It shapes the effective potentials felt when a system is steered slowly, the adiabatic story translated into the leaky setting. It also controls how Wannier states, the localized wave packets used to describe electrons in crystals, spread in periodic non-Hermitian lattices. Most strikingly, the non-Hermitian quantum metric appears directly in how the system answers a periodic wiggle in time. Which hands experimentalists a way to measure the metric rather than merely compute it.
arxiv-2512-07364:
S M Holme and co-authors chart how particles and gyroscopes would move around a vorton, a hypothetical ring of cosmic string carrying a persistent current. Vortons interest high-energy physics as possible dark matter and as fossils of grand unified theories. Working from a recently derived weak-field description of a circular chiral vorton, the team traces both the paths of massive particles and the routes of light.

The catalog of motions is rich: bound orbits that precess, circles, oscillations shaped like tori and crowns, and unbound fly-bys. Maps of the motion show orderly and chaotic regimes trading places as the string's tension and the starting conditions vary. Gyroscopes carried along the paths precess at rates with features no black hole produces. Including divergences near the ring's core and multiple minima, echoes instead of the naked singularities of spinning solutions.
arxiv-2512-07964:
Tom J. L. C. Bakx and Hiddo S. B. Algera wrote this 2025 astronomy paper, with Jean-Baptiste Jolly and many co-authors. Early galaxies look reddened, as if dust already filled them. Yet telescopes keep failing to catch that dust glowing in the far infrared.

The PIXIEDust project pooled deep hours from two great millimeter arrays. ALMA and NOEMA together stared at ten galaxies from the universe's first era. No significant dust emission appeared at any of the wavelengths probed. The silence caps how much dust those galaxies can hold on average. Dust-to-stellar mass ratios are squeezed to very low ceilings as well. Bins by era, color, or mass change nothing. Every bin returns the same stringent non-detection story. Combined with other studies, the picture favors inefficient early dust build-up. Supernovae may produce little dust, grains may grow slowly, or outflows may expel it.
arxiv-2512-08164:
Reiko Harada, Heather Fong, and Kipp Cannon, gravitational wave astronomers, posted a methods paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their goal is to estimate the Hubble parameter, the expansion rate of the universe, from catalogs of merging compact objects. Earlier dark siren studies leaned on galaxy catalogs or mass and redshift patterns, and they used only clearly significant merger candidates.

The authors present a framework that skips detailed analysis of each candidate and works only with detection level information. That means a raw candidate list from a search pipeline can feed the population inference directly, with no extra selection cuts. The approach is built to draw value from marginal candidates, the faint events other methods throw away. Those faint mergers are essential for probing the distant universe, and the method could widen the usable catalog as detectors find weaker signals.
arxiv-2512-08264:
Rachana Mysore, Preksha Girish, Kavitha Jayaram, Shrey Kumar, and colleagues, researchers in India, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 on the mathematics of very wide neural networks. In the infinite width limit, training is governed by the neural tangent kernel, a mathematical object that describes how network outputs change. The team proposes an architecture designed so this kernel behavior can be analyzed rigorously.

Their network, called NTK ECRN, combines Fourier feature embeddings, residual connections with scaling at each layer, and stochastic depth. With that design, they derive bounds on how the kernel evolves during training. They also characterize how its eigenvalues move, and link the spectrum to generalization and stable optimization. Tests on synthetic and benchmark data matched the predicted kernel behavior. The authors report steadier training and better generalization as well. The work aims to bridge deep theory about infinite width networks and the architectures people actually train.
arxiv-2512-08364:
Erich Novak and Friedrich Pillichshammer, mathematicians in Germany and Austria, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is discrepancy, a measure of how evenly points fill a space, studied for random points in high dimensions. Classical results suffer from the curse of dimensionality, and the gap between upper and lower bounds stays large, worst for small values of the exponent.

The authors study a generalized version that lets random points be drawn from non uniform densities, with matching weights. Using the probabilistic method, they show that well chosen product densities give much better upper bounds. For one key exponent the new bounds are exact and optimal, and for the rest they are sharp in the limit. The gain reads as importance sampling tuned to the underlying function space. Even so, the curse of dimensionality survives for random points, and bites hardest at small exponents.
arxiv-2512-08464:
Jungjin Park, Osamu Kaneko, and Kiminao Kogiso, control engineers in Japan, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025. Their subject is tuning controllers on encrypted data, so a cloud service can adjust a system without ever seeing its private measurements. The method they secure, called confidential fictitious reference iterative tuning, encodes data with quantization before encryption, and bad parameter choices can cause overflow that wrecks the computation.

The authors give a systematic design procedure for the two knobs that matter: the quantization gain and the security parameter. From operating data, the range of quantization errors can be estimated in advance. They derive conditions on both parameters that guarantee no overflow, and quantify how the error shifts tuned gains from the unencrypted answer. A numerical example confirms the procedure hits a target accuracy within tolerance while staying overflow free. Charts of the allowed region give practitioners a practical design map.
arxiv-2512-08664:
Junho Park studies swirling flow between rotating cylinders, known as Taylor Couette flow, when the fluid is stably layered and highly diffusive. Layering normally calms the centrifugal instability that creates vortices in that flow. Strong heat diffusion, at low Prandtl number, weakens that calming effect in ways the author checks with local stability analysis.

Direct simulations then trace the nonlinear life of the instability. Classic axisymmetric Taylor vortices form first, then lose stability to wavy patterns or to chaotic states as speed rises. A second stability analysis on the vortex state finds when that secondary change sets in, and how layering and diffusion delay it. Torque based measures show how angular momentum transport grows with speed, and how it differs between steady vortex and chaotic regimes.
arxiv-2512-08764:
Nicolas Reche, Elvys Linhares Pontes, and Juan Manuel Torres Moreno compare methods for summarizing financial news, from simple extractive tools to large language models. Markets move fast on news, and investors need short summaries to react in time. With tens of thousands of articles published each day, manual summary is not feasible, so automation is essential.

Using a challenge data set for financial models, the authors find that language models write more coherent and informative summaries. Those models are costly, though, and can invent facts, which is risky in finance. Extractive methods, which lift sentences from the source, do well on short and well structured texts and cost far less. The best scores come from a fine tuned language model, but the authors warn that their corpus has limited reliability. That caution shapes how strongly the ranking should be read.
arxiv-2512-08864:
Steve Barrett and a large team apply quantitative risk modeling to cybersecurity risks created by misuse of advanced artificial intelligence. In the most recent year studied, AI enabled cyber offense has become a concrete concern rather than a purely hypothetical one. The report uses a methodology that a companion paper describes in full.

Nine detailed cyber risk models are built, each breaking an attack into steps with a standard attack framework. The models estimate how AI changes attacker numbers, attack frequency, success probability, and resulting harm, giving different forms of uplift. Estimates come from human experts in a structured Delphi study and from simulated experts based on language models. Both map benchmark scores from cyber evaluations to risk factors, and Monte Carlo simulation combines the estimates with uncertainty. Results show systematic uplift in attack power, speed, and reach. The authors aim to help defenders, evaluators, developers, and policymakers set priorities.
arxiv-2512-09364:
Shengchao Zhou and colleagues present ASSIST-3D, a pipeline that manufactures training data for 3D instance segmentation, the task of separating every object in a scanned scene without knowing object classes in advance. Progress is limited by scarce labeled 3D scenes and noisy labels lifted from 2D images. Synthetic scenes could help, but earlier generators could not deliver variety, complexity, and layouts at once.

ASSIST-3D combines three ideas. It samples objects randomly from collections of 3D models to maximize diversity. It arranges them using a language model for spatial reasoning plus a depth-first search for sensible placements. Then it renders multi-view color and depth images and fuses them into point clouds that mimic real sensor data. Models trained with this synthetic data beat existing methods on the ScanNetV2, ScanNet++, and S3DIS benchmarks. The authors also show their pipeline outperforms general 3D scene synthesis approaches.
arxiv-2512-09464:
Antoine Van Muylder, Andreas Nuyts, and Dominique Devriese build a type theory that supports nominal techniques, the tools used to handle names and binders. Languages with binders, where a name is tied to a subterm, are awkward in ordinary frameworks. Nominal frameworks fix this with abstraction types, making terms that differ only by renaming equal, but they come in two flavors with opposite strengths.

Existential abstractions support matching on binding patterns but have clumsy typing rules, while universal ones have clean rules and no matching. The authors recover matching and the nominal features inside a type theory built from three parts. One part is a nullary internally parametric type theory. Another is a type of names with an induction principle, and nominal data types. The result is a framework with both kinds of abstraction, a freshness type former, swapping, and local-scope operations, with nominal pattern matching recovered through parametricity.
arxiv-2512-09664:
Antonio Terpin and colleagues describe SynthPix, software that makes synthetic images for particle image velocimetry, a technique that measures fluid flow by photographing seeded tracer particles. Machine learning pipelines for this technique are data-hungry, and building datasets offline is slow and storage-heavy. SynthPix instead streams image pairs into those pipelines as they run.

Implemented in JAX for speed and parallelism on accelerators, the generator produces image pairs from prescribed flow fields. Its configuration matches imaging parameters: seeding density, particle image size, illumination nonuniformity, noise, blur, and timing. Because images are made on the fly, users can run closed-loop procedures such as adaptive sampling and design of acquisition and parameters. They can sweep nuisance factors for robustness testing without high input-output costs. The authors show compatibility with scenarios from experiments to river surface velocimetry, and present the package as a tool for the flow measurement community.
arxiv-2512-09964:
Donghyeon Lee and colleagues build an AI agent that runs genomics analysis for researchers without deep biology training. Next generation sequencing is routine in genomics, but the downstream work is not. Turning raw results into lists of changed genes and biological meaning demands both computing skill and domain knowledge. Their agent, built on a large open language model with retrieval augmented generation, automates that chain through a web application.

The system identifies differentially expressed genes, clusters samples, and runs pathway enrichment. Uniquely, it searches the medical literature through PubMed to back its interpretations with evidence. In a cancer case study, it found significant gene changes, charted clinical correlations, and drew literature based insights, such as linking a BRAF mutation to prognosis. When the user chose, it then ran advanced survival modeling. The authors aim to lower the barrier from raw data to tested hypotheses.
arxiv-2512-10164:
Maelle Magnan and colleagues test whether a galaxy's bar strength controls how much gas it funnels to its center. Bars are elongated stellar structures in disk galaxies that can torque gas inward, feeding central activity and star formation. Strong bars were known to drive rapid inflow; weak bars were uncertain. The team gathered spectra with the Isaac Newton Telescope for eighteen nearby galaxies: strongly barred, weakly barred, and unbarred, drawn from a citizen science classified sample. They mapped the strength and velocity spread of ionized gas from the hydrogen alpha line across each galaxy.

Strongly barred galaxies show a distinctive three peaked pattern in gas emission strength, consistent with gas being funneled inward. Weakly barred systems lack the pattern entirely, suggesting little inflow. The gas velocity spread also separates the groups, running significantly higher in strong bars. Bars, it seems, must be strong to matter.
arxiv-2512-10264:
Alon Ziv and colleagues align music generation with human taste using several rewards at once. Flow matching models can compose plausible music, but plausibility is not preference, and musical judgment is subjective and split across dimensions. Their method adapts direct preference optimization to flow matching generators, guided by three off the shelf reward models. One scores how well the music matches its text prompt, one scores audio production quality, and one scores semantic consistency.. The rewards serve twice: they build the preference pairs used for training, and they are woven into the text prompting itself.

A new semantic scoring mechanism stabilized rhythm. Evaluation combined music specific objective metrics with a human listening study. Listeners and metrics agreed: the method significantly improved overall quality and was consistently preferred over strong baselines on audio quality, text alignment, and musicality.
arxiv-2512-10364:
Yueli Han and Lu Lu analyse the spectrum of the vertex-weighted Laplacian. This operator extends the familiar graph Laplacian to simplicial complexes. Those complexes are the higher-dimensional cousins of networks, built from triangles and tetrahedra. Weights on the vertices let the operator reflect uneven importance. And its eigenvalues encode shape and connectivity in ways earlier work had only partly mapped.

Building on Lew's foundational techniques, the authors first show how joins, complements, and Alexander duals change the spectrum, yielding a sharp ceiling for the spectral radius in terms of the weights. They then pin down a sharp floor for the spectral gap and say exactly when equality holds. Further bounds tie the remaining eigenvalues to those of a related weighted graph, and new relations link a complex to its subcomplexes, unifying many older theorems.
arxiv-2512-10464:
Satyandra Sharma, Varun Sheel, and Martin Pätzold hunt for a recurring bump in the upper ionosphere of Venus. Earlier missions had reported a local rise in electron density on the planet's topside, at heights of roughly a hundred and sixty to two hundred kilometres. But its shapes and causes were loosely catalogued. Venus has no magnetic field of its own, so its ionosphere meets the solar wind head-on.

The team used more than two hundred dayside profiles from the Venus Express radio science experiment. An automatic gradient-based sorting method then divided the bulge into three types. They range from a clear second peak to a hidden form found only in residuals. The bulge appeared in most profiles. It showed up more often when solar activity was low and the Sun was high. That points to outside drivers such as the solar wind, rather than local chemistry alone.
arxiv-2512-10564:
Paola Martire and co-authors run the first end-to-end three-dimensional simulation of a star being torn apart by an intermediate-mass black hole, one about ten thousand times the Sun's mass. Such tidal disruption events flare brightly, but where the early light peak comes from is still debated. Their radiation-hydrodynamics code followed the whole event with realistic numbers.

The shredded star's debris never settled into a tidy disc. Instead, a thin, radiation-driven wind formed near the closest approach and ballooned outward almost spherically, carrying radiation with it and releasing light at a huge, hot photosphere. The flare briefly outshone the Eddington limit, the usual ceiling for steady shining, then settled near it. Tests at three resolutions held up, and the authors note that the Rubin Observatory and ULTRASAT could spot such events across a modest slice of the universe.
arxiv-2512-10764:
Patrik Veres spotlights a class of cosmic flare that hides in plain sight. Tidal disruption events, stars shredded by a supermassive black hole, are normally found in quiet galaxies, where the flash stands out. A few, though, have turned up inside active galactic nuclei, galaxies whose black holes were already feeding and glowing. And telling a fresh disruption apart from ordinary active-galaxy flickering is genuinely hard.

Writing in conference proceedings, Veres discusses AT2019aalc, a promising disruption candidate inside an active nucleus, and compares it with similar sources. He also examines Bowen fluorescence flares, a newly recognised class of flaring black holes, as possible members of the same family. The aim is to match what telescopes see against what simulations of disruptions inside active nuclei predict, sharpening the criteria for a class of event that surveys have mostly overlooked.
arxiv-2512-10964:
Laslo Hunhold proposes a new way to write real numbers for computing hardware based on three valued, or ternary, logic. Modern machines almost all use binary, yet ternary logic offers possible gains in energy use and memory efficiency that have drawn little attention. Hunhold revives tapered precision, where numbers near one get more digits, in a balanced ternary form.

The new format, called tekum arithmetic, is compared with the posit and takum formats used in binary work. Several basic design problems for ternary tapered numbers are worked through along the way. In many respects the proposed format performs better than both rivals. The study lays groundwork for real number computation designed from scratch for future ternary hardware.
arxiv-2512-11064:
Travis Yeager and colleagues release an open benchmark of one million simulated spacecraft trajectories in cislunar space, the region from high Earth orbit out past the Moon. That region will host future exploration, science, and security missions, yet shared reference data for testing methods have been scarce. The trajectories were computed with an open source space awareness package.

Each path includes detailed Earth and Moon gravity, the Sun's pull, and radiation pressure, and runs for up to six years from a single shared start time. Starting conditions sample the ranges mission designers commonly use. The team notes patterns such as a stable band near five times geosynchronous distance and long lived orbits near two Lagrange points. The dataset supports navigation, awareness, and machine learning research.
arxiv-2512-11164:
David Brewster, Yichen Huang, Michael Mitzenmacher, and Martin Nowak study evolution on networks where the rules of replacement themselves are mixed. In evolutionary graph theory, individuals sit on graph vertices and compete to replace neighbours. Two standard rules differ in order: one picks an individual to die first, the other picks a parent first by fitness.

Their mixed updating flips a coin each step, using the death first rule with some probability and the birth first rule otherwise. They examine how the chance and timing of one type taking over depend on that mixing probability, under both neutral drift and steady selection. The dependence can rise, fall, or bend in between. Despite that variety, they prove nearly all unweighted undirected graphs fixate quickly and give an efficient algorithm for the probabilities, plus exact formulas for rings, stars, and richer structures.
arxiv-2512-11464:
Han Lin and a large team let multimodal language models plan images and videos in latent space instead of merely captioning them for a generator. In current pipelines, a strong reasoning model is demoted to a global text encoder for a diffusion model, wasting its grasp of layout, attributes, and world knowledge. Generation then shows weaker control than the same model's understanding would suggest.

MetaCanvas is a lightweight framework connecting the language model directly to the internal representations that diffusion generators use. The model can reason and plan where things go and how scenes evolve, then hand that plan to the generator. Implemented on three diffusion backbones and tested across six tasks, from text to image and video generation to editing, it consistently beat global conditioning baselines. The authors argue latent space planning can close the understanding generation gap.
arxiv-2512-11964:
Sourabh Paul and co-authors release the first data from the MeerKLASS UHF radio survey, taken with South Africa MeerKAT array. The survey tests an on the fly mapping style, where the telescope scans nonstop and images form from the flowing data. Twelve hours of early observations covered about 800 square degrees.

The mosaic reaches noise near 35 microjanskys per beam at its deepest, with detail of about 32 by 17 arcseconds at 816 megahertz. The team cataloged 95,483 radio sources. Cross checks with other surveys confirm positions to under an arcsecond and a sound brightness scale. Source counts match past work. The release proves the scanning style for the full survey and for the future SKA.
arxiv-2512-12264:
Abhay Srivastava, Sam Jung, and Spencer Mateega introduce Market-Bench in a 2025 paper. The benchmark tests large language models on basic quantitative trading. Given a plan in plain words, a model must write a working backtester, code that replays a trading plan on past prices, and match a known correct version.

Each task uses one of three plans: timed trading on Microsoft, pairs trading on Coca-Cola and Pepsi, or delta hedging on Microsoft. Thirteen top models were tested over many rounds. Most ran the simplest plan, averaging 4.08 passes out of 5 rounds, but errors varied widely. Gemini 3 Pro, Claude 4.5 Sonnet, and GPT-5.2 stood out.
arxiv-2512-12664:
Sreehari Rajan, Kunal Bhosikar, and Charu Sharma present InteracTalker, a framework for motion generation with speech and objects, in a 2025 paper. Interactive digital experiences need human motions that respond to both spoken words and physical objects. Past methods handled speech driven gestures or object interaction separately, and no integrated data set covered both at once.

InteracTalker learns a unified space for motion, speech, and prompts through multi-stage training. The team enriched a text to motion data set with detailed object interaction notes. A motion adaptation module trains on each condition apart, then combines them at inference, while adaptive fusion reweights signals during diffusion sampling. The system beat earlier methods on both gesture generation and object interaction synthesis.
arxiv-2512-13064:
Szu-Chi Chung, Chien-Hong Cho, and Strong Wen revisit EEPAS, a model for medium to long term earthquake forecasting. Its name says that every earthquake may act as a precursor for larger ones, scaled by size. The model beat time-invariant rivals in regional studies, but its math was poorly documented.

The authors derive EEPAS and a companion model inside a rigorous point process framework. They clarify how older scaling fits connect to likelihood based inference. They also release an open-source Python version with fast compiled code and standard evaluation hooks. On an Italian data set, it reproduced published results within an hour and improved the fit.
arxiv-2512-13264:
Devibala Esakkimuthu and Basherrudin Mahmud Ahmed Abduljaffer show how to distill photonic qudit states, multi-level quantum states of light, from single photon sources alone. High fidelity continuous variable states are vital for quantum technologies, but making them usually demands strong nonlinearities or large photon numbers.

Their setup strings beam splitters in a cascade and uses only single photon sources and detectors. It produces displaced multi-level states with unit fidelity and Schrodinger cat states above 98 percent fidelity in their analysis. Grid states used for quantum error correction reached about 99 percent. They also model detector inefficiency and imperfect sources to keep the claims realistic.
arxiv-2512-13364:
Aisling Power, Cara-Lena Nies, and Stefan Schulz build a valence force field model for wurtzite semiconductors. Force field models find where atoms settle in a crystal, enabling large simulations of layered devices. Well-tested models exist for the cubic zinc blende phase, but wurtzite parameters were often borrowed without a rigorous check.

Exploiting the likeness between wurtzite and zinc blende viewed along a diagonal, they project the cubic model onto wurtzite with no added parameters. Trained on elastic tensors, bond asymmetries, and band gaps, the model also predicted untrained traits well. It matched density functional theory on strongly mismatched alloys.
arxiv-2512-13564:
Yuyang Hu and a large team survey memory for AI agents built on foundation models. Memory is now a core skill for such agents, but the field is fragmented. Works differ in aims, builds, and tests, and loose terms blur key ideas, while old labels like long-term and short-term no longer fit.

The survey sorts agent memory by forms, functions, and dynamics. Forms cover token-level, parametric, and latent memory, while functions split into factual, experiential, and working memory. Dynamics tracks how memory forms, changes, and is recalled. The authors also compile benchmarks and open tools, and map frontiers such as multimodal and multi-agent memory and trust issues.
arxiv-2512-13664:
Yang Chu studies a biased form of the infinity Laplacian through a new extension concept. The work sits in variational analysis, where best extensions of a function from a small set to a larger space are sought. Chu defines an exponential absolute minimizing extension on any length space, with a bias parameter.

The definition generalizes the classical absolute minimizing Lipschitz extension, which returns as the case of zero bias. Chu also defines an exponential McShane-Whitney extension and a biased convexity that match the new notion. In Euclidean space, the extension matches viscosity solutions of an Aronsson-type equation. He shows it arises as the limit value of a biased tug-of-war game, and proves a linear blow-up trait for biased infinity harmonic functions.
arxiv-2512-14464:
Sujoy Chakraborty and Saurav Holme Choudhury prove a connectedness result in algebraic geometry. Their objects are moduli stacks, spaces whose points stand for vector bundles on a smooth curve of genus at least two, with rank and determinant held fixed. The question is whether these spaces are connected in the A1 sense, a homotopy notion built for algebraic varieties.

They show the stack of semi-stable bundles is indeed A1-connected. The same holds for quasi-parabolic bundles, which carry extra flag data at marked points on the curve. For small, generic weights and coprime rank and degree, the open stack of semistable parabolic bundles is connected as well.
arxiv-2512-14564:
Arthur Capozzi mined forty thousand political ads that ran on Meta platforms in Switzerland from 2021 to 2025, asking how social media campaigning interacts with direct democracy. Swiss referenda happen often, so the ads can be studied outside normal election cycles. Together they racked up hundreds of millions of impressions aimed at millions of voters.

Heavier exposure to pro-Yes ads tracked closely with referenda passing. Targeting split by party family: centrist and right-wing parties aimed mainly at older men, left-wing parties at young women. Parties also talked past each other, each promoting only its own signature issues. Their habits were so distinct that a model could guess an ad's sponsor from its audience and topic alone.
arxiv-2512-14964:
Sourav Das and four coauthors work out exactly what happens when a single photon bounces off a lone quantum emitter that shakes. The emitter is a two level system coupled to a vibrational bath, like a molecule that wiggles as it interacts with light. Such shaking blurs the light matter interaction, a problem for quantum light spectroscopy.

The authors derive the full quantum state of the scattered photon pulse for this four part system. With that solution they measure how vibrations cut the quantum Fisher information for estimating the emitter's linewidth. The loss mostly reflects Franck-Condon suppression, where vibration steals overlap from the transition. Comparing ways to detect the photon, they find frequency resolved detection carries more information than time resolved when the coupling is strong.
arxiv-2512-15164:
Harbir Antil and three coauthors build a general well posedness theory for a class of evolving systems whose rules depend on their own state. The systems are pseudo parabolic gradient systems, driven by an energy functional with variable coefficient fields. Such state dependence appears in grain boundary motion of KWC type and in anisotropic image denoising, among other models.

Two main results anchor the framework. Energy dissipating solutions exist. And solutions are unique and depend continuously on the starting data, the two traits that make a model trustworthy. The authors then show an anisotropic denoising model and a new pseudo parabolic KWC model for anisotropic grain boundary motion both fit the abstract structure. The work gives analysts one theory for many nonlinear evolution problems with state dependent operators.
arxiv-2512-15364:
Oren Becker and Emmanuel Breuillard prove a uniform spectral gap for random walks on algebraic groups in a 2025 math paper. A spectral gap measures how fast a random walk spreads out and forgets its start. Getting one bound that holds uniformly across many groups is the central challenge.

The authors show that such walks do not concentrate on proper algebraic subvarieties, with a uniform exponential rate. Their method leans on Diophantine heights and the Height Gap theorem. They also derive a non abelian version of the Littlewood Offord inequalities and logarithmic bounds for escape from subvarieties. A planned sequel will turn the gap into uniform expansion for Cayley graphs.
arxiv-2512-15464:
Yingxiang Hu and Mohammad Ivaki solve a capillary shape problem in a 2025 geometry paper. The Lp Christoffel Minkowski problem asks when a desired measure comes from the shape of a convex body. The capillary version places the body in a half space, where it meets the boundary at a set contact angle, like a droplet on a surface.

The authors solve the capillary Lp version for p between 1 and k plus 1, within the class of even hypersurfaces. A key step is a non collapsing estimate that bounds both the height and the capillary support function from below. The result extends an earlier capillary Christoffel Minkowski existence theorem by other authors.
arxiv-2512-15664:
Peter Humphries proves a quantitative equidistribution result on hyperbolic surfaces in a 2025 paper, with arithmetic applications. Equidistribution says special points spread evenly over a surface as their number grows. Putting a rate on that spread, through the Wasserstein distance between probability measures, is the harder task taken up here.

Humphries proves an analogue of the Berry Esseen inequality for the Wasserstein distance on a finite area hyperbolic surface. The bound runs through averages of Weyl sums built from Maass cusp forms and Eisenstein series. Applications bound the distance in Duke's theorems on Heegner points and closed geodesics, and in Watson's theorem on Hecke Maass cusp forms, the last conditional on a Lindelof type hypothesis.
arxiv-2512-15764:
Anshul Kumar, Gagan Raj Gupta, and Manisha Chawla present AdaGradSelect, a gradient guided layer selection method for fine tuning small language models, in a 2025 paper, dated December 12. Full fine tuning is costly, and low rank adapter methods restrict training to a narrow subspace that can cost performance. Small models need efficiency most.

AdaGradSelect picks which transformer blocks to update based on gradient norms, adapting the choice as training proceeds. Dirichlet based sampling favors blocks updated often before, balanced by epsilon greedy exploration. In tests the method trains about 12 percent faster and uses 35 percent less GPU memory than full fine tuning, with near equal quality. On GSM8K it beats a high rank LoRA baseline by about 3 percent.
arxiv-2512-15964:
Diana Blanco and co authors test DESI data for calibrating photometric redshifts, using KiDS-1000 as a case study, in a 2025 paper. Weak lensing cosmology needs accurate redshift distributions, and spectroscopic samples anchor them. DESI has gathered over 50 million redshifts since 2021, including more than 256,000 high quality spectra in deep fields.

The team calibrates KiDS-1000 galaxies that share self organizing map cells with DESI COSMOS spectra. Results broadly match published distributions, with mean redshift shifts of minus 0.028 and median shifts of plus 0.011 across tomographic bins. Incompleteness within map cells can still distort the inferred distributions. Larger aligned photometric catalogs would unlock more of the DESI data.
arxiv-2512-16464:
Peter Thalmeier analyzes unusual magnets in a paper posted on arXiv during 2025, an extended published version. Singlet ground state magnets, found in certain f-electron compounds, have nonmagnetic atoms that can still order through induced moments. Without nuclear effects, a quantum critical point separates their paramagnetic and ordered regimes.

Thalmeier adds the hyperfine coupling between electron and nuclear spins, plus the nuclei's quadrupole splitting. The coupling erases the sharp critical point, replacing it with a gradual crossover between electron-driven and nucleus-driven order. He predicts how the ordering temperature and the specific heat's peak pattern, three peaks melting into two, shift with nuclear spin size, splitting, and applied field. Reentrant behavior appears: order can vanish and return as conditions change. The phase diagram's full evolution under quadrupole coupling is mapped.
arxiv-2512-16564:
Kirill Mazur, Marwan Taher, and Andrew J Davison rebuild moving scenes in an arXiv paper made public in 2025. A single casual video shows each part of a scene only briefly, yet humans remember the whole room. Their system aims for the same persistence: a complete, replayable reconstruction covering everything the camera ever saw.

The scene is decomposed into rigid 3D primitives, chunks assumed to move as solid pieces. Dense 2D correspondences between frames drive an optimization that infers each chunk's motion, producing a 4D reconstruction, geometry evolving through time. A motion-grouping mechanism extrapolates objects that leave view, preserving object permanence. On object scanning and multi-object data sets, the system beat existing methods clearly in both numbers and visual quality. Replayable reconstructions of articulated objects are among the enabled uses.
arxiv-2512-16764:
Emma Godden and Katherine M. Blundell refine how astronomers model the effective point spread function, the blur pattern a telescope stamps on star images. Sharp blur models are vital for exact light and position measures, above all when images are undersampled.

Building on a standard open-source routine, the pair show that several small changes lift accuracy a lot. They test choices such as oversampling, interpolation, grid placement, smoothing, star spread, and dithering on fake star fields, tracking flux and position errors tied to pixel phase. They then apply the tuned routine to Global Jet Watch images, where it recovers a truer blur than before, with plain advice for other instruments.
arxiv-2512-16964:
Faisal Ahmed presents PseudoColorViT-Alz, a vision transformer system that sorts brain MRI scans into four Alzheimer disease classes, from non-demented to moderate dementia. Subtle brain changes make the task hard for standard deep models reading gray scans.

The method first maps scans through colormaps, turning gray levels into pseudo-color that boosts texture and contrast cues. A vision transformer then learns global features from the colored scans. On the OASIS-1 data set, the model reached 99.79 percent accuracy with a perfect AUC score, past recent CNN and Siamese tools that scored 96.1 to 99.68 percent. The author offers it as an aid for early detection and clinical calls.
arxiv-2512-17064:
Aditya Dendukuri, Shivkumar Chandrasekaran, and Linda Petzold present a flux-preserving adaptive method for stochastic reaction networks, where molecule counts jump by random reactions. The finite state projection trims the huge state space to a finite set with known error bounds.

Multiscale networks with rates split by orders of magnitude break plain adaptive versions, since rare bottleneck states can carry key probability flux. Their rule prunes by flux, shielding low-probability states with large outgoing flux, and picks time steps from the live total flux. On stiff, oscillatory, and bottleneck test networks, the method held accuracy while using much smaller state spaces, a gain for systems biology models.
arxiv-2512-17264:
Yuming Xu and ten co-authors present SPIRE, an index that can search billions of vectors spread across many machines. Vector search finds the stored items closest to a query, and it powers tools from image search to chatbots. At huge scale, systems must trade off accuracy, delay, and speed, and older designs struggle to hold all three.

SPIRE makes two key choices. It picks a balanced size for splitting data across machines, so reads do not blow up in cost. It then builds the index level by level in a way that guards accuracy as it grows. In tests with up to 8 billion vectors on 46 nodes, SPIRE ran up to 9.64 times faster than leading systems.
arxiv-2512-17464:
Thomas Eiter, a mathematician in Berlin, examines a model for how rock like material slowly deforms, in a 2025 analysis paper. The model comes from geophysics, where rock over long time scales behaves as a visco elasto plastic material: part springy, part flowing, part permanently bent. Eiter studies what should count as a solution to its equations.

The model is written in the Eulerian view, following the material's current shape rather than a fixed reference shape. Density is treated as constant, which would normally block pressure waves from traveling through the material. An added internal force, following an approach due to Temam, keeps the material slightly compressible so those waves survive. Work like this puts models used for the Earth's outer layers on firmer math ground.
arxiv-2512-17564:
The Fermilab E906 SeaQuest collaboration, led in this report by C. H. Leung, publishes its final measurement of the flavor balance inside the proton's sea of short lived quark antiquark pairs. The team fired 120 GeV protons at liquid hydrogen and liquid deuterium targets and studied the Drell Yan process.

Combining all the data gives the cross section ratio between the two targets over the momentum fraction range 0.13 to 0.45, and from it the team extracts how the down antiquark share compares with the up antiquark share. Down antiquarks outnumber up antiquarks across the whole range, with tighter errors than earlier measurements. The final numbers now stand as a benchmark for the parton distribution fits and theories that describe the proton's inner makeup.
arxiv-2512-17764:
Kangchen Lv and four co-authors give robots a way to keep track of a cable even when most of it is hidden. Ropes, wires, and hoses flop into endless shapes, and in a cramped workspace other objects block the camera's view. A robot that loses the cable's shape mid-task cannot plan its next grip.

UniStateDLO treats seeing as educated guessing: a diffusion model generates the full cable shape that best fits the visible fragments, for one frame and across a whole motion. It copes with self-hiding bends and multi-object pileups. Training used only synthetic scenes, yet the system transferred to real robots with no retraining. Plugged into a working manipulation loop, it kept control stable in clutter. Cable handling is a quiet bottleneck in factories and surgery alike.
arxiv-2512-17864:
Balram Singh, Ram Prakash Sharma, and Somnath Dey aim to spot plant diseases from leaf photos in a way farmers can trust. Their model pairs a standard image network with an attention block at each stage. The block helps the network focus on the sick spots of a leaf rather than the whole picture.

Trained on five plant disease data sets, the model reached accuracy as high as 98.87 percent and held up well on new data. The team also shows why each call was made, using heat maps and related tools that mark the leaf regions behind a diagnosis. Such openness matters when a wrong call can cost a harvest.
arxiv-2512-17964:
John K. Nino reports a link between giant black holes and the dark matter halos around their galaxies. Working with three large universe simulations, he compares black hole mass with how tightly each halo's matter is packed toward its center. At a fixed halo mass, tighter halos tend to hold heavier black holes.

The link was clear in the TNG100, EAGLE, and CAMELS-TNG runs, with correlation values of zero point two four, zero point three four, and zero point six six. It was absent in the SIMBA run, which feeds its black holes by a different rule. Nino reads the split as a clue: when growth follows the density of nearby gas, a packed halo core feeds a bigger black hole.
arxiv-2512-18164:
Retardation, the finite-speed delay in how particles affect each other, complicates the quark forces inside hadrons. The delay terms are studied here in coordinate space, by adapting a procedure from classical electrodynamics.

The author also weighs whether a matching quantum operator can be built, and backs the discussion with numerical matrix element calculations. Getting the delay right matters for hadron models that aim at accurate spectra and structure. The paper gives theorists a careful comparison of the methods on offer for including the effect, and a check on which survive quantization.
arxiv-2512-18264:
Yucheng Fan, Jiawei Chen, Yu Tian, and Zhaoxia Yin shield social media photos from AI snooping. Modern vision language models can guess private traits, like age or job, from a casual picture. Older shields either wrecked the photo's looks or broke the site's own image features.

Their method tunes a photo guard that hides private traits while keeping harmless content readable and the image looking the same. To judge fairly, they built VPI-COCO, a public set of 522 images with layered privacy questions and clean twin questions. Across several models, their guard pushed private guesses below 25 percent while harmless answers stayed above 88 percent, and it held up on fresh, reworded questions.
arxiv-2512-18364:
Cole Comfort and Jean-Simon Pacaud Lemay work in category theory, a branch of math that maps the structure shared by different systems. Their December 2025 arXiv paper connects two tools for handling probability. Markov categories describe chance processes in abstract form. The Moore-Penrose inverse is a matrix tool used to compute conditional probabilities for Gaussian data.

The authors introduce the Gauss construction, which turns a category with a Moore-Penrose structure into a Markov category with conditionals. Applied to real matrices, it recovers the standard Gaussian example. Applied to complex or quaternionic matrices, it yields new Markov categories for those kinds of Gaussian distributions. They also pin down every possible conditional the construction allows.
arxiv-2512-18664:
Panagiotis Charalambous, Laura Donnay, and Alexandru Lupsasca revisit a hidden symmetry of black holes in this 2025 relativity paper. In 1983 Couch and Torrence found that waves on an extremal black hole keep a radial inversion symmetry that swaps the horizon with infinity. The trio asks how far this symmetry extends beyond the extremal Reissner-Nordström and Kerr cases where it was first seen.

Using a static lukewarm de Sitter black hole, they show that neither the horizon-infinity swap nor the preservation of radial singularities is essential. Reading the inversion through its action on photon spheres unifies the picture, reaching the extremal Kerr-Newman geometry. For scalar fields there, the inversion's fixed point ties simply to superradiant scattering, and a hidden symmetry appears in the Kerr Laplacian for all spins.
arxiv-2512-19064:
Nicole Fontana and four co-authors build a method for health causes whose effects change over a lifetime. Mendelian randomization uses genes as instruments to judge whether an exposure causes an outcome. Standard versions assume one fixed effect, and handle several exposures only under that same flat assumption.

Their framework, MV-FMR, models several time-varying exposures at once. It uses functional principal components, picks its basis by cross-validation, and allows shared instruments and indirect paths through mediators. In simulations with nonlinear effects, pleiotropy, mediation, and sparse data, the method recovered the true effect curves. Joint modeling beat separate fits in the cases they tested.
arxiv-2512-19264:
Patrick Copinger and Shi Pu build a worldline framework for watching quantum fields evolve inside pair-creating electric fields. Strong fields can pull particle-antiparticle pairs from the vacuum, the Schwinger effect. Standard tools give start-to-finish amplitudes, while many questions ask what happens during the process, the in-in view.

Working from both the Bogoliubov method and the closed-time-path formalism, they derive the framework to all orders in the field coupling. The in-in corrections appear as a non-local term built from singularities in complex proper time. Resumming gives vacuum decay and an exact count-style definition for creating a set number of pairs.
arxiv-2512-19464:
Noy Cohen revisits how a temperature-sensitive gel can hold two phases at once under mechanical load. PNIPAM gels swell in cool water and collapse past a threshold temperature, as single chains curl from coils into globules. An older study found swollen and collapsed zones coexisting in one rod held under constraint.

Collapsed patches crept into a fixed swollen rod over time, and stretched collapsed rods sprouted swollen patches. Cohen builds a statistical-mechanics model of single chains below and above the threshold, then a probabilistic model on top of it. The framework aims to explain how local chain switching, steered by load, writes the patchwork pattern.
arxiv-2512-19764:
Chathuranga Wijerathna Basnayaka leads an eight-author team designing downlinks for smart satellites. Low Earth orbit systems now run AI on board. They spot events in images up there, then must send word down. Weak links, path loss, and fading make raw images a bad cargo. Their scheme sends only the traits that matter for the task at hand. It is called deep joint source-channel coding.

The team also adds a new metric. It pairs how stale the news is with how often it is wrong. A threshold check counts users who meet the time limits their tasks set. In tests, the smart scheme beat the classic split scheme. It won on accuracy, on the new stale-and-wrong score, and on meeting time limits. The target is image event spotting for future 6G space networks.
arxiv-2512-19964:
Bruno Farias, José Flauzino, and Elias Duarte put the cache inside the network itself. Key-value databases serving distant clients suffer latency on every lookup, and classic caching near the server does little for geography. VNF-Cache is a caching service built on network function virtualization with computing in the network, an IETF-standardizing technology that runs arbitrary services on the data path.

The service intercepts packets in flight, processes and stores values, and answers clients directly whenever the answer is already held. A proof-of-concept deployment spanned geographically dispersed servers in Brazil, the United States, and Japan. Experiments there showed significant cuts in response time and clear gains in requests processed per second, evidence for in-network caching as a practical tool.
arxiv-2512-20564:
Abhishek Bhattacharjee, Hemanadhan Myneni, Manoj K Harbola, and Prasanjit Samal design a kinetic energy functional that refuses all adjustable knobs. Orbital-free density functional theory promises fast simulations, but its nonlocal ones are costly and tuned per system. Their semilocal functional, KGE2, aims for nonlocal accuracy at gradient-level cost.

The design revives the Thomas-Fermi-von Weizsäcker approach, balancing its two terms through physical constraints while keeping the exact second-order gradient expansion in the uniform gas limit. Despite its simple form, KGE2 matches leading nonlocal and meta-GGA rivals across metals, semiconductors, and finite clusters. No knob fitting is involved anywhere. The result is a candidate general-purpose tool for large-scale orbital-free runs that previously needed empirical tuning.
arxiv-2512-20664:
Shinobu Miya builds a gate that rejects fluent nonsense. Language models often rate their own made-up claims as highly likely, so checking by score cannot catch them; the flaw is one of structure, not of confidence. Eidoku recasts the checking task as a constraint problem that ignores how likely a claim sounds.

Each step of reasoning is scored by what it costs to fit that step into the graph of the context around it. The score mixes how well the step links into the graph, how well it fits the feature space, and whether logic carries it. Steps whose cost passes a limit drawn from the context's own spread are refused outright. On a controlled test set, the gate turns away smooth falsehoods, claims that sound likely yet hang loose from the context, which score-based checks cannot in principle catch.
arxiv-2512-20864:
Suhyeon Lee, Dieu-Huyen Nguyen, and Donghwan Lee ask whether blockchain challenge systems actually pay people to police fraud. Systems like optimistic rollups compute off-chain and call the chain only when someone challenges a result. That design assumes at least one honest challenger will bother, an assumption about incentives rather than code.

The authors model a colluding minority, varied participant costs, and three ordering modes. Two goals must hold together: honest challengers should never lose money, and fraud should be deterred. In single-winner designs, they prove both goals cannot reliably be met at scale. In multi-winner designs, simple explicit conditions achieve both, giving protocol designers a clear fork in the road.
arxiv-2512-20964:
Ji Hyuk Jung and Ji Won Yoon demonstrate an attack on one of the strongest defenses a self-driving vehicle has. Vehicles cross-check their satellite position against an internal inertial measurement unit, whose motion readings expose spoofed GPS signals that disagree with physics. The authors set out to defeat exactly that check.

Their attack model steals the vehicle's dynamic state using an external inertial sensor, then feeds spoofed position values shaped by that stolen state so the fusion filter sees nothing anomalous. In experiments built around extended Kalman filter sensor fusion, the injected values passed without triggering detection. The result is a warning for defenders: a single internal sensor cross-check is not enough, and spoofing detection needs signals an outside attacker cannot mimic.
arxiv-2512-21064:
Hongsong Wang, Jie Gui, and two co-authors teach machines to recognize human actions from skeleton data gathered in several kinds at once. Fusing the kinds late is accurate but expensive; fusing them early through one shared backbone is cheap but weaker. Their self-supervised framework, Decomposition and Composition, splits the difference. It first pulls fused features apart into single-kind features and aligns each with its true single-kind counterpart, then recomposes the parts so each kind guides the joint features.

On the NTU RGB+D 60 and 120 benchmarks and PKU-MMD II, the approach lands a rare good balance of computing cost against accuracy. For action-recognition systems that must run on modest hardware, drones, cameras, rehabilitation monitors, getting fused quality without fused bills is the practical win.
arxiv-2512-21164:
Jifeng Ge, Bastien Vieuble, and Juan Zhang split the arithmetic itself to solve huge sparse linear systems faster. Their method builds on the alternating-direction implicit family, which splits a matrix so the full problem becomes a chain of easy structured subsystems. In their three-precision version, the subsystems are solved in cheap low precision. Residuals and solution updates are computed in high precision to protect accuracy. Modern graphics hardware rewards that division of labor.

A rounding-error analysis pins down how far forward and backward errors converge and which splitting matrices guarantee success for a given precision mix. A Gaussian-process model trained on small problems picks the regularization parameter. On an A100 graphics card, problems reaching 130 million unknowns run between two and three times faster than full double precision, across convection-diffusion and reaction-diffusion tests. Simulation pipelines gain speed without surrendering accuracy guarantees.
arxiv-2512-21464:
Ho Yun and Yoav Zemel study optimal transport between Gaussian measures, including degenerate ones, on possibly infinite-dimensional spaces. Optimal transport asks for the cheapest way to reshape one distribution into another. For Gaussians, the natural geometry is the Bures-Wasserstein space, but degenerate measures break the classical theory: the usual map formally comes from a convex function infinite almost everywhere.

Working operator-theoretically instead of through duality, the authors prove that the Kantorovich problem between any two Gaussian measures reduces to a Monge problem. A genuine transport map exists in at least one direction, not just a coupling. They give explicit formulas for all optimal maps and couplings, prove uniqueness, and describe all geodesics between degenerate measures. Uses include transport maps for Gaussian processes and a new construction of Wasserstein barycenters.
arxiv-2512-21664:
Nizar El Idrissi and Hicham Zoubeir build probability measures on infinite-dimensional Banach spaces with a striking property: every finite-dimensional subspace receives measure zero. Such measures matter where there is no analogue of ordinary volume. Gaussian measures and infinite-product builds were already known to have it.

The authors add a new construction based on prime numbers. Their method adds to the Gaussian and product approaches and is fairly elementary. They argue such measures are in fact generic among measures not supported on any finite-dimensional subspace. Along the way, they prove that any infinite-dimensional Banach space contains an uncountable family of independent vectors, as many as the continuum itself. The note widens the toolbox for building such measures, a setting where intuition from finite dimensions often fails.
arxiv-2512-22264:
Tzamn Melendez Carmona and five co-authors present LuxIA, a system for simulating and training photonic neural networks, chips that compute with light. Photonic designs promise fast, efficient machine learning, but current simulators choke on large networks because transfer matrix calculations eat memory and time. LuxIA's answer is a new computation approach the authors call the Slicing method.

Slicing computes transfer matrices in a way that stays compatible with back-propagation while sharply cutting memory use and run time. Integrated into LuxIA as a unified simulation and training tool, it was tested across photonic architectures and standard datasets including MNIST, Digits, and Olivetti Faces. LuxIA always surpassed current tools in speed and scalability, opening the way to larger photonic designs.
arxiv-2512-22464:
Sukhyun Jeong and Yong-Hoon Choi refine text-to-motion generation, where typed descriptions become 3D human movement, and text-guided editing of current motion. Pose-code systems like CoMo translate measurable pose attributes into discrete codes that people can interpret and control, but frame-by-frame codes miss subtle timing and fine detail, hurting reconstruction quality and local editing.

Their method, pose-guided residual refinement, keeps the interpretable pose codes and adds residual codes learned by residual vector quantization for the fine-grained variation. Residual dropout stops the model leaning too hard on those extra codes, protecting editability. Two transformers then predict pose codes first and residuals second. On HumanML3D and KIT-ML, the system improved generation and editing scores over CoMo and recent rivals, and users confirmed intuitive, structure-preserving edits.
arxiv-2512-22664:
Qiankun Li and five co-authors present CLAdapter, a small add-on that aims giant pretrained vision models at science fields where labeled data is scarce. Vision models trained on web-scale sets like LAION and ImageNet hold rich knowledge, yet narrow domains, from microscopy to agriculture, still starve for training examples. CLAdapter refines the pretrained features using attention methods and cluster centers that personalize how features are enhanced.

Distribution correlations and transformation matrices let the adapter learn forms tailored to each downstream feature set. Its unified design plugs into CNNs and transformers alike, in two and three dimensions. Across ten datasets spanning medicine, industry, materials, geography, and more, models fine-tuned with CLAdapter reached state-of-the-art results, which the authors offer as evidence for flexible transfer over retraining.
arxiv-2512-23364:
Jidu Yu and co-authors build a physics-based model for concrete that knows how to stop. How concrete flows decides casting quality and how long finished structures last. The Bingham model misses flow stoppage, though, and leans on ad hoc fixes to stay stable at low shear rates. The model is an elasto-viscoplastic constitutive model that treats fresh concrete as a solid-like material with a rate-dependent yield stress.

Inside the model, material responds like a spring until yielding, then flows with Bingham rheology, and can restiffen in reverse. Flow cessation emerges, not by imposed cutoff. A thixotropy law tracks the strengthening from flocculation and its breakdown under shear. The model is built in the Material Point Method, whose particle form handles the history variables and shape changes of pours. Examples reproduce concrete flow cases, offering a consistent tool for better construction and fewer defects.
arxiv-2512-23464:
Tencent's Hunyuan team, led by Yuxin Wen and many collaborators, built HY-Motion 1.0, a family of large models that turn text descriptions into 3D human motion. Earlier motion generators were small compared with language and image models. HY-Motion scales a diffusion transformer trained with flow matching up to a billion parameters, a first for this field.

Training came in full stages: pretraining on more than three thousand hours of motion data, fine-tuning on four hundred hours of cleaned data, and reinforcement learning from human feedback and reward models. The system covers over two hundred motion categories, from everyday actions to sports. Released openly, it aims to push text-to-motion tools toward commercial use in animation, games, and virtual characters.
arxiv-2512-23564:
I. Lovrekovic classifies one-parameter subgroups of the group SO(3,2), a symmetry group of interest in conformal gravity and related theories. A one-parameter subgroup is a continuous family of transformations generated by a single element, and listing them all amounts to sorting the possible generators into types. The corresponding classification for the smaller group SO(2,2) was already understood.

Comparing against that known case, Lovrekovic finds two genuinely new types of subgroup that appear only in SO(3,2). Explicit examples are constructed for each of the new types, so the classification is not just abstract. The paper closes by locating existing conformal gravity solutions within the classification, showing which subgroup types those known solutions actually realize. The note runs to just eleven pages, with some extra parts set out at the end.
arxiv-2512-23864:
Guo Ye and six co-authors give robot hands a sense of touch that can imagine the future. Vision-language-action models generalize well from web-scale knowledge, but they are blind to contact, so tasks hinging on force, texture, and slip defeat them. Earlier touch signals miss the rich dynamics of a fingertip pressing, sliding, or gripping.

DreamTacVLA treats high-resolution tactile images as a third kind of vision, alongside wrist-camera and third-person views. A hierarchical alignment loss ties tactile tokens to their spatial counterparts in the visual streams. A tactile world model, used in fine-tuning, teaches the policy to predict upcoming touch signals before acting. Training mixes a high-fidelity digital twin with real tests to work around scarce, wear-prone sensors. Across contact-rich tasks the system beat leading baselines, reaching success rates as high as ninety-five percent.
arxiv-2512-23964:
Carlo Malapad Acosta and five co-authors build a flood forecasting model meant to run in real operations, where physics simulators are too slow. Flood prediction guides disaster management, and graph neural networks suit the problem because river and terrain networks are naturally graphs on unstructured domains. Their model, DUALFloodGNN, adds physics directly into the learning rather than hoping the network discovers it.

Physical constraints enter as explicit loss terms at global and local scales, and one shared message-passing framework predicts both water volume at nodes and flow along edges. Training uses a multi-step loss with a dynamic curriculum, tuned for the autoregressive way the model is run in forecasting. Against standard and state-of-the-art graph flood models, DUALFloodGNN improved predictions of volume, flow, and depth while staying computationally cheap. Code and data set are open. The paper appears at an IJCAI-ECAI 2026 track.
arxiv-2512-24264:
Partha Rana and Sriparna Bandopadhyay return to sign patterns, matrices of plus, minus, and zero. A pattern is sign k-potent when raising it to the k-plus-first power returns the pattern itself. The smallest such k defines the property. For k equal to one, the pattern is sign idempotent. Building all such patterns has a tangled history.

Eschenbach gave a construction algorithm in the nineteen nineties. Huang later showed its outputs were not always idempotent. Park and Pyo repaired the algorithm for reducible patterns. The present paper shows their version may need many iterations. The count can grow with the pattern's order. A new algorithm fixes this. It finishes in a single iteration and builds every reducible idempotent pattern. A second algorithm builds sign k-potent patterns. Conditions for a pattern to allow k-potence close the paper.
arxiv-2512-24364:
Dibyendu Das studies the symmetries of finite algebras. The algebra is commutative, with a unity, over a closed field. Its group of symmetries has an identity component. The question is when that component is a solvable group. Pollack's work inspired this line of study.

Saorín and Asensio began the analysis under a restriction. They fixed the size of one quotient built from the algebra's radical. Das removes that restriction. New conditions on the algebra are enough to force solvability. No bound on the radical quotient is needed. The result widens the known territory a great deal. Readers in algebra gain tests that apply to all such algebras. The paper continues a program of reading group structure off algebra structure.
arxiv-2512-24464:
Wolfgang Wagner reviews thirty years of top quark research. The top quark is the heaviest known elementary particle. Its discovery came three decades ago. The field remains a thriving area of basic research. Wagner's article distills the eighteenth Workshop on Top-Quark Physics. Hanyang University in Seoul hosted the meeting.

The highlights follow the experimental summary talk's selection. New scattering processes involving top quarks keep appearing. Precision measurements of top properties continue to sharpen. Top quarks also serve as tools for exploring other physics. A newer trend stands out. Ever subtler effects are now observed through refined experimental techniques. Wagner presents the most striking results from the conference. The article reads as a field entering an age of refinement and subtlety, in his phrase.
arxiv-2512-24964:
Alessia Ando, Giusy Bosco, and Dimitri Breda build a general approach for approximating evolution maps of linear delay equations, where the present rate depends on past values. Spectra of those maps govern stability of nonlinear delay equations through linearized stability. Their analysis reformulates the maps through a fixed-point formula.

A list of hypotheses ties regularization traits of the formula to convergence of chosen approximation methods on suitable subspaces. The approach unifies proofs for several pseudospectra-based methods. Numerical analysis readers get one convergence theory instead of case-by-case arguments. Delay equations model everything from control systems to group motion, so reliable spectra matter widely.
arxiv-2512-25064:
Qinan Wang, David Jones, and Justin Pierel build a robust ultraviolet template for type Ia supernovae within the SALT3 framework, to prepare for coming cosmological surveys. Many future observations will be in rest-frame ultraviolet light, yet how standardizable these supernovae are in the ultraviolet is uncertain. Training uses open-source software and a Hubble Space Telescope spectroscopic sample with precise calibration.

Unlike earlier training spectra, the Hubble spectra need no extra warping to match photometry. Redshift dependence of the ultraviolet template is also constrained. Cosmology readers get a better standard candle model for the ultraviolet era, where systematic errors could otherwise spoil distance measurements.
arxiv-2601-06964:
Alessandro Fontanella and colleagues wrote a 2026 arXiv preprint. The work covers hardware-in-the-loop wind-tunnel testing of wake interactions between two floating wind turbines. ArXiv posted the preprint in 2026 under its PAPERS collection. Wake interactions in floating wind farms are inherently coupled to platform motion. Yet most experimental studies to date neglect this two-way coupling by prescribing platform movements.

This work presents a hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) wind-tunnel methodology to investigate wake interactions. Between two floating wind turbines with fully coupled aerodynamic loading and platform dynamics. The work gives specialists a compact account of the problem and one proposed way to handle it.
arxiv-2601-07064:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Mohd Mujtaba Akhtar and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers bridging attribution and Open-Set detection using Graph-Augmented instance learning in synthetic speech. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. The authors propose a unified framework for not only attributing synthetic speech to its source but also.

For detecting speech generated by synthesizers that were not encountered during training. This requires methods that move beyond simple detection to support both detailed forensic analysis and open-set generalization. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07164:
A 2026 arXiv preprint by Min Wang and co-authors appeared in 2026. It covers offline Meta-Reinforcement learning with Flow-Based task inference and adaptive correction of feature overgeneralization. It was posted on arXiv in 2026 in the PAPERS collection. Offline meta-reinforcement learning (OMRL) combines the strengths of learning from diverse datasets in offline RL with the adaptability to new tasks of meta-RL. Promising safe and efficient knowledge acquisition by RL agents.

However, OMRL still suffers extrapolation errors due to out-of-distribution (OOD) actions. Compromised by broad task distributions and Markov Decision Process (MDP) ambiguity in meta-RL setups. Readers get a clear, focused account of the problem and the method the authors set out.
arxiv-2601-07264: Weihao Xuan and co-authors published a 2026 arXiv preprint. The preprint covers confidence dichotomy. It appeared in the arXiv PAPERS collection for 2026. Autonomous agents based on large language models (LLMs) are rapidly evolving to handle multi-turn tasks, but ensuring their trustworthiness remains a critical challenge. A fundamental pillar of this trustworthiness is calibration, which refers to an agent’s ability to express confidence that reliably reflects its actual performance. The preprint gives researchers a focused account of the problem and the approach the authors take.
arxiv-2601-08064: Yuxi Xia and five co-authors test how much users should trust language model confidence scores. Their 2026 arXiv paper notes that confidence estimates shape user trust and real choices. Past work judged these methods mostly by calibration and by how well scores rank right over wrong answers. Calibration checks whether stated confidence matches accuracy in practice. The authors argue that this is not enough, and they test confidence methods across changes in language instead. That shift matters when the same question is worded in new ways.
arxiv-2601-08164: Udomlerd Srisuchinwong and a large team wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on year-long swings in the radial velocity of 2 Draconis, a K0 giant star in the red-clump group. Slow stars that have left youth often show such swings, which can hint at a planet. The team weighs four roots for the swing: the star's own acts, flaws in the tool's profile, a beat from the sample plan, and a planet. A false claim here would be easy to make.
arxiv-2601-08364:
Sanjukta Kundu and five co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a check for a quantum link. The link is entanglement, a tie where two parts act as one. The pairs in view are photon pairs, made by a step called spontaneous parametric down conversion. The tie sits in the side-to-side place of each photon. The team checks the tie with no need to catch one of the photons.

Most checks count pairs that hit two sensors at the same time. The team skips that step in full. They use a nonlinear interferometric method, based on how one photon's waves add and cancel. With that one photon, they show a breach of the Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen rule. They also show a breach of the Mancini-Giovannetti-Vitali-Tombesi rule. A full theory account backs the lab work.
arxiv-2601-08464:
Evgenii Maslov and co-authors present CoMa, a framework that generates building massing designs with vision-language models. Their 2026 arXiv paper targets the conceptual design phase in architecture and urban planning. Massing sets a building's basic shape and volume, and it still leans heavily on designer intuition and manual effort.

An automated framework would generate massing from functional requirements and site context. A primary obstacle has been the lack of suitable datasets for data-driven methods. CoMa uses vision-language models to work around that scarcity. Early massing choices lock in cost, light, and energy use, so faster grounded options could improve whole projects.
arxiv-2601-08764:
Haven Kim, Yupeng Hou, and Julian McAuley work on song picks made by AI. New pick systems turn each song into a short code of parts. The code can mix sound, words, and cover art facts. Past work codes each type of fact on its own, which wastes space.

Their method is called FusID. It fuses the types of fact into one shared code for each song. That cuts waste from codes that say the same thing twice. It also lets the types shape each other, so the code holds more sense. A reader who builds music picks gets a lean code plan. It may help a system find songs a user will like with less cost.
arxiv-2601-08964:
Jiahao Tian works on tasks where one item can hold more than one true tag at once. A news text can be on sport and on cash at the same time. Tags can also link: if one tag is true, a next may be more prone to be true. A good tag tool must learn both the trait links and the tag links.

He uses a tree sum tool with a Bayes frame, called BART. Trees split data by traits in steps. The Bayes frame keeps doubt in the calls, not just one firm call. His form is built for multi tag work from the start. A reader who tags large sets gets a tool that shows its doubt, which helps on edge cases.
arxiv-2601-09064:
Cunyuan Jiang reports that a famed bump in how glass like stuff shakes is a mass act, not a rare one. Glass and like stuff shake more at a set rate than a plain law by Debye says they should. That extra shake is called the Boson peak. Late work laid it on a few odd spots that shake in a local way.

Jiang splits the total shake count by each free move of the stuff. The split shows near all parts take part in the peak. It is not the act of a few odd spots. A reader in stuff physics gets a shift in view. The peak is a trait of the whole crowd, not a flaw of a few.
arxiv-2601-09164:
Masaki Michiwaki and Tsutomu Kobayashi build ghost free theories that link a scalar field to gravity with deep terms. A ghost here is a fake state with bad energy that breaks a theory. The scalar can have up to third order rates of change in their build. Most past builds stop at a low order, to stay safe from ghosts.

They write the build in a frame split by time slices. They then set rules that kill ghosts and keep just three free modes: one scalar, two from gravity. Past the known Horndeski class, new sound builds may live. A reader in gravity theory gets a recipe for new builds that stay sound.
arxiv-2601-09364:
Radim Zedka, Roman Marsalek, Marek Bobula, and Arman Farhang work on a newer wireless scheme called OTFS, short for orthogonal time frequency space. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies channel estimation, the step where a receiver learns how the air has warped the signal. They focus on oversampled OTFS in channels with fractional delay and Doppler shifts.

The paper uses unique word signaling to probe the channel. Oversampling and pulse shaping have been studied for OTFS, but not much in the context of channel estimation. Filling that gap matters because fast-moving users smear signals in delay and Doppler. A good estimator keeps links reliable for trains, cars, and other moving receivers.
arxiv-2601-09664:
Ozan Sargın studies an inflation model inside a modified theory of gravity. His 2026 arXiv paper treats constant-roll inflation with a beta-exponential potential in the Palatini formalism. A scalar field couples to quadratic gravity, with both R and R-squared terms.

In this model, the inflaton is the field that sets the size of an extra dimension. Constant-roll conditions slow the field's motion in a controlled way. The Palatini approach treats the metric and connection as separate, which changes the dynamics. The authors check what expansion history this mix predicts for the early universe.
arxiv-2601-09864:
Adway Girish, Shlomo Shamai, and Emre Telatar find the best input for a noisy channel when entropy is capped. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies the entropy-constrained Gaussian channel at high signal-to-noise ratio. Capacity tells how much information a channel can carry reliably.

The authors show that as the signal-to-noise ratio grows without bound, the best input is a discrete Gaussian on a scaled integer lattice. A smooth problem lands on a discrete answer. Such asymptotics guide code design for links that run hot and fast. They also close a neat theoretical question in information theory.
arxiv-2601-09964:
Taekyun Kim and Dae San Kim bring chance into a classic count. Stirling counts split a set into blocks. Bell counts sum all such splits. Past work made mixed forms of these counts. The pair now add a chance twist.

They fix a chance variable with set mean facts. From it they build new Stirling counts and Bell sums. The counts mix two past forms and add the chance part. The paper works out traits of these new counts. It finds sums, links, and closed forms. Such counts show up in work on sums, codes, and chance walks.
arxiv-2601-10064:
Zhenghao Liu and co authors teach small models to reason in long chains. Large models can work out hard math in long step chains. Small models can learn from those chains. But the chains are often too long and too rich in form. A small model may fail to learn them as is.

The team trims those chains by prefix match. They line up the start of the teacher chain with what the small model can take. That match adapts as the small model grows. The aim is a chain the small model can learn in full. It should gain skill, not just copy length.
arxiv-2601-10164:
Themistoklis Diamantopoulos, Dimosthenis Natsos, and Andreas Symeonidis hunt malware by how it uses a machine. Cloud and smart device nets link vast rigs. Bad code can spread fast in such nets. Old hunts read the code itself. New hunts watch what the code does.

The team watch use of CPU, memory, and disk over time. Bad code tends to leave a trace in those loads. They seek a live hunt that flags bad code as it runs. The trace is at the level of the running task. Such a hunt can act fast, before harm spreads wide.
arxiv-2601-10464:
Mikkel Meyer Andersen and co authors gauge how rare a full mitochondrial genome is in a crowd. Such genomes are passed down the mother line. In crime work, a match on one can be strong proof. Its worth rests on how rare that type is. For full genomes, crowd data is thin.

The team made MitoFREQ to fill that gap. It starts from top level groups and single point variants. From those two facts, it gauges the rate of the full genome. That lets labs state the worth of a match with more care. The work aids courts and labs that use this proof.
arxiv-2601-10564:
