Eduardo Magalhães studies rewriting, the step-by-step replacement of symbols by fixed rules. Classic rewriting works on strings of symbols, which form a free monoid. He asks what happens when the rules act inside any monoid at all. A push for this comes from logic, since free monoids cannot be pinned down by first-order axioms.

He defines monoidal rewriting systems, where each reduction step takes place inside a chosen ambient monoid. To study them, he builds a 2-category of systems that always halt and never fork into rival results. The work gives rewriting theory a broader, more abstract home. It may help logicians apply first-order tools to rewriting problems.
arxiv-2601-10864:
Daniel Irving Bernstein writes an expository survey on rigidity theory in statistical inference. A statistical model is a family of probability distributions. Fitting picks the member that best matches data. For Gaussian models, the maximum likelihood threshold says how many samples are needed before a best fit is sure to exist.

Bernstein sums up what is known about these thresholds. He stresses their links with rigidity theory, the study of when frameworks of bars and joints hold firm. The tie is a surprise bridge between statistics and geometry. Survey papers like this one let newcomers enter a field through its results and its open problems in one read.
arxiv-2601-10964:
Nicholas J. C. Papadopoulos and Ramin Ayanzadeh pursue universal fault-tolerant quantum computation that works for any stabilizer code. Such protection lets quantum computers run while noise strikes. Many error-correcting codes exist, but none alone supports every operation a universal computer needs. Workarounds like code switching or magic state distillation are costly and tied to one code.

The authors seek one route to universality that works across codes. A method that works across stabilizer codes would free builders from per-code tricks. It could also cut the overhead that now dominates quantum hardware plans. The work matters for the long build toward large, useful quantum machines that must correct errors as they go.
arxiv-2601-11064:
Xiang-Wei Shi and Sheng-Qin Feng study heavy quarkonia inside a rotating, anisotropic quark-gluon plasma. Quarkonia are bound states of a heavy quark and its antiquark, like the J/Psi and the Upsilon. In hot plasma, they melt at rates that report the plasma's traits. The authors compute their in-medium spectral functions and effective masses with holography.

The plasma here both spins and squeezes unevenly, closer to real collision debris. Rotation and anisotropy can shift how each quarkonium state survives. Heavy-ion experiments read those survival patterns as thermometers. A holographic map for spinning, uneven plasma helps interpret what colliders see when quarkonia emerge from the fireball changed.
arxiv-2601-11864:
Zhiyuan Li, Yuan Wu, and Yi Chang aim to steady the training of large language models. A common fix for wild gradients is to clip them to a set size. The usual fix treats all parts of the model as one block.

That can hurt, since wild parts force cuts on calm parts too. The team call this spill-over. Their method, named AGGC in the work, clips each group of parts by its own scale. Group-wise clips could keep training calm with less harm to calm parts. The work tests this idea on large model runs.
arxiv-2601-12464:
Yanrui Lu and a large team build a benchmark for cell images from electron microscopy. The task is to segment organelles, the small parts inside a cell, one by one. Exact masks for each organelle aid counts of shape and studies of how organelles touch. Past benchmarks rest on small, hand picked datasets, though.

Real microscopy data are far more varied and cover wider fields of view. That gap limits patch based methods that see only small windows. The team present a large scale benchmark drawn from data in the wild. A test set of this kind can show which methods truly scale. It can also steer the field toward tools that work on raw, messy images.
arxiv-2601-12564:
John Gough and Dylon Rees, at Aberystwyth University, derive a quantum filter for systems with squeezed noise. A quantum filter tracks the state of an open quantum system as measurements come in. Their setup uses quadrature measurements, a scheme called homodyning. The input field is in a general quasi free state, a broad class of noise.

Past work handled thermal input noise, a narrower case. This work extends the filter to squeezed inputs, where noise is lower in one quadrature than usual. Squeezed light is a real tool in labs, so filters must handle it. A correct filter lets engineers estimate and control quantum devices in real time. The result serves quantum optics and quantum control alike.
arxiv-2601-12664:
Elisa Goncalves Ribeiro and three co authors, at Brazilian universities, study federated learning for cancer images. Deep learning on histopathology images clashes with privacy rules in clinical settings. Federated learning helps by keeping patient data local at each site. Its performance still depends on hyperparameter choices, though.

Client datasets in real federations are not identically distributed. The team ask whether settings tuned on one cancer dataset generalize to others. They test that transfer across non IID federated scenarios. If good settings travel well, hospitals could skip costly local tuning. If not, each site faces its own search. The answer matters for practical medical AI deployment.
arxiv-2601-12764:
Sikarin Yoo-Kong shows how a famed law of relativity can grow out of the math of data and chance. The law links energy and momentum for a fast object. He starts from a less used form of a Hamiltonian, the function that tracks total energy. He then treats the swings of an extra parameter with a max entropy rule.

That rule fixes one chance law and no other. The bounds that pick it come from the shape of the space of chance laws. In this view, the law of relativity is an average effect, not a base fact. Work of this kind asks how much of physics is deep and how much is an effect of scale. It joins two fields that rarely meet.
arxiv-2601-12864:
Giovanni Bocchi, Alessandra Micheletti, Paolo Nota, and Alessandro Olper study how abnormal temperatures affect crop yields in Italy. They apply functional regression to find which within season periods matter most. Temperature and precipitation anomalies can help or harm a crop based on timing. A heat spike at flowering may hurt far more than one in winter.

Their data cover Italian provinces from 1952 to 2023. They analyze two major cereals, maize and soft wheat. Quantile regression in function form shows effects across the yield distribution, not just the mean. Long records let them separate true signals from noise. Results can guide adaptation as the climate of Italy warms.
arxiv-2601-12964:
John Waithaka, Gustave Bwirayesu, and Moise Busogi improve self supervised learning for satellite imagery. Pretraining in remote sensing mostly uses mid resolution image datasets, due to their high availability. High resolution datasets have now been released as well. The team ask how high resolution data can join pretraining to help mid resolution tasks.

Their cross scale pretraining aims to enhance representation learning across resolutions. The downstream test is semantic segmentation on mid resolution images. Better features at low resolution matter for land cover and agriculture maps. Many regions are only covered by coarse imagery, so gains there have wide reach. The work links two data scales that are usually trained apart.
arxiv-2601-13264:
Tyler Lizzo and Larry Heck survey how a trained model can be made to forget. Large language models score well on many text tasks. Their wide use, though, raises fears on privacy, rights, and bias. Full re train to drop bad data is too costly to be a fix.

Unlearning aims to cut just the bad part out. It seeks to drop set facts or data from a model while the rest stays sound. Lizzo and Heck map the main routes to do so. They also map how each route is judged and what hard tasks stay open. For firms that must pull data on call, the survey sorts real tools from mere claims.
arxiv-2601-13664:
Tiancheng Fang and co-authors build a model to repair rough 3D voxel shapes in 2026. Voxels are small cubes that make up a 3D form, like pixels in space. Raw voxel data is often noisy or has holes and gaps. Photos from many views hold clues that could fix those flaws.

Their model, VIAFormer, aligns voxels with multi-view images. It uses a transformer, an AI design that weighs how parts relate to each other. Calibrated images tell the model where each view was taken from. The aim is high-fidelity repair, shapes that stay true to the real object.
arxiv-2601-14364:
Omri Lesser, Joon Young Park, Yuval Ronen, and their co-authors build a theory of odd superconductors in this 2026 paper. A Josephson junction joins two superconductors with a thin weak link. In standard junctions, the critical current swings with magnetic flux in a Fraunhofer-like pattern. The team studies Corbino junctions, a ring-shaped form of the device.

When the superconductors sit on a three-dimensional topological insulator, the pattern shifts a bit. Chiral Majorana modes on the surface cause that shift. The title names the paper's focus: reentrant superconductivity in these junctions. Reentrant means the superconducting state returns after it fades. The work gives a theory for that return in this setup.
arxiv-2601-14664:
Erick Pastén, Claudia Álvarez Rojas, and Norman Cruz clarify a concept in general relativity in this 2026 paper. Their topic is angular momentum, the measure of rotation. In relativity, its role is tricky. The authors examine it from both heuristic and fully covariant perspectives. Their aim is to clarify conceptual ambiguities.

Those ambiguities arise when Newtonian intuition is extrapolated into the relativistic regime. In Newton's world, angular momentum is simple and absolute. In Einstein's, rotation depends on the observer and the frame. Readers get a careful sorting of which parts of the classic picture survive, and which must be rebuilt.
arxiv-2601-14764:
Thomas Eiter, Tobias Geibinger, and Zeynep G. Saribatur survey explainable logic programming in this 2026 paper. Answer Set Programming, or ASP, is a popular declarative reasoning and problem solving approach in symbolic AI. Its rule-based formalism makes it inherently attractive for explainable and interpretive reasoning. That attraction gains importance with the surge of Explainable AI, or XAI.

The authors give an XAI view on explainable ASP. They cover methods, systems, and perspectives. Declarative rules can be read by humans, unlike the weights of a neural network. The survey sorts how ASP systems explain their answers today. Readers get a map of a symbolic field whose explanations come built in.
arxiv-2601-15064:
Simran Kaur, Sara Salimzadeh, and Ujwal Gadiraju study how pay and rewards shape the studies that test human-AI teamwork. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with joint decision-making. Human judgment still rules in high-stakes calls, so teams of people and AI are widely studied.

Those studies often recruit crowd workers. How the workers are paid can sway how hard they try and what they report. The authors examine incentive schemes as a design choice in its own right. They call their approach incentive-tuning, and they ask how it should be set and tuned.
arxiv-2601-15264:
José C. Martín studies maps through a topology that the maps themselves create. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with self-maps of a set and the primal topology each one induces. He then examines a whole series of dynamical concepts inside that topology.

The list runs from non-wandering and recurrent points to minimal sets. It covers transitive and mixing maps in weak and strong forms. Lyapunov stable maps join the list, as do chaotic maps in two senses, those of Auslander-Yorke and of Devaney. Pairs of points with special closeness properties close the study.
arxiv-2601-15364:
Szymon Łukaszyk sorts pure qubit states by the pattern of their support. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with separability, the question of whether a joint quantum state splits into independent parts. He studies registers of qubits in the computational basis.

The pattern of basis states that appear is called the support. Łukaszyk shows that bipartite separability hinges on that pattern's combinatorial shape. Using Boolean cube geometry, he builds a taxonomy. Some support shapes guarantee separability outright. In the rest, entanglement depends on the probability amplitudes themselves alone in the final end.
arxiv-2601-15464:
Alessandro Neri and Ferdinando Zullo write on rank-metric codes in a 2026 arXiv paper. These codes are sets of matrices over a finite field. Distance between codewords is measured by rank, not by counting changed entries. The codes draw interest for their use in network coding. They also link to many other areas of math.

The history here runs back to Delsarte in 1978. Gabidulin later rediscovered the same idea. Since then the codes have become a central topic in coding theory. The title states the paper's two aims. It gives bounds that limit how good such codes can be. It also gives constructions, over arbitrary fields, that show how to build them.
arxiv-2601-15664:
A team signing as Skywork presents an image model in a 2026 arXiv paper. The model is Skywork UniPic 3.0. It handles multi-image composition: merging several images into one result. Recent hits like Nano-Banana and Seedream 4.0 show strong public interest in this task. Composition is much harder than editing a single image. Consistency and quality are harder to hold across sources.

Many leading models have not shared how they achieve good fusion. The title names the team's route: unified composition via sequence modeling. Treating images as a sequence lets one model handle varied inputs. For creators, multi-image tools promise posters, product shots, and storyboards from mixed sources. The paper speaks to builders racing in that space.
arxiv-2601-15764:
Silvia De Nicolò, Beatrice Biondi, and Mario Mazzocchi probe a workhorse research design in a 2026 arXiv paper. Triple difference is a method for estimating treatment effects. It compares changes across groups and time with an extra layer of contrast. The design assumes control groups stay clean. Spillover effects can break that assumption. When treatment leaks into controls, the contrasts blur.

The authors study identification under such contamination. They show that, under conventional assumptions, the model fails to identify both effects at once. Neither the treatment effect nor the spillover effect can be pinned down. That is a sharp warning for applied work. Many policies spill over by nature. The paper tells researchers when their design cannot answer the question they posed.
arxiv-2601-15864:
Tanmay Inamdar, Pallavi Jain, and Pranjal Pandey study fair house allocation in a 2026 arXiv paper. House allocation assigns n houses to n agents. The goal is a fair division under some criterion, such as envy-freeness. The problem is extremely well studied in fair allocation theory. Classic versions often assume all agents value houses identically. Real people do not. Tastes differ, and envy gets harder to avoid.

The authors move beyond identical valuations, per the title. Their aim is minimum envy under differing values. Envy is unavoidable in some instances; measuring its least possible level is the task. Such work informs real allocation problems, from dorm rooms to public housing lotteries. Theory that respects differing values travels better to practice.
arxiv-2601-16164:
Emmanuel Abbe, Colin Sandon and Oscar Sprumont build codes from grid maps of many vars. Their 2026 preprint sets out Tensor Reed Muller codes. Code words come from values of maps with sets of vars. Each set has its own grade cap for the maps. Such codes join traits of the known Reed Muller codes in a grid form.

The team shows these codes can reach the top rate for a channel. They also give a read back method with near straight time cost. Top rate with fast read back is a rare pair. It makes the codes fit for real links and stores. The work is a step in code theory.
arxiv-2601-16364:
Jongmin Mun and Jeong Hoon Jang mix curve and count data in one shrink fit. Their 2026 preprint stems from kidney scan work. Kidney tests give renogram curves plus drug and trait counts. Past shrink fits oft take one data type at a time. Types that move as one then lose their joint tale.

The new fit, called Hybrid PLS, shrinks both types as one. It cuts size in a guided way while it fits the reply. Joint shrink keeps links that span curve and count facts. Those links may hold the true signs of kidney state. The work seeks fits that use all test facts well.
arxiv-2601-16464:
Yipei Wang, Zhaoying Pan and Xiaoqian Wang test how foe tweaks bend spread strength. Their 2026 preprint deals with two kinds of model strength. One kind stands firm to small foe tweaks of inputs. The next stands firm when test data shifts in kind. Past work found a trade twixt the two kinds of strength.

The team asks how foe tweaks in train shape that trade. Tweak trained models may gain one strength and lose the next. Clear trade maps help teams pick train terms by need. High stakes tools need both strengths in fair share. The work adds terms to the trade tale.
arxiv-2601-16864:
G. M. Gusev and a team of four co-authors probe how charge flows in a mixed flat band. Their flat stuff joins light Dirac bands with heavy hole bands. Charge-charge pushes shift flow in flat stuff in known ways. How those pushes shift flow in a magnet field was less clear. Plain band tales oft say the shift should be nil.

Their 2026 preprint puts that nil claim to a lab test. They track flow as the field and charge mix shift. Flat bands like this show up in new quantum stuff. Sound maps of their flow traits aid chip and sensor design.
arxiv-2601-16964:
Mohamed Amine Ferrag, Abderrahmane Lakas, and Merouane Debbah build a test set for AI in self-drive cars. Cars with AI must sense, plan, and act with care. Tests for such thought need vast, safe-scene sets. Real crash-risk scenes are too dear to stage. Their 2026 preprint shares AgentDrive, an open set of made scenes.

Big chatbots wrote the scenes in that set. Scenes span hard and risk-full road cases. Teams can train and grade car AI on them. Shared scene sets make grades fair across labs. They may speed safe self-drive work for all.
arxiv-2601-17564:
Aadam presents JaxARC, a fast environment for research on the Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus. ARC tests if AI can reason from a few example pairs. It is a prized test of human-like induction. Old Gymnasium-based tools are slow. That slowness caps the scale of tests teams can run. JaxARC rebuilds the environment in JAX for speed.

An open-source, high-performance tool lets more labs join ARC work. Fast runs allow broad sweeps over tasks and agents. Scale matters when each idea needs many trials. JAX also fits GPU and TPU hardware well. The work is infrastructure, but key infrastructure. Better tools can speed the search for reasoning methods that generalize.
arxiv-2601-17764:
Md Asgor Hossain Reaj and co-authors probe gender bias in Bengali language models. Large models have scored big gains in recent years. Intrinsic gender bias persists inside them. Most bias research centers on English. Bengali and other Global South languages get little study. Their linguistic and cultural biases may differ in kind. The team uses cross-lingual probing for the task.

They add a community-grounded analysis to the probes. Local voices can say which biases harm in context. Bengali has many millions of speakers who deserve fair tools. English-only bias fixes may not transfer. This work builds the evidence base for Bengali. It models how bias study should adapt per culture.
arxiv-2601-17864:
Fabrizio Canfora, Anibal Neira, and Seung Hun Oh build a bridge between two theories of gravity and matter. Their 2026 preprint links Einstein-scalar-Maxwell theory with gauged Skyrme-Maxwell-Einstein models. The link is exact, and the authors say it is the first of its kind. They find it by building the simplest setup that fits the gauged Skyrme-Maxwell frame and working out what it implies.

Inside that setup, a sector appears with strong magnetic fields and nonzero baryonic charge. Baryonic charge counts the matter content tied to Skyrme-type fields. An exact bridge lets results from one theory be read in the other. That can speed work on charged, magnetized bodies in strong gravity.
arxiv-2601-17964:
Brian C. Albrecht and Mark Whitmeyer study how cost shocks move prices when prices differ across sellers. Their 2026 preprint starts from a gap in the standard story. Classic pass-through analysis assumes one single price in a market. Real studies find wide price spread even for the same good. The authors build a tractable frame that splits the problem into two tiers, so spread and shocks can be studied together.

The split lets them ask who bears a cost shock when buyers face many prices. The answer can differ from the one-price story in size and in who pays. Firms, tax planners, and trade watchers all care about pass-through. A frame that fits real price spread gives them sharper tools.
arxiv-2601-18064:
Hasi Hays introduces a brain-inspired network design built on sparse, shifting links. His 2026 preprint presents Resonant Sparse Geometry Networks, or RSGN. Transformer models use dense attention, whose cost grows with the square of the input size. RSGN instead places its nodes in a learned hyperbolic space. Link strength falls off with distance in that space, and the wiring organizes itself. Only nearby nodes talk much, so the network stays sparse.

Input-dependent wiring lets the network reshape itself for each input. Hyperbolic space suits tree-like data, which is common in language and biology. If the design scales, it could cut the cost of attention sharply. The paper offers a fresh route past a known bottleneck.
arxiv-2601-18464:
Wenbin Wei, Suyuan Yao, Cheng Huang, and Xiangyu Gao build a full chain AI tool for glaucoma, a disease that steals sight bit by bit. The disease is a top cause of sight loss that cannot be undone. Early finds and steady checks can save sight, but care now leans on one test at a time. Those tests leave room for whim and for gaps in care.

Their tool joins many kinds of test in one flow, from first screen to long term watch. It aims to give the same grade of care in each place, not just where top kit and top staff sit. A fair chain could help more people keep their sight. It could also cut the load on eye clinics that now face long lines. The team frame the tool as one that users can trust, with clear steps from test to choice.
arxiv-2601-18664:
Zihao Guo and eight colleagues add step-by-step thought to smart shop tools that build a pick list word by word. Such tools read a user's past picks and then write out the next pick as a code. Past tools jump straight from the past picks to the code. That jump skips the kind of step thought that has made text tools so strong on hard tasks.

Their plan breaks the jump into steps led by sense. Each step narrows the kind of thing the user may want next. By the last step the code is picked with the full chain in view. A chain of steps could give picks that fit taste with more care. It could also let staff see why a pick was made, step by step.
arxiv-2601-18764:
Sahil Satapathy, Projjwal Kanjilal, and A. Bhattacharyay give a plain way to chart the phases of a trapped cloud of cold atoms with three spin states. Such a cloud sits in a trap that holds it in a near line. Its atoms can pair their spins to pull close or push off, and that choice sets the phase of the whole cloud. To chart the phases by the full rules is slow and dear.

Their way takes a smart guess at the cloud's form and tunes the guess to the least force. From that tuned guess they read the form of the cloud in each spin state. The full phase chart drops out at low cost. A cheap chart helps labs pick trap sets that land on the phase they want. It also gives a first map for more strict work to check.
arxiv-2601-18964:
Karen Meagher and Hermie Monterde study quantum walks that refuse to leave home. In a quantum walk, a particle spreads across a graph's nodes by quantum rules. A node is called sedentary if a walk that starts there tends to stay put, which is odd for such a spread prone process.

The pair prove that almost all planar graphs and almost all trees have at least two such stay at home nodes. The result holds for any choice of edge weights. Sedentariness, it seems, is not a quirk but a common trait of these graph families, a fact that may shape quantum search design.
arxiv-2601-19064:
David Bryant, Celine Scornavacca, and David L. Swofford present a new way to score an evolutionary tree. Few tools in the field are used more than Felsenstein's pruning method, which computes how likely a tree is given DNA data. Their method, LvD, rests on a different split of the tree's structure.

LvD works for all standard models of how DNA letters change over time. A rival route to the same score gives software writers a check on old code and, in some cases, a faster path. Tree scores sit under nearly all modern work on how species relate, so even small gains spread wide.
arxiv-2601-19764:
Guram Donadze, Manuel Ladra, and Pilar Páez-Guillán revisit a classic theorem in group theory. Schur's theorem links a group to its Schur multiplier, an object that measures how the group can be extended. A natural hope is that the multiplier of a Noetherian group is always finitely generated. The authors show this hope is false.

They give cases where the multiplier of such a group is not finitely generated. They also study the non-abelian tensor product of groups, a construction with wide algebraic use. They prove it preserves the polycyclic property, even when one factor is only Noetherian. New versions of Schur's theorem round out the paper. The results correct assumptions that specialists may have taken for granted.
arxiv-2601-19864:
Thomas Bieske and Frederic Bowen study a kind of solution to partial differential equations in an unusual geometry. Martinet spaces lack the algebraic group law of Carnot groups. They also lack the triangular vector fields of Grushin-type spaces. That makes standard methods hard to apply.

The authors establish the basic properties of viscosity solutions in these spaces. Viscosity solutions are a weak notion designed for equations with no smooth solutions. They then prove uniqueness for strictly monotone elliptic equations and for the infinite Laplace equation. Uniqueness matters because a model with several right answers predicts nothing. The work extends a workhorse theory to a setting that had resisted it. The proofs are strict and step by step. Each claim rests on the last.
arxiv-2601-20164:
Jim Maar, Denis Paperno, Callum McDougall, and Neel Nanda ask whether language models plan ahead while they write. A model picks one word at a time, yet it may pick a word now to set up a word it expects later. A prior study of rhyming verse suggested this kind of implicit planning in one model.

The authors build metrics to measure such planning and apply them to rhyme generation and question answering. Clear measures would help researchers test when a model is truly planning and when it is only reacting. That question bears on how much trust to place in model outputs on longer tasks.
arxiv-2601-20464:
Alejandro Benito-Santos and five colleagues survey how research where visualization meets the humanities is evaluated. The field, called VIS*H, is marked by a tension between chasing analytical insight and interpretive meaning. Standard evaluation frameworks judge tools by analytical utility and communicative power.

That yardstick can mismatch the interpretive aims of humanities scholarship, which does not always seek a single right reading. The authors survey evaluation practices across this borderland. Their map can help both sides judge work by goals the work actually has, rather than by imported standards. The field is young, and its rules are still being set by the work now in print.
arxiv-2601-20664:
Dimitrios Karapiperis and three colleagues present ALER, an active learning system for entity resolution. Entity resolution links records that refer to the same real thing across datasets. Supervised deep models do it well but need massive labeled datasets that are expensive to build, which blocks many real uses.

Active learning cuts the labeling need by asking humans about the most informative pairs. Existing approaches, though, hit scalability bottlenecks. ALER is a hybrid design aimed at efficient resolution. Cheaper record linkage would help hospitals, governments, and firms merge messy data with confidence.
arxiv-2601-20764:
Saeed Akbar, Muhammad Waqas, and Rahmat Ullah design control software for fog computing. Their 2026 paper presents Agentic Fog, a policy-driven framework. Fog computing places small servers near users, between devices and the cloud. These systems face strict latency limits and workloads that change by the minute. They also see only part of the picture at any time.

Recent agentic AI tools lean on large language models to reason. The authors argue such tools fit infrastructure poorly. They cost too much compute, act at random, and resist formal analysis. Their framework instead drives agents with explicit policies. The paper aims at distributed intelligence that stays fast, cheap, and open to checking. It speaks to builders of edge systems that cannot wait on the cloud.
arxiv-2601-20864:
Chloe Cheng and a large team of co-authors argue that early galaxies hide more mass than they seem to. Their 2026 paper concerns the initial mass function, the mix of star masses a galaxy is born with. JWST has shown that massive galaxies formed far faster than models predicted. Many had built a large mass in stars about twelve billion years ago. That speed strains the standard picture of galaxy growth.

The authors point to a bottom-heavy mass function as the key. Bottom-heavy means far more small, dim stars than usual. Such stars add mass while adding little light. A galaxy can then be heavier than its glow suggests. This hidden mass could ease the clash with models. The paper reframes how astronomers read the light of the first galaxies.
arxiv-2601-21564:
Antonio Almudévar and Alfonso Ortega remove the trace of chosen training data by compressing a model's inner representations. Unlearning is needed for privacy law and for fixing models trained on bad data. Most methods tweak the model's weights, which can be unstable and costly.

Their framework works in representation space instead of weight space. Compression squeezes out the information tied to the data to be forgotten. Working one level up may give cleaner removal with less damage to other skills. The approach offers a fresh route for honoring deletion requests in trained models.
arxiv-2601-21864:
Jinhao Pan and co-authors study how large language models pick up social bias. Models can repeat harmful stereotypes, which limits their safe use. Most attempts to debias them work by suppression: changing parameters, prompts, or the neurons tied to biased behavior.

The authors argue that suppression is brittle, generalizes weakly, wastes data, and can damage general ability. Their 2026 preprint, called KnowBias, takes the opposite road and enhances neurons tied to knowledge about bias itself. Strengthening a model's own grasp of stereotypes, rather than muting parts of it, could offer a steadier fix. The debate matters because these models now answer questions for millions of people every day.
arxiv-2601-22164:
Christos Tsourveloudis tests whether detectors that find anything in ordinary photos can cope with the view from above. Open-vocabulary detection uses vision-language models to recognize new categories from text alone, with no retraining, and it performs strongly on natural images. Aerial imagery is a different world of tiny objects and odd angles.

Tsourveloudis presents the first systematic benchmark of this transfer. Five state-of-the-art open-vocabulary models are evaluated on an aerial dataset of several thousand images across eighty categories. His 2026 preprint maps which models survive the move to drones and satellite views. That map matters for search and rescue, farming, and disaster mapping, where new object types appear without warning.
arxiv-2601-22364:
Eghbal Hosseini and four co-authors show that the shape of a text can bend how a model lays out its inner states. Past work found that models straighten these paths in deep layers, which may aid next-word calls. Their 2026 preprint asks how the build of the context itself reshapes that layout.

They track how the inner paths curve or align as the input form changes. The work links surface form to deep structure inside the model. That link can help explain why some prompts work and others fail. It also guides safer, clearer prompt design.
arxiv-2601-22564:
Takashi Shimada and Kunihiko Kaneko show that microbes feeding on each other's leaks can coexist in wild, chaotic swarms. Species trade chemicals: each leaks metabolites that others take up. Their 2026 preprint studies a simple model of that cross-feeding web.

In the model, many species persist past what the exclusion rule would allow. The system can even fall into high-dimensional chaos, with counts swinging in complex ways. The result helps explain the rich mix seen in real microbial worlds. It ties food-web shape to diversity itself. The model is simple, which makes the result striking.
arxiv-2601-22664:
Zixuan Huang and a team align reward models with human taste in real time, past mere word sense. RLHF trains models from human likes, yet the policy can overfit the reward model and game its quirks. Their 2026 preprint targets that reward overoptimization, where scores rise while true quality stalls.

Their reward model updates as it is used, staying in step with the policy it grades. A live, aligned grader should cut gaming and drift. The work matters for every lab that trains by feedback. It treats alignment as a moving target. That honesty is the point.
arxiv-2601-22764:
Deepak Kumar, Emmanouil Karystinaios, Gerhard Widmer, and Markus Schedl test how far pre-trained language models go on symbolic music. Music and language share deep parallels, which invites the swap. Their 2026 preprint runs controlled comparisons of supervised tuning against preference-based tuning for music tasks.

The checks cover both grasp of music and generation of it. Knowing which tuning wins, and by how much, guides music AI design. It also shows where language skill fails to transfer. The work is a careful bake-off, not a hype claim. Its value is the clean comparison.
arxiv-2601-22964:
Yufei He and a large team present EvoClinician, a medical AI that learns as it works through a case. Most medical AI judges a complete patient file in one shot. Real diagnosis is a chain of questions and tests, chosen step by step while watching cost and time.

Their agent evolves at test time, improving its approach across many turns with one patient. Stepwise inquiry matches how good clinicians actually narrow down a disease. An agent that asks better questions could cut needless tests and reach answers sooner. Test-time evolution lets the agent adapt within a single case, rather than waiting for a future round of retraining.
arxiv-2601-23064:
Hari Krishna Gadi and six co-authors locate photos by learning geography's natural hierarchy. Visual geolocation predicts where an image was taken, a hard task at global scale. Older methods need huge image stores, ignore how places nest inside each other, or blur fine detail.

Their HierLoc embeds entities in hyperbolic space, a geometry that fits tree-like structure well. Continent, country, and city levels can then guide the search together. Better geolocation helps organize photo archives and verify where images were really shot. Hyperbolic embeddings fit geography's nesting naturally, since space in that geometry grows like a tree of regions.
arxiv-2601-23164:
Daniel Ezer, Alon Peled-Cohen, and Yishay Mansour study bandit learning where the reward rule itself is noisy. In their stochastic linear bandit model, each action's reward depends on a parameter vector. That vector is resampled independently, adding parameter noise on top of ordinary randomness.

Bandit algorithms must learn well despite never seeing a stable target. The model fits settings like ads or dosing, where each user's response rule differs. Theory for noisy parameters helps set realistic expectations for adaptive systems. Independent resampling of the parameter vector each round defines the noise model whose regret behavior the study analyzes.
arxiv-2603-01464:
Finding facts about a protein often means searching text and also reading the protein code itself. Congying Liu, Taihao Li, Ming Huang, and colleagues built a search agent for that dual task in 2026. Older agents search once, use text only, and get scored only on the final answer, so errors in the search path slip past.

Their agent, ProtRLSearch, searches in rounds and uses both the protein sequence and text to guide each step. Training rewards judge the search path as well as the final report. To test it, the team built a set of three thousand choice questions in three grades of hardness. Scores rose sharply at all three grades, which matters for work on disease-linked protein changes.
arxiv-2603-01664:
D. D. Solnyshkov, V. Paquelier, C. Balmisse, and G. Malpuech simulate black hole mergers in a lab fluid in this 2026 work. Analogue gravity uses fluids to mimic effects like Hawking radiation, but past setups held the fake hole fixed in place. A fixed hole cannot move, gain mass, or merge with another hole.

Their setting uses polariton condensates, where loss tied to speed makes each quantum vortex act like a small black hole. Such vortices can move through the fluid, so mergers enter reach at last. Two vortices alone cannot form a shared horizon, the edge past which flow cannot escape. Four or more can, and the shared edge size follows a simple geometric law. The team also clarifies how the true horizon differs from the apparent one here.
arxiv-2603-01864:
Alexander Prutsch, David Schinagl, and Horst Possegger predict traffic paths in a continuous stream, not as lone snapshots. Their 2026 work serves self-driving cars, which must forecast nearby road users with low delay. Snapshot methods treat each scene alone and waste what prior forecasts already learned.

Their lightweight method carries context forward from one time step to the next. Endpoints of prior forecasts act as anchors that guide the scene encoder to key context. That targeted encoding skips refinement rounds and segment-wise decoding, which cuts latency a lot. Tests show the context relay works as planned across consecutive steps. On a leading traffic benchmark, the method sets top streaming scores for both single and multi-agent cases. It does so while using far fewer resources than refinement-heavy rivals.
arxiv-2603-02064:
Tom Jacobs, Chao Zhou, and Rebekka Burkholz ask how the choice of trainer shapes learning in this 2026 theory paper. Trainers such as Adam update model weights in set ways. The authors group steep update rules under one flow model. That lens shows how update shape steers what a model learns and what it ignores.

In simple test networks, steep updates escaped stuck points and learned features well. Plain gradient steps needed huge step sizes to escape the same points. Such sizes are rare in real fine-tuning work. Tests backed the claim that escaping stuck points is a core hurdle. The authors also show that split weight decay, as in AdamW, steadies feature learning.
arxiv-2603-02164:
Sami Abuzakuk, Anne-Marie Kermarrec, Rafael Pires, and colleagues speed up vector search in this 2026 systems paper. Vector search finds the stored items closest to a query. Graph indexes do this well, but each query walks the same graph from set starts. Real query streams cluster, so much of that walk repeats past work.

Their add-on, CatapultDB, learns from that clustering and adds shortcut links. Each shortcut jumps a query from its region to a node that past queries visited often. The base graph and search code stay unchanged, so key features still work. In tests, speed rose up to about two and a half times at equal recall. The shortcuts also adapted well when query patterns shifted.
arxiv-2603-02364:
Kirill Borodin, Vasiliy Kudryavtsev, and colleagues test fake-speech detectors across languages in this 2026 paper. Synthetic speech can mimic real voices, and detectors are meant to catch it. Most detectors are built and tested on a few major languages. The team built a huge corpus to check whether they hold up worldwide.

Their corpus holds thousands of hours of fake speech in sixty-six languages. Twenty-four open text-to-speech systems generated the audio. Forty-five of the languages count as low-resource in their setup. Eleven public detectors were tested with thresholds set on outside data, so no local real speech was needed. Rejection rates varied sharply by language, even under controlled conditions. Language itself acts as a source of domain shift, they conclude.
arxiv-2603-02864:
Oktay Cebecioğlu and Salih Kibaroğlu derive cosmic expansion laws inside a gravity theory with built-in twist. Their 2026 paper uses AdS-gauged gravity, a gauge-style extension of general relativity with extra symmetry generators. The extra gauge field creates torsion, a twisting of spacetime geometry beyond ordinary curvature.

For a uniform, direction-free universe, they work out the modified Friedmann equations, the rules linking expansion to contents. The new terms allow steady de Sitter-like acceleration driven purely by the theory's structure, with no exotic matter added. The gauge field's moving parts act like an effective cosmological constant source. One regime mimics cosmic-string-like behavior, tying spacetime twist to a known cosmic defect picture.
arxiv-2603-03064:
Kiminad Mamo proposes a new way to read a hadron's gravitational properties from its entanglement. His 2026 paper defines the radius flow of a ball-shaped region's entropy inside a single hadron state, with the empty-space contribution subtracted. On a lattice, this quantity can in principle be measured, making it a practical observable rather than a formal curiosity.

In the continuum limit, changing the ball's radius acts like a rescaling, so the flow isolates the trace part of the energy-momentum response. Mamo organizes the flow into a surface term plus a remainder fitted by templates built from gravitational form factors. For sample nucleon inputs, the spin-zero and spin-two templates peak at clearly different radii. Lattice data could thus reveal which contribution controls the hadron's interior.
arxiv-2603-03364:
Jasem Hamoud, of the Moscow Institute of Physics and Technology, works out formulas for a graph measure called the Sombor index. Introduced in 2021, the index sums a degree-based score over every edge of a graph and is used to describe molecular and network structure. Simple shapes like paths and stars have known formulas, but layered hierarchical trees with uneven branching did not.

Hamoud derives a general recursive formula for a family of trees built on a central spine path, with pendant branches attached level after level. Branches on odd and even spine vertices follow different rules, one with a plain replication factor and one with an offset that propagates upward. The result pushes the theory of degree-based descriptors toward the complex, repeatedly built graphs where closed forms were missing.
arxiv-2603-03764:
Maximilian Weber, Daiki Suenaga, and Masayasu Harada dissect an exotic four-quark particle and find its energy budget upside down. The Tcc tetraquark is modeled as a heavy diquark bound to a light antidiquark. Intuition says exciting the motion between those two clusters should cost less than exciting the light pair inside the antidiquark. Solving the Schrödinger equation with a standard potential and a Gaussian expansion method, their 2026 paper finds the opposite.

The between-cluster excitation costs more, not less. The inversion traces to centrifugal force acting on the light degree of freedom, which inflates the wider motion's price. The same framework applied to the bottom-quark sibling and to two heavy baryons shows the identical behavior, marking the mechanism as robust rather than a fluke of one system. The result reshapes how modelers should budget mass in exotic hadrons.

burton-mission-gelele-vol1-1864:
Richard Burton went to Dahomey in West Africa in 1863 as Britain's envoy to King Gelele. Volume One of A Mission to Gelele, published in 1864, tells of the trip and the court. Burton was already famed for his pilgrimage to Mecca in disguise.

His orders were to press Gelele to end human sacrifice and the slave trade. Burton records the Fon kingdom's army, its famous women soldiers, the Amazons of Abomey, and court rites in close detail. He is frank, curious, and often harsh in judgment. The volume is firsthand ethnography from a kingdom few Europeans had entered.
burton-mission-gelele-vol2-1864:
Volume Two of Burton's Mission to Gelele completes his 1864 account of Dahomey. Burton had spent months at Gelele's court at Abomey, delivering Britain's message. What he saw there changed few British minds but filled two vivid volumes.

This volume treats the customs of the Fon people: festivals, sacrifices, oaths, and the palace guard of women. Burton adds notes on language, trade, and the slave ports of the coast. His mission failed in its aims, as he admits with dry irritation. The ethnography survived the diplomacy, and historians still mine his close, if biased, reporting. A route map and word lists support the main narrative.
bury-st-edmonds-tryal-witches-1664:
Amy Duny and Rose Cullender, two widows of Lowestoft, were tried at Bury St Edmunds in 1664 for bewitching children. A Tryal of Witches, printed in 1682, preserves the court record of their case. Judge Matthew Hale, one of the age's most prized legal minds, sat on the bench.

The report sets out the girls' fits, the toads and other signs, and the proof the jury heard. Hale let the case go to the jury, and the women were hanged. Lawyers and historians have argued over the trial ever since. It remains the most cited witch trial in English law.
busk-pithecoid-gibraltar-1864:
George Busk, an English surgeon and man of science, sent this short letter on a Gibraltar skull in July 1864. The skull had been dug from a quarry at Gibraltar in 1848 and left unheard of for years. Busk saw that it matched the famed Neanderthal skull from Germany.

He named the Gibraltar find ape like, or pithecoid, in the terms of his day. Its match with Neanderthal showed that odd skull was no freak or sick man, but a race. The letter is short, yet it gave the Neanderthal claim its key second proof.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-martin-1400-1: This 1913 reference piece on Martin — the Bohemian abbot. Francis Mershman outlines his abbacy. His rule steered the cloistered house. cia-0000012364:
