cieza-travels-peru-markham-part-1-1864:
Pedro Cieza de León came to the Americas as a teenage soldier and spent years walking Peru with a notebook. His Crónica del Perú of 1553, in Clements R Markham's Hakluyt Society translation of 1864, forms Part One of The Travels of Pedro de Cieza de León. The travels themselves cover 1532 to 1550, from first landfalls to the wars of the conquerors.

Cieza describes the Inca road system, cities, and peoples as the first European to survey them with care. He asked questions everywhere and wrote down what the Andean world told him. His chronicle became the great eyewitness record of the Inca conquest. Few sources bring a reader so close to Peru at the moment of its fall.
civil-rights-act-1964:
The 88th Congress passed the Civil Rights Act of 1964 after fierce debate. All eleven titles of the full text stand in this record. Segregation in public places is banned outright by its terms.

Hiring bias is outlawed across the land in the act's strong clauses. Hotels, theaters, lunch counters, and schools must open on equal terms. The law broke the legal back of Jim Crow in the South. Long filibusters and street marches both stand behind its hard passage. The century's greatest legislative win for equality reshaped daily American life at once. Its enforcement clauses gave the paper rights real teeth in court.
europmc-pmc10184764:
Kurwadkar and co-authors critically review PFAS chemicals in water and wastewater in a 2022 paper. PFAS are a large family of man-made chemicals prized for resisting heat, water, and grease. They persist in nature for very long periods, build up in living tissue, and have been tied to health risks.

The review maps where PFAS appear around the world and in what amounts. It covers how they spread through water systems and how treatment plants handle them. It also weighs removal methods. The paper is a full guide to the forever chemicals problem.
europmc-pmc10196664:
De Coster and Rademakers present NanoPack2, tools for checking and processing long-read DNA sequencing data at large scale, in a 2023 paper. Long-read machines from Oxford Nanopore and PacBio can read very long DNA stretches. As study groups grow to thousands of samples, scientists need faster software to judge data quality.

The paper describes new tools that summarize experiments and filter reads efficiently. The authors show the tools handle population-scale data with modest computing power. The work supports the quality control that big genome projects depend on. It is freely available to labs.
europmc-pmc10767964:
The CNCB-NGDC Members and Partners gave the 2024 update of the National Genomics Data Center of China. The centre runs a family of data banks for gene research world-wide. Data from many omics fields pour in at a record pace. The centre archives that flood, merges it, and adds curated value.

Fresh banks headline this round, the report notes. New sets cover protists, bacteria, and plants, from soy to a plant pan-genome. Trait and disease banks grew too, with sets on fatty liver and virus parts in human DNA. Staff also upgraded core banks and kept smooth data swaps with world partners. All sets sit free at the centre's public site.
europmc-pmc11332364:
He and colleagues show that a stress protein protects against liver cancer by blocking iron-driven cell death in this 2023 study. Liver cancer is a leading cause of cancer death, tied to viral hepatitis, fatty liver disease, and alcohol damage. All three stress the cell's protein-folding compartment and trigger cell death and inflammation. One stress effector, ATF4, had an unknown role in this cancer.

In stress-prone mice fed a high-fat diet, removing ATF4 from liver cells worsened fatty liver cancer, they found. ATF4 switches on a transporter called SLC7A11, also known as xCT. That transporter blocks ferroptosis, the iron-driven death path. Restoring the transporter in ATF4-deficient liver cells restored protection. The authors conclude ATF4 suppresses liver tumour formation through this axis. The work names a concrete stress-to-death pathway in the liver.
europmc-pmc11351064:
Lam and a large panel of Canadian experts update clinical guidelines for treating major depression in adults in this 2024 document. Major depressive disorder is a leading cause of disability, and treatment evidence has advanced since the network's 2016 guidelines. CANMAT, Canada's national network for mood and anxiety treatments, convened academic clinicians and patient partners to revise the advice.

The editorial group ran a systematic review focused on reviews and meta-analyses published since 2016. Recommendations are organised by lines of treatment, meaning the order in which options should be tried. Each rests on graded evidence plus expert consensus on safety, tolerability, and feasibility. The guidelines span eight topics in question-and-answer format. They map a care journey from assessment through treatment choice to preventing recurrence. Patient partners and peer reviewers revised the drafts.
europmc-pmc1241864:
Pope and co-authors studied air particles, heart rhythm, and inflammation in 2004. Eighty-eight elderly subjects lived in three Utah communities. Each wore heart monitors for 24-hour sessions and gave blood. Fine particle levels were matched to each session.

A rise of 100 micrograms per cubic meter in fine particles brought a clear change. A key heart rhythm variability measure fell by about 35 milliseconds. Blood markers of inflammation were tested alongside the rhythm data. Pope probes two suspected paths from dirty air to heart harm. Autonomic control shifts and body-wide inflammation are the candidates.
europmc-pmc1277864:
Barr and co-authors charted urine creatinine across the United States population in 2005. Creatinine adjustment corrects urine tests for sample dilution. The practice assumed fairly uniform creatinine levels. Diverse national samples broke that assumption.

Data covered 22,245 participants in a national health survey. Creatinine ranges differed across demographic groups. Those differences can misclassify exposure status for individuals. The authors show how adjustment choices shift study results. Barr recommends regression-based adjustment over simple division. Their ranges give body monitoring studies a firmer footing. The data came from a big national health survey of the late 1980s and 1990s. Men and women of all ages and groups took part in the count.
europmc-pmc1332664:
Alonso-Magdalena and co-authors showed bisphenol A disrupts insulin control in mice in 2006. Pancreatic beta cells store and release insulin to manage blood sugar. BPA mimics the hormone estradiol in the body. Adult mice got a single low dose of either compound.

A dose of 10 micrograms per kilogram rapidly lowered blood sugar. Plasma insulin rose at the same time. Longer exposure raised beta-cell insulin content within two days. After four days, mice showed chronic high insulin and altered tolerance tests. Alonso-Magdalena links environmental estrogens to insulin resistance and diabetes risk.
europmc-pmc1413964:
Shaky RNA samples can ruin gene tests before they start. Schroeder and co-authors built a fair grading method in 2006. Labs had long judged RNA quality by eye, using a rough ratio of two RNA bands. That old check proved patchy and hard to repeat between users.

The team fed a large set of machine traces into a learning method. It picked the trace traits that best foretold decay. The result is a single score, the RNA integrity number, or RIN. Schroeder shows the score is steady and free of user bias. It gives labs one shared yardstick for sample quality.
europmc-pmc1783664:
Friedrich, Adhikari and Beyene tackled in 2007 a quiet inconsistency in how study results are pooled. A meta-analysis combines many trials into one overall estimate. Trials with zero events in both the treated and the control group are kept when effects are stated as a risk difference, but dropped for relative risk or odds ratios.

The authors reran three published meta-analyses with and without those zero-event trials. Adding them pulled the pooled effect closer to no effect, narrowed its confidence interval, and reduced differences between studies. For relative risk and odds ratios the shifts stayed small, even when such trials were most of the set. For risk difference the shifts grew large. They urge reviewers to include the trials whatever measure is used.
europmc-pmc1865564:
Grönke, Kühnlein and co-authors showed in 2007 that fruit flies run two fat-burning systems in parallel. Storage fat sits in droplets inside cells, and the machinery that moves it is shared between insects and mammals. The team knocked out the receptor for adipokinetic hormone, the fly's main fat-mobilizing signal.

Flies lacking that receptor built up fat over time and could not release it quickly when needed. The defect matched loss of Brummer, a fat-cutting enzyme akin to the main mammalian one. Losing both systems at once caused extreme obesity and fully blocked fast fat release. Either system alone could partly cover for the other. The dual control keeps body fat steady across the fly's life and lets it respond to sudden energy demand.
europmc-pmc1885964:
Reznick, Shulman and co-authors reported in 2007 that aging dulls a key energy sensor in rat muscle. The sensor is AMPK, a protein kinase that boosts fat burning and orders new mitochondria, the cell's power plants. Aging already brings weaker mitochondria, messy fat handling inside cells, and insulin resistance.

In old rats, a drug that switches AMPK on, and exercise itself, both activated the muscle sensor far less than in young rats. Long-term stimulation through diet also built fewer new mitochondria in old muscle. The blunted response centered on the alpha2 form of the enzyme. The authors argue that fading AMPK activity helps explain why mitochondria falter with age. Restoring that signal is a candidate route to protect muscle metabolism in older animals and perhaps in people.
europmc-pmc2124964: A medical paper on complement fixation in syphilis with spirochaeta culture antigens. The pox test. This article preserves that serology. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later.
europmc-pmc2125164: A medical paper with a further study of nitrogen retention in the blood in experimental acute nephritis. The kidney's nitrogen. This article preserves that nephrology. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
europmc-pmc2128064: A medical paper on physiological causes for the varied character of stasis bile. The stagnant bile. This article preserves that physiology. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
europmc-pmc2128464: A medical paper with studies on virulence, the increase in virulence in vitro of a pneumococcus strain. The strengthened germ. This article preserves that bacteriology. Later readers can locate it. It holds its historical place.
europmc-pmc2128564: A medical paper on methemoglobin formation by sterile pneumococcus culture filtrates. The brown blood again. This article preserves that bacteriology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2131164: A medical paper on local progression with spontaneous regression of tuberculosis in the bone marrow. The marrow TB. This article preserves that pathology. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past.
europmc-pmc2131464: A medical paper on cholesterol and cholesterol ester content of bovine colostrum. The cow milk's fat. This article preserves that biochemistry. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
europmc-pmc2131764: A medical paper on the chloride content of the tissues of the dog after experimental gastrointestinal procedures. The dog's salt. This article preserves that biochemistry. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
europmc-pmc2180264: A medical paper with immunological studies with herpes virus, considering the herpes-encephalitis link. The cold sore virus. This article preserves that virology. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact.
europmc-pmc2363864:
Fallowfield, Ratcliffe, Jenkins, and Saul measured how often cancer doctors miss mental illness in 2001. Depression and anxiety are common in cancer and, untreated, tend to persist. The team wanted a hard number for how much of this suffering goes unseen in clinics.

Across 34 UK cancer centres, 2,297 patients filled in a short mental health questionnaire before their appointment. Doctors then rated each patient's distress. The questionnaires flagged likely psychiatric problems in 36.4% of patients, but doctors spotted only about 29% of those cases, while correctly clearing about 85% of healthy patients. Overall, the wrong call was probably made for 797 patients. The authors said doctors need communication training to draw problems out, plus clear routes to refer patients for psychological help.
europmc-pmc2495064:
Elliott and colleagues measured how common disease-causing mitochondrial DNA changes are in the general population in this 2008 study. Mitochondria are the cell's energy producers, and faults in their small loop of DNA cause genetic disease. The team screened newborn cord blood for ten known harmful point mutations.

They tested 3,168 samples from consecutive live births, plus matched blood from the mothers. Fifteen babies, which is 0.54 percent of the sample, carried one of the mutations, and nearly all had inherited it rather than gaining it fresh. The commonest fault was the change known as m.3243A to G. The authors conclude that at least one in 200 healthy people carries a mutation that could cause disease in the children of female carriers.
europmc-pmc2557064:
Baird and colleagues introduced in 2008 a cheap way to find DNA differences and map genes by sequencing short DNA tags. Genetic mapping needs many markers called SNPs, single-letter DNA differences, but finding them was slow and costly. Their method, RAD sequencing, cuts DNA at fixed points with enzymes and reads only the DNA beside each cut.

With less than half of one run on a sequencing machine, they found more than 13,000 SNPs. They also mapped three traits in two model organisms. One mapping pinpointed the gene behind lost armour plates in stickleback fish, using barcoded samples pooled together. They also mapped a pelvic reduction in fish and a mutation in a fungus. Choosing different cutting enzymes lets users tune how dense their markers are.
europmc-pmc2584664:
Bihari and colleagues worked out in 2008 a reliable recipe for dispersing nanoparticles in the salty, protein-rich fluids used in biology experiments. Nanoparticles clump into coarse agglomerates in such solutions, which ruins toxicity and imaging studies. The team used titanium dioxide particles and varied the ultrasound energy, the preparation order, and which stabiliser to add, checking sizes by light scattering and electron microscopy.

A specific ultrasound dose broke the clumps apart, and more energy gained nothing. The winning order was to sonicate in water first, add the stabiliser second, and add buffered salt solution last. About 1.5 milligrams per millilitre of serum albumin, from human, cow, or mouse, kept dispersions stable for at least a week. The method also worked for zinc oxide, silver, silica, carbon nanotubes, and diesel particles.
europmc-pmc2634664:
Muirhead and co-authors published in 2009 the third large analysis of deaths and cancers among British radiation workers. The group followed more than 174,000 people listed in a national registry, with records running to 2001. For the first time, the analysis also used cancer registration data, not deaths alone.

Overall, the workers died less often than the general public, a pattern the authors call a healthy worker effect. Within the group, though, deaths and new cases rose as the radiation dose rose. This held for leukemia other than one slow type, and for cancers as a whole. The size of the rise matched estimates drawn from Japanese atomic bomb survivors. A weaker rise in deaths from heart and circulation disease might reflect smoking instead of radiation.
europmc-pmc2649164:
Smedley and co-authors presented in 2009 BioMart, a single doorway to many biological databases. Biologists often need to ask complex questions across several data stores at once. Each store had its own search page to learn, and copying results between sites by hand wasted hours.

BioMart lets users build a rich query once and run it across stores held in different countries as if they were one. A query can then be saved and rerun with one click, which suits large routine jobs. The system plugs into tools scientists already use, such as R-based analysis packs and pathway drawing software. Big projects including Ensembl and UniProt run on it. The paper walks through real tasks, like picking gene variants for a screening study.
europmc-pmc2654964:
Hughes and co-authors compared in 2009 the daily gene rhythms of mouse liver with those of cells grown in dishes. The body clock switches genes on and off in roughly 24-hour cycles in most tissues. The team sampled gene activity at very fine time intervals, far denser than earlier studies, to catch rhythms others might have missed.

The liver showed a surprise: besides the daily cycle, many genes rose and fell every 12 or 8 hours, at the second and third harmonics of the day. These faster waves appeared in heart, kidney, and lung too. Dish-grown cells showed almost none of them, and far fewer cycling genes overall, by about a hundred-fold. Restricting feeding times wiped the harmonics out. Clock studies based only on cells, the authors warn, miss much of what the clock does in a living animal.
europmc-pmc2661364:
Hidalgo and colleagues built in 2009 a network of human diseases from the medical histories of more than 30 million patients. Diseases that often strike the same people are linked, forming a map of how illnesses cluster and follow one another. The team released the map, called the Phenotypic Disease Network, as a public resource.

Clear patterns emerged from the map. Patients tended to develop new diseases close to ones they already had. The paths of spread differed between men and women, and between ethnic groups. People whose diseases sat at busy hubs of the map tended to die sooner than those with lonely, rarely linked diseases. Diseases that usually came late in a chain were also more connected and more deadly. Disease, the authors argue, advances along this map like traffic along roads.
europmc-pmc2717464:
Dubin and co-authors tested in 2009 whether raising blood pressure with norepinephrine, a drug that tightens blood vessels, improves tiny-vessel flow in septic shock. Septic shock is a severe infection state where pressure falls and organs starve despite a strong heartbeat. Doctors often aim above a mean pressure of sixty-five, assuming higher pressure means better flow to tissues.

In twenty ventilated patients, raising mean pressure in steps to seventy-five and then eighty-five raised heart workload but did not improve flow under the tongue. The share of open capillaries, the smallest vessels, stayed flat, and perfused capillary density trended down. Patients who started worst tended to worsen most, which warns that higher targets may harm some.
europmc-pmc2725864:
N'Guessan, Corbel, Akogbéto, and Rowland tested in 2007 whether treated mosquito nets and indoor spraying still control malaria in a pyrethroid-resistant area of Benin. Pyrethroids are the insecticide class used on nets and for wall spraying across Africa. Resistance through the kdr mechanism, a nerve mutation, had become common in the local Anopheles gambiae mosquitoes.

In experimental hut trials against the resistant population, both nets and spraying performed poorly compared with their known effect on sensitive mosquitoes. Mosquito survival was high and malaria control was weakened, which suggests these tools may no longer work well in such areas. The results argue for new insecticide classes where kdr resistance is widespread.
europmc-pmc2731764:
Henderson and co-authors tested in 2009 AC-1202, a ketogenic compound taken by mouth, in a ninety-day trial for mild to moderate Alzheimer's disease. Brains in Alzheimer's use glucose poorly in specific regions early on. Ketone bodies, made when glucose is scarce, offer the brain an alternate fuel that it can still burn.

In one hundred fifty-two patients on normal diets and usual Alzheimer's drugs, the compound raised a blood ketone marker within hours. Thinking scores favored the compound over placebo at day forty-five in all analysis groups. Among patients without the APOE4 risk gene form, the benefit was larger and still present at day ninety. A stronger ketone response also tracked with better scores.
europmc-pmc2763764:
Surjushe, Vasani, and Saple gave in 2008 a short review of Aloe vera, a plant long used for health, beauty, and skin care and now common in cosmetics. The plant has served medicine for millennia across Greece, Egypt, India, Mexico, Japan, and China, from royal beauty routines to treating soldiers' wounds. Its gel, latex, and rind layers carry distinct active compounds.

They summarize the plant's properties, how its compounds are thought to act, and its clinical uses in dermatology and beyond. Controlled trial evidence, though, is thin for many claimed uses. They note plainly that rigorous trials must still test whether it truly works, rather than relying on tradition. The review also traces the plant's history and its anatomy, including the water-rich inner gel that holds most active ingredients.
europmc-pmc2784464:
Stommel and Schoenborn examined in 2009 how accurate body mass index values are when they rest on self-reported height and weight. They used the national NHANES and NHIS surveys from 2001 to 2006. Interviews gather such figures cheaply, but people misreport them, so the error pattern needed mapping. They compared self-reported values against physical measurements and hunted for traits that predict the gaps.

Self-reported BMI ran too high at the low end of the scale, below about twenty-two. It ran too low at the high end, especially above twenty-eight. Errors also varied with age, sex, and ethnic background. Adjusting for those traits narrowed the mistakes but still misclassified some obese people as merely overweight. Health risk estimates, however, came out virtually the same from self-reported and measured values. Corrected self-reports, they conclude, can serve risk estimation well.
europmc-pmc2827364:
Tan, Cang, Ma, Petrillo, and Liu reviewed in 2010 a new family of cancer drugs that block enzymes called histone deacetylases, or HDACs. These enzymes remove small chemical tags from the proteins that spool DNA, which can silence tumor suppressor genes, the genes that hold cancer back. Blocking them can switch those genes back on.

One blocker, vorinostat, had already won United States approval for a skin lymphoma after standard treatments failed. More than eleven agents were in at least eighty clinical trials, covering blood cancers and solid tumors, alone and in drug combinations. Early results showed real promise in several cancers, and the review maps which agents reached which trial stage.
europmc-pmc2846864:
Daley, Abbott, Doyle, Nader, and Larson pulled together three decades of research in 2010 comparing beef from grass-fed and grain-fed cattle. Consumer interest in grass-fed beef had grown fast, raising questions about whether its fat profile and antioxidant content truly differ. The review weighs measured fatty acid and nutrient differences alongside taste and cooking trade-offs.

Grass-based diets clearly raised conjugated linoleic acid, its precursor trans vaccenic acid, and omega-3 fats per gram of fat. Total saturated fat matched grain-fed beef, but grass-fed carried more harmless stearic acid and less of the cholesterol-raising kinds. Grass-fed beef also packed more vitamin A and E precursors plus protective enzymes, ran leaner overall, and brought a distinct grass flavor and yellowish fat.
europmc-pmc2874364:
Mugnier, Poirel, Naas, and Nordmann traced in 2010 how a resistance gene that defeats last-resort antibiotics spread around the world. The gene, blaOXA-23, makes an enzyme that breaks carbapenems, drugs kept for the worst infections. Its carrier, Acinetobacter baumannii, haunts intensive care units with pneumonia and blood infections that resist many drugs.

First found in Scotland, the gene has since been reported on every inhabited continent. It travels inside a mobile DNA package flanked by insertion sequences that also switch it on strongly, and a harmless relative species appears to be its original source. Hospital clones carrying it match across countries, which shows patients and equipment move it. Stopping the spread will be hard, the authors warn plainly.
europmc-pmc2898064:
Wu, Feng, and Stein built in 2010 a human protein interaction network based on functional links and showed it can spotlight cancer genes. Rather than physical contacts alone, their network connects proteins that work in the same pathways, drawn from curated pathway knowledge and expanded by prediction. Projecting gene lists onto such a network lets patterns emerge that single-gene ranking misses.

Applied to cancer datasets, the network pulled out candidate driver genes that sit amid known cancer players, even when the candidates' own signals were modest. Network neighbors of a suspicious gene proved strong evidence in its favor. The resource and its cancer workflow were released for other analysts, offering a route to interpret the flood of tumor sequencing results gene by gene.
europmc-pmc3144464:
David Habier and colleagues extended a family of statistical methods for predicting breeding value from DNA in a 2011 paper in BMC Bioinformatics. Breeders now score animals at tens of thousands of DNA markers, most with no effect, and the methods must guess how many markers matter. Two new variants learn that share from the data instead of fixing it beforehand.

In simulations and in records from North American Holstein bulls, one variant gave steadier guesses about how many trait genes exist, and it ran faster than its sibling. Milk and fat yield appeared driven by larger-effect genes than protein yield or cell counts. Prediction accuracy was similar across all variants, so the authors recommend the faster, self-tuning one for routine breeding work.
europmc-pmc3185064:
Ewan Gibb and colleagues compiled the first atlas of long non-coding RNAs across human tissues and cancers in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. These long RNA copies make no protein and were once dismissed as genome dark matter, yet mounting work gives them real jobs in cell control. Nobody had charted them comprehensively, so the team mined hundreds of gene-tag libraries.

Parsing tens of millions of short tags, they profiled the RNAs across more than two dozen normal tissues and nearly twenty cancers. Normal tissues each ran a distinctive, tightly tissue-specific pattern. Cancers broke those patterns extensively, with widespread abnormal levels. The atlas gives cancer researchers a first map of where these RNAs act and which ones go wrong.
europmc-pmc3219664:
Denny Borsboom and colleagues proposed a network view of mental disorders in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. People with one disorder often have another, and the usual explanation, a single hidden cause for each diagnosis, struggles with that overlap. The team instead modeled symptoms themselves as a connected web, using the symptom lists of the DSM-IV diagnostic manual.

Half of all listed symptoms turned out to be connected, and the web had a small-world shape: tight local clusters linked by short paths. Distances between disorders in the web predicted real-world comorbidity rates. Simulations of depression and generalized anxiety reproduced population statistics well. The authors argue disorders are inherently complex systems, which may explain why simple genetic or brain-based explanations keep falling short.
europmc-pmc3222064:
Lucienne Cardoso and colleagues examined whether waiting for an intensive care bed harms critically ill patients, in this 2011 cohort study in Critical Care. When demand exceeds beds, patients wait in other wards, and delay had been blamed for worse outcomes. The team followed adults admitted to one Brazilian unit through 2005, comparing immediate admissions with delayed ones.

Of four hundred and one patients, about two-thirds waited for a bed. Mortality rose significantly with delay, and the authors estimate roughly three in ten intensive care deaths were attributable to the wait. Each additional hour of waiting was independently linked to a higher risk of death, even after accounting for age, diagnosis, and severity scores. The findings argue that getting patients into intensive care early saves lives.
europmc-pmc3234264:
Martin Ganal and a large consortium built a high-density genotyping array for maize in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Such arrays, which read tens of thousands of single-letter DNA differences at once, power genetic mapping and breeding. The team selected markers mainly from genes, spread evenly across the maize genome, and tested the array on diverse breeding material.

Nearly fifty thousand markers proved reliable, with low failure rates across North American and European inbred lines, crosses, and wild teosinte relatives. The team then genotyped two mapping populations to build dense linkage maps carrying tens of thousands of markers. Comparing those maps with the reference genome assembly exposed several regions where the assembly's order looks wrong, and placed markers missing from it. The array is offered as a durable resource for maize genetics and breeding.
europmc-pmc3241564:
Antoine Lecharpentier and colleagues searched the blood of lung cancer patients for circulating tumor cells caught mid-transition, in this 2011 paper in the British Journal of Cancer. Tumor cells that shed into the blood drive metastasis and carry prognostic information. A process called epithelial-mesenchymal transition is thought to prepare them, but direct evidence in patients' circulating cells was scarce.

Using a filtration method that traps tumor cells by size, the team stained cells from six patients. All had non-small cell lung cancer that had already spread. Every patient carried tumor cells, singly and in clusters, that strongly displayed both an epithelial marker and the mesenchymal marker vimentin. Cells bearing only the mesenchymal marker were rarer, and none bore only the epithelial one. The authors present these hybrid cells as the first direct evidence of the transition in this disease.
europmc-pmc3254664:
Anna Protasio and a large team delivered a thoroughly rebuilt genome for the human blood fluke Schistosoma mansoni, in this 2012 paper in PLoS Biology. The parasite causes schistosomiasis, a disease affecting millions in poorer countries, and its earlier draft genome was highly fragmented. Using two sequencing technologies on clonal worms, the team upgraded the assembly and re-examined its genes.

The new assembly collapsed the sequence into under nine hundred scaffolds, with most bases placed on chromosomes. Sequencing the parasite's RNA at four life stages refined the gene catalog, cutting the predicted gene count while extensively revising nearly half of the genes. The team mapped expression changes for more than nine thousand genes across the life cycle and found a splicing trick, trans-splicing, at work in at least a tenth of genes. All data feed two public databases for parasite researchers.
europmc-pmc3314964:
Scheres set out a cleaner statistical way to build three dimensional structures from electron microscope images, in a 2012 paper. The method, called cryo-EM, photographs huge numbers of frozen particles and averages them into a structure. The images are extremely noisy, so the math can accidentally sculpt noise into fake detail, especially near the sharpness limit.

Traditionally, researchers filtered their maps by hand picked rules, which let personal judgment creep in. Scheres instead frames the whole task in Bayesian terms, a style of statistics that weighs the data against prior expectations in a principled way. The approach builds in smoothing automatically and gives an honest estimate of sharpness. Tested on real data, it produced more trustworthy structures than standard methods and could even spot small hidden groups of differing particles.
europmc-pmc3315464:
Sun and colleagues worked out how warm weather makes young plant stems stretch, in a 2012 genetics study. Seedlings of the small plant arabidopsis grow tall, thin stems in heat, a change thought to help the plant cope. Two players were already suspected, a gene switching protein called PIF4 and the growth hormone auxin, but how they connected was unclear.

The team showed that heat raises the activity of both PIF4 and a hormone making gene named YUCCA8. PIF4 binds directly to that gene's control region and switches it on, raising hormone levels in the plant. Plants with a broken YUCCA8 gene barely stretched in heat, even when PIF4 was overactive. A second mutation that blocks hormone signaling did the same. The results draw a straight line from temperature sensing to hormone production.
europmc-pmc3317864:
Wiltsey Stirman and colleagues reviewed what research says about keeping new health programs alive after their launch, in a 2012 article. Getting proven practices into clinics has drawn heavy study, but far less is known about whether those practices survive once the launch support ends. The team gathered one hundred twenty five studies that followed programs past their first rollout.

Most studies looked backward rather than following programs forward, and about half relied on what staff said about themselves. Few checked quality or faithfulness to the original program with hard measures, and among those that did, only a small number found full survival. Programs also quietly changed over time, a topic barely studied. Workplace setting, staff capacity, everyday processes, and the design of the program itself all shaped survival. The authors call for clearer definitions and studies planned from the start.
europmc-pmc3318764:
Yeung and Summerfield reviewed how people judge their own decisions, in a 2012 article on the science of self monitoring. People often sense their confidence in a choice and notice their own mistakes, even with nobody telling them the right answer. This self knowledge, called metacognition, helps people avoid repeating errors and stops them wasting effort on shaky choices.

The review brings together two research lines that grew up apart, one on confidence judgments and one on error spotting. Both, the authors argue, rest on extra processing that happens after a decision, inside the same systems that made it. That shared machinery explains why confidence and accuracy usually rise and fall together. The authors note that nearly all the evidence comes from quick, simple lab choices, and question how well the ideas stretch to long, real world decisions.
europmc-pmc3323564:
Waldenström, Gennebäck, Hellman, and Ronquist showed that heart muscle cells send out tiny parcels carrying genetic messages, in a 2012 study. Many cells release such membrane wrapped parcels, which can influence the cells that receive them. The team collected parcels shed by mouse heart cells grown in the lab and examined them under powerful microscopes and by sorting instruments.

Inside, they found hundreds of kinds of RNA messages forming a connected biological network, plus hundreds of distinct stretches of chromosomal DNA. The parcels could deliver DNA into connective tissue cells, reaching even the cell nucleus. Receiving cells changed the activity of hundreds of genes afterward. The authors propose that heart cells use these parcels, which they nickname cardiosomes, to coordinate metabolism with their neighbors.
europmc-pmc3384264:
Stuhrmann, Suslow, and Dannlowski reviewed brain-scan studies in 2011 on how people with major depression read emotion on faces. Theories of depression predict a bias toward sad or threatening expressions. The team gathered twenty-five functional MRI studies comparing acutely depressed patients with healthy controls.

Patients showed a shared pattern of overreaction to negative faces and underreaction to happy ones. The amygdala and several face and feeling regions drove the effect, with further changes in cingulate and frontal areas. Results varied in some frontal regions, likely because tasks and patient groups differed. Whether the pattern marks a passing state or a lasting trait, they say, needs studies of recovered patients.
europmc-pmc3393664:
Eaton led twelve modeling teams in 2012 to compare forecasts of how HIV treatment itself could prevent new infections in South Africa. Each model had tackled slightly different questions before, making their answers hard to compare. Here all twelve ran the same standard treatment scenarios and reported the same measures.

Under an ambitious scenario, the models agreed new infections would fall by roughly a third to a half within eight years. Long-range forecasts spread much wider, leaving deep doubt about wiping HIV out with treatment alone over four decades. Seven models judged that today's real rollout already cuts incidence meaningfully below the no-treatment path. The exercise shows where modelers agree and where honest uncertainty remains.
europmc-pmc3428864:
Nik-Zainal and a large team reconstructed the life histories of twenty-one breast cancers in 2012 from the mutations written into their genomes. A cancer evolves as cell families replace one another under shifting pressures, and the genome keeps the diary. The team built algorithms to read that diary in order.

Mutational processes, they found, change across a cancer's lifespan, with several switching on late yet adding huge variation. Most mutations sit in only a fraction of tumor cells, showing rich branching, but every tumor kept one dominant family making up over half its cells. That family's takeoff seems to need hundreds or thousands of mutations first, and its expansion may be the final step that brings the cancer to notice.
europmc-pmc3443064:
French and colleagues demonstrated a systematic way in 2012 to build behavior-change programs that push medical evidence into everyday practice. The gap between what studies prove and what clinics do is notorious, yet intervention design lacked a standard recipe. Their four-step method leans on a framework cataloguing the domains that drive professional behavior.

The steps ask who must act differently, which barriers and enablers theory points to, which techniques and delivery modes could shift them, and how change will be measured. They illustrate with a program to improve back-pain care in primary practice, delivered through two interactive workshops plus a DVD. Outcome measures were chosen to expose the mechanisms of change. Other teams, they argue, can reuse the scaffold.

europmc-pmc3621664: South Africa got an HIV lifespan study. This 2013 paper tracks lifespan gains on HIV drugs. The authors reveal the gains. Their work guides policy. Johnson's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped treatment access.
europmc-pmc3627464: Drugs got microneedle patches. This 2012 paper builds jelly microneedles for drug delivery. The authors reveal the patches. Their work guides pharma. Donnelly's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. It shaped painless vaccines. The study shaped drug delivery.
europmc-pmc3629564: Alu elements got a splicing guard. This 2013 paper shows the hnRNP C protein blocks Alu misuse. The authors reveal the guard. Their work guides genetics. Zarnack's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic. The study shaped gene research.
europmc-pmc3637064: Gene lists got Enrichr. This 2013 paper introduces Enrichr for gene-list analysis. The authors reveal the tool. Their work spread through labs. Chen's team led the work. It is open source. The paper is widely cited. Labs use it worldwide.
europmc-pmc3655264: AP2 got a shape-change study. This 2010 paper shows AP2 shape change couples docking to cargo. The authors reveal the change. Their work guides cell biology. Jackson's team led the work. The paper is widely cited. It is a classic.

fossil-man-abbeville-again-1864:
An unsigned piece in the Anthropological Review took up the Abbeville fossil man row once more in 1864. Its blunt title ends with the word 'Again.' The row dealt with a jaw found at Moulin-Quignon, near Abbeville in France, the year past.

Fresh bones kept turning up, and each new find fed the fight on both sides. The piece tells where the row stood, what was claimed, and what was doubted or charged as fraud. It shows a key case of man's deep age stuck in doubt, in the words of its own time.
french-art-of-distillation-1664:
John French teaches distillation in The Art of Distillation, from 1664, a great English manual of the craft. Stills draw out the virtues of plants, minerals, and animals drop by drop. Waters, oils, and spirits for medicine fill his practical, workmanlike pages of recipes and furnace lore for the laboratory.

French writes for the working chemist of the seventeenth century here. Herbs for the sick, metals for the seeker, all pass through his alembics. The book blends alchemy's aims with a tradesman's plain method throughout. It served as the chemist's handbook before chemistry had the name, a bridge between the spagyric art of Paracelsus and the science that followed.
frus-1861-d164:
William Preston wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 25 May 1861. Preston had lately held the Madrid post for the United States. The dispatch is document 164 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Preston's letter comes from the handover season in Spain, as Schurz came to take the post. An outgoing envoy's report could still guide the new chief at home. His May page adds a Kentucky voice to the Spanish file of 1861. Preston, a Kentuckian of the old school, knew Spain from his years at its court. A clear thread in the whole volume runs through the hands of such aides.
frus-1861-d264:
30 October 1861 brought James Shepherd Pike a fresh letter from Secretary Seward in Washington. The printed record keeps it as Document 264 in the President's message volume for 1861. The letter comes from the autumn of the war's first year, a time when each foreign capital watched the war with care.

Outbound letters like this one told the envoy what line to take and what to report back. Read in order with its neighbors, it shows diplomacy as daily work rather than grand speeches. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d64:
From Washington on 29 July 1861, William H. Seward addressed a letter to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 64 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

A week after Bull Run, Seward's aim abroad was plain: no panic, no threats, no open door. This late July letter carries that aim to London. It shows a Secretary chastened by defeat at home but steady in his handling of the most risky front of the war. A week of such letters rebuilt abroad the calm that Bull Run had broken at home. Calm rebuilt abroad was worth regiments to a cause that had lost its first battle.
frus-1862-d164:
Dated 20 October 1862, Document 164 is a Seward dispatch to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It was printed in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, the State Department's yearly account of its work abroad during the Civil War.

The tempo of the London mail tells its own story: letters every few days, each one short and businesslike. Through them Washington tracked British shipyards building warships for the South, a sore point Adams raised again and again. This dispatch belongs to that grinding, vital strand of the wartime correspondence. Adams held the London post from 1861 to 1868, the longest run of any Union envoy in Europe.
frus-1862-d264:
William H. Seward, as Secretary of State, opened April with a dispatch to William L. Dayton in Paris dated 1 April 1862, printed as Document 264 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

April 1862 would bring Shiloh's slaughter and the fall of New Orleans. Events that cut both ways in foreign eyes: proof of Union power and proof of the war's cost. Seward wrote at the month's start with his usual aim, to keep France from giving the South the one thing it lacked, a great-power friend. The letter starts the spring run of the Paris file. Southern agents were active in Paris too, seeking loans, ships, and friends at court.
frus-1862-d364:
Henri Mercier, the French minister in Washington, wrote to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 16 May 1862, in a letter printed as Document 364 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume.

Mercier wrote three weeks after his return from Richmond, where his April visit had stirred Union anger and Confederate hope. Relations between the minister and the Department were strained that spring. A letter from his hand in mid-May belongs to the repair and testing that followed. Both men were sounding out how much trust the channel still held. The channel, like the British one, stayed open and civil through the whole of 1862.
frus-1862-d464:
On 25 August 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to George Perkins Marsh, the American minister to Italy at Turin. The instruction is Document 464 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Marsh had spent the summer reporting Italian goodwill, and Seward's late-August order reached him as Union armies fell back in Virginia. Italy's government, still securing its new unity, had every reason to wish the Union well and little power to help it. Instructions to friendly but minor courts still mattered: they kept sympathy alive and denied Confederate agents any opening. The dispatch shows Seward tending the whole map of Europe, not just its great capitals, in a hard month.
frus-1862-d564:
On 14 January 1862 Henry Shelton Sanford reported from Brussels to Secretary of State William H. Seward, five days after his previous dispatch. The report is Document 564 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Sanford's quick second letter of the year is characteristic: he wrote when he had something, not on a fixed day. Brussels gave him early word of moves in London and Paris, and January 1862 was full of moves, as Europe digested the Trent settlement. His reports fed Seward's sense of where the real dangers lay. The Belgian file's value lies in this flow of well-placed observation, offered by a minister who treated information as the whole of his job.
frus-1862-d64:
15 May 1862 is the date on a dispatch from Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London to William H. Seward. The printed record keeps it as Document 64 in the 1862 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs volume. By then, in the spring of 1862, a year into the war, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

The text is the view from the post abroad: local mood, official talk, and the envoy's own judgment. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1862-d664:
On 1 August 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote straight to the ministers for foreign affairs of Japan. Most letters in this file went through the American legation; this one speaks government to government. It is document 664 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Direct notes like this one carried the formal voice of the United States to the shogun's court. They dealt in the courtesies and claims that held the young tie between the two lands in place. The letter is a rare formal piece in a file of working mail. It shows Washington treating Japan as a full partner in talks, not a mere port of call.
frus-1863p1-d164:
On 22 April 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent this second letter of the day to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 164 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

The mate to a late-April letter held the day's last point for the London brief. Seward's pairs, all through this file, let each claim stand on its own page. This one closes both the pair and the three-day run behind it. Read in line, the run shows a secretary who treated the British file as the war's second front. He staffed it with paper as others staffed forts.
frus-1863p1-d264:
On 20 August 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, sent this dispatch from London to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It stands as document 264 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1863. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

Mail crossed the Atlantic by steamship, taking roughly ten days or more each way. News in a dispatch like this one was already old when Seward read it, yet it guided his next orders. Set in its place in the volume, it helps readers trace how two governments talked their way past repeated crises.
frus-1863p1-d364:
The British minister in Washington, Lord Lyons, took up his pen on 17 January 1863 to write Secretary of State William H. Seward. His note is document 364 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The channel between Lyons and Seward was the main safety valve of Anglo-American relations in the war. Papers like this one are the valve at work. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it forms part of the fullest record of how the Union handled its most dangerous foreign relationship.
frus-1863p1-d464:
Dated 16 April 1863, document 464 is a letter from William H. Seward, Secretary of State to Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily.

Students of the war use this mail to see foreign policy as the men on the spot lived it, page by page. What the page shows is process, not drama. Claims, protests, and replies moved back and forth until small disputes stayed small. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d564:
Writing on 15 June 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington in an official letter. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. It forms part of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official printed record of American diplomacy.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d64:
From the State Department on 26 January 1863 went this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London. The letter is document 64 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863, answering the thick mail Adams had sent that month.

Seward's letters did more than reply. They set the claims Adams was to press and the tone he was to use with Lord Russell. By early 1863 the two men had a rhythm: reports in by steamer, orders out by the next. This letter is one turn of that wheel, sent in the depths of a war winter.
frus-1863p1-d664:
Document 664, dated 14 November 1863, records a letter from William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams. Adams was the American minister in London, and Seward was Secretary of State in Washington. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. Adams in London was the Union's front line in Britain, pressing its case with the British government week after week.

The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. From the London end, the work was pressure and reporting. Adams pushed the British government on Confederate shipbuilding and sent home his reading of British politics and opinion.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d164: The British delegation to the Moscow Conference set down a memorandum dated October 24, 1943, preserved as Document 164 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Delegations traded such papers to state a position in writing where speeches might blur it, and the American editors kept this British text among their own files. The record gives the source and the date. The memorandum is printed in the Foreign Relations series' Moscow section.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d264: A luncheon meeting at Cairo on 24 November 1943 between General Marshall and Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek left no official record, and an editorial note in the volume covers it instead. Later that afternoon Marshall reported to the Combined Chiefs of Staff on a discussion with Chiang about proposed operations in the Southeast Asia Command. The editors presume that discussion took place at this luncheon. The Stilwell Papers show that Stilwell and Madame Chiang were also present. Where the luncheon was held is not indicated.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d364:
Minutes of the Combined Chiefs of Staff meeting at Tehran on 29 November 1943, at half past ten in the morning, record the first three-power military session. General Sir Alan Brooke leads, running through the war as the British see it, with General Marshall invited to interrupt where he disagrees.

Brooke's theme is keeping German divisions pinned down during the five or six months before Overlord can sail, at the earliest on 1 May. In Italy, amphibious hooks around the flanks should drive the Germans north of Rome and wreck the eleven or twelve divisions in the south. In Yugoslavia, where he counts twenty-one German and eight Bulgarian divisions, the Partisans should get arms and air help to deepen German troubles. Turkey's entry, he adds, holds great military advantage, whatever the politics.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d464:
John J. McCloy, the Assistant Secretary of War, wrote to John Gilbert Winant, the American ambassador in London, on December 2, 1943. The letter falls between the Tehran Conference, which had ended the day before, and the Second Cairo Conference, which opened on December 4. The State Department printed it in the Cairo-Tehran conference volume.

McCloy was one of the War Department's central fixers, and Winant was Washington's man at the center of the British war effort. Their exchange belongs to the back-channel traffic that kept the alliance running while the leaders traveled. Readers see how business moved between Washington and London even at the height of summit season.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d564:
Harry Dexter White, assistant to the Secretary of the Treasury, wrote this memorandum on August 13, 1944. White was the Treasury's chief technical mind and a main designer of the postwar monetary system agreed at Bretton Woods that summer. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

White's papers matter because the peace was being designed in economic offices while armies fought. Questions of money, trade, and Germany's economic future ran from Tehran's discussions into the Quebec Conference that autumn. For readers, this memorandum shows the Treasury's hand in that design work, written by the official who more than any other shaped America's postwar financial plans.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d64: On October 27, 1943, Roosevelt wrote to Chiang Kai-shek, less than a month before the two men were to meet at Cairo. The letter is Document 64 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Keeping China's leader close was a steady task for Washington that fall. The record supplies the date and the names and leaves the subject to the text. It is part of the Foreign Relations series' road to the Cairo Conference.
frus-1944-quebec-d164:
Abbot Moffat, chief of the Division of Southwest Pacific Affairs, sent Hull a short covering note on September 8, 1944. It introduces the attached memorandum for the president on Indochina and Southeast Asia, the long paper that follows it in the volume. Moffat explains why policies toward Indochina appear inside a broader Southeast Asia paper.

The policies, he writes, were included to stress correlating Indochina with the other regions of Southeast Asia. They stated the objectives the department's European, Far Eastern, and Near Eastern offices agreed were most desirable. If Churchill raised the subject at Quebec, the president would have them before him. The department also hoped for basic guidance to develop its own policies and procedures.
frus-1944-quebec-d264:
One sentence kept the Octagon basic policies from full agreement, and the secretaries' note C.C.S. 654/8 of September 12, 1944, isolates it. Every other policy for the final report to Roosevelt and Churchill had been settled informally before the conference. The exception was paragraph 6(i), on reorienting forces from Europe to the Pacific as a matter of highest priority.

The British text spoke of regard to other inescapable commitments. The American text said agreed commitments instead. The difference mattered. Britain feared being trapped by promises; America feared unilateral excuses. The Combined Chiefs were asked to decide. Their eventual compromise kept both words: agreed and/or inescapable.
frus-1944-quebec-d64:
Prime Minister Churchill wrote to President Roosevelt on September 12, 1944, the opening day of the Second Quebec Conference. The two men were in the same city, yet the written habit held. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume.

Letters exchanged inside a conference fixed points between sessions and carried proposals too formal for talk. Churchill, installed at the Citadel with Roosevelt, used paper as he always did. For readers, an opening-day message shows the conference starting in the leaders' own words, at the summit remembered for the Morgenthau Plan and the final division of the war's work.
frus-1945-50-intel-d164:
A telegram from the President’s Chief of Staff (Leahy) reached President Truman on 21 August 1946. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 164, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. At the time, a new National Intelligence Authority oversaw central intelligence, and the Central Intelligence Group did its daily work.

Writers chose a letter when they wanted a stance to count. The text gives the sender's side in full. Replies in the same file show the exchange from both sides. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d264:
Dated 31 March 1948, this memorandum runs from the Assistant Secretary of State for Public Affairs (Allen) to Acting Secretary of State Lovett. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 264 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. It was the CIA's first full year, and the Council was setting the rules for both open analysis and secret work.

Inside the government, memos were how business got done between meetings. One put the question and the facts in front of the reader at once. The reply, if any came, would build on the points laid out here. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d364:
Dated 9 February 1949, this memorandum runs from the Chief of the Intelligence Coordinating and Planning Staff (Childs) to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. It survives in print as document 364 of the State Department's Foreign Relations volume on intelligence, 1945 to 1950. The Council had sent in an outside team to grade the CIA, and the whole town knew a blunt report was coming.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Its worth lies in the trail it leaves: a dated, signed step in the long build-up of the CIA and the Council.
frus-1945-50-intel-d64:
Sidney Souers, deputy director of naval intelligence, wrote to Clark Clifford on 27 December 1945. Clifford was then a naval aide and adviser at the White House, close to President Truman. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

This letter is a hinge in the volume. Within weeks, Souers would become the first director of central intelligence, and Clifford one of the new system's architects. A paper between them, days before the January directive, shows the settlement being readied by the men who would run it. Readers should mark the names: the volume's story turns here from tearing down the wartime service to staffing the peacetime one that replaced it.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d164:
The Polish ambassador brought his government's latest terms to Washington on 22 January 1945. Acting Secretary Grew sent them to the President the next day with a cool judgment. His memorandum, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, finds no real basis for an approach to Moscow in them.

The London Poles would rather leave frontiers until the war ends. But they will talk now, if gains in the north and west make up for losses in the east. They seek an alliance with Moscow inside the new world body. They refuse one-sided solutions and claim the right to order their own home life. If Moscow will not negotiate, they propose an inter-allied military commission to run local rule in Poland for those loyal to London.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d264:
The Joint Staff Planners sent the chiefs a fresh report on Russia and Japan on 18 January 1945. Their paper, J. C. S. 1176/6, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. It was drawn up on the planners' own initiative, and a memorandum by General Arnold rides with it as an enclosure.

The coming allied staff conference at Malta, the report begins, offers a favorable chance to advance American planning. That planning rests on Russian participation in the war against Japan. General Deane's recent talks in Moscow had aimed at the information and agreements the planners need. They had not yet been able to win them. The report therefore goes to the Joint Chiefs for their consideration, days before the President's party sails for the Crimea.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d364: The Joint Chiefs asked the President to intervene in person in this short memorandum of February 6, 1945. They judged it necessary to win Stalin's approval for a meeting with the Soviet staff. The subject was details of possible Soviet participation in the war against Japan. They suggested Roosevelt speak to Stalin to obtain his agreement. An endorsement on the paper records that Admiral Leahy delivered it to the President that afternoon, at 4:15. The few lines trace how a staff question became a leader's errand.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d464:
Hiss's notes of the final foreign ministers' meeting, February 11, 1945, return to the question of credit. Bridges reported on the communiqué text. Molotov relayed Stalin's view: the communiqué should say what was agreed on voting, not that the President's proposal had been adopted. No other place, Molotov noted, said on whose initiative a step was taken.

Stettinius answered that the point had been discussed that morning with Stalin and the President present. It would be very hard for him to agree to strike the reference. Molotov replied there had been no agreement on this special point. The notes break off mid-bargain, with the wording — and the credit — still contested.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d64:
President Roosevelt wrote to Marshal Stalin on 22 January 1945 to settle press rules for the conference code-named Argonaut. His short top secret telegram is printed in the Foreign Relations volume on the Malta and Yalta conferences. It carries the plan already agreed with Churchill.

Roosevelt says he has decided to have no press representatives at the meeting. Only a small group of uniformed photographers from the American Navy will take the pictures the leaders want. He notes that Churchill agrees. Stalin's reply, quoted in the editors' note, raised no objections and said the same answer had gone to the Prime Minister.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d164:
Secretary Stettinius commented on the draft American agenda from San Francisco on June 22, 1945. His telegram to Grew is document 164 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It works through the items in Noyes's list of June 20, point by point.

Stettinius asks whether free access for foreign correspondents in places like Yugoslavia, Poland, and Czechoslovakia has been considered. On Italy, he wants the item on joining the United Nations moved to last place, and asks whether abolishing the Advisory Council for Italy should be raised. On international bases, he advises that the United States not take the lead in proposing discussion, though the delegation should be ready if others raise it. The comments show the agenda being sharpened at the top.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d264:
A briefing paper traced the long history of international control of the Danube, dated July 6, 1945. The paper is document 264 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It gave Truman's staff the legal background for a question the settlement would raise: who governs Europe's greatest river.

The principles began with the Treaty of Vienna in 1815: navigation free to all nations, no charges beyond the cost of upkeep, and rules set by common consent of the river states. The Treaty of Paris in 1856 applied them to the Danube and created a European Commission to run its maritime section. After the First World War the Danube was declared an international river. By 1945 the Soviet Union held both banks of the lower river and meant to run it alone, which the West resisted.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d364:
Frustration boils over in Pauley's letter of July 3, 1945, to Maisky, chairman of the Reparations Commission in Moscow. For the third time, Pauley writes, Maisky had put off the Commission's full meeting. The meeting was to discuss the Soviet proposal set out in Maisky's own Memorandum No. 2, the plan named in the Crimea Protocol.

The American delegation, Pauley notes, had now waited twenty-two days in Moscow. It had not received a single figure to support the Soviet proposal. Nor had Moscow tried to explain the plan's basis to the Americans or, so far as he knew, the British. The letter is a formal protest against allied stalling.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d464:
Italy is redefined as an American interest in an undated briefing book paper on policy toward that country. The objective, it states, is to strengthen Italy economically and politically. A stronger Italy could withstand the forces that threaten to sweep her into a new totalitarianism. The paper lists those forces one by one.

They include economic distress and national humiliation. They include doubt about British intentions, and about America's readiness to carry out a friendly policy. They include Soviet power, shown in Tito's nearly successful move in Venezia Giulia, a well organized Communist party, and no real experience of democratic government. American troops, it notes, are being withdrawn, and with them a sense of protection.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d564:
A secret priority wire from Belgrade charge Harold Shantz reached Washington on June 21, 1945. It is document 564 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It reports the signing of the Duino military deals and the gap left in them.

Shantz cites a British colonel who said the deals were signed without article 3 of the Belgrade agreement. The Yugoslavs meant to raise that point again at government level. They hoped to have their liberation committee named the sole agency under Allied military government. Shantz adds that the Yugoslav press twists the U.S. stand, since the Belgrade text was never published there. He suggests Washington and London issue a joint statement of facts and broadcast it into Yugoslavia.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d64:
Churchill proposed a royal visit to Berlin in telegram number 92 to President Truman, sent June 15, 1945. It is document 64 in the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. King George VI would be in France and Germany inspecting his troops while the Big Three met, and he wished to spend a day in Berlin.

Churchill's plan has the King take no part in the talks. He would lunch with the Russians if Stalin agreed, then dine in the British sector with Truman and Stalin as fellow heads of state, and leave early the next day. The King would also hand out decorations to Allied officers. Churchill says he has sent the same news to Stalin and asks Truman's view so he can advise the King.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d664:
Ambassador Caffery described a British bid to read Soviet motives on Tangier from Paris on July 4, 1945. His secret wire is document 664 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It reports a talk with Peake, head of the British team at the talks.

Peake read out a private letter he had sent to the Foreign Office. In it he guessed that Moscow wanted above all to embarrass Franco's Spain. A foothold at Tangier, he thought, would aid a subversive campaign against Franco. The U.S. team found that reading plausible, but framed the issue more widely. They saw an expanding Russian interest in the Mediterranean at work. As a way out, they proposed a Soviet observer, drawn from the Paris embassy, to follow the talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1064:
Soviet delegates presented this proposal on Greece to the foreign ministers on July 20, 1945. It is framed under the Yalta Declaration on Liberated Europe. The printed text gives extracts only; the remaining paragraphs appear elsewhere in the volume. Greece, the paper charges, still lacks due order, and law goes unrespected there.

Terror, it says, rages against the democratic elements who bore the main burden of fighting the German invaders. The Greek government is also accused of breaking the peace with its neighbors, threatening Albania and Bulgaria. The Soviets urge urgent measures. One is to press Greece's Regent to build a democratic government at once, in the spirit of the Varkiza Agreement of February 1945.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1164:
Nikolai Novikov, secretary of the Soviet team at Potsdam, wrote to Assistant Secretary Dunn on 23 July 1945. Team secretaries handled the daily traffic between the three staffs. They passed papers, set up meetings, and smoothed the small frictions that summits breed.

A note from one team's office to another's is backstage work. No speeches ride on it, but the talks could not run without it. This one shows the Soviet staff writing to the American staff in the ordinary way of business. Readers rarely see this layer of a summit. Here it survives in the record, dated and signed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1264:
On 21 July 1945 the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. Behind each choice the leaders made stood staff work of this kind. The chiefs' papers turned the services' knowledge into advice the team could weigh at the table.

By the end of the first week the chiefs had a full file running at Potsdam. Their notes covered the fronts and the forces that would hold the peace. This memorandum is one entry in that file. It shows the staff-level writing under the headline choices, done by the men who would have to make those choices work.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1364:
The State, War, and Navy Coordinating Committee sent a paper to its own panel at Babelsberg on 18 July 1945. Babelsberg was the suburb of Potsdam where the American delegation lived and worked during the conference. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

A committee in Washington writing to its forward panel shows how the summit was staffed. Men at Babelsberg needed questions answered and positions cleared by the home machinery, and this paper is part of that flow. It gives readers a rare look at the plumbing of a summit. The staffs pass paper between Germany and Washington to keep the talks fed, far from the leaders' photograph.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-164:
A second set of State Department minutes records further business on August 1, 1945. The closing day held more than one meeting, and staff minuted each. This set joins the other records of the final day in the second Potsdam volume. Together they cover the conference's last working hours.

Two formal records for one day show the end's density. As one session closed, another took up the next task. Readers can follow the handoffs in sequence. The minutes preserve the order in which the last business was cleared. They give the conference a fully written finish, not a fade.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-64:
Truman and Churchill conferred for an hour at Truman's quarters on July 22, 1945, beginning at 12:15. No official record of the talk's substance has been found. An editorial note in volume two covers the meeting, resting its account on the President's log.

The editors connect the talk to the atomic report Churchill had read that morning. They quote his memoir account of inviting the President to confer with him forthwith. General Marshall and Admiral Leahy were with Truman at the meeting, Churchill writes. The editors also quote Truman's own memoirs on the decision at stake. The final decision of where and when to use the atomic bomb was up to me, Truman writes. He regarded the bomb as a military weapon and never doubted it should be used. Churchill, he adds, unhesitatingly favored its use if it might aid in ending the war.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d764:
Kirk wrote again from Rome on July 29, 1945, in document 764. The ambassador in Italy kept the Acting Secretary supplied as Potsdam neared its end. Two reports in three days suggest pressing business. This one joined the second Potsdam volume beside its fellow.

Repeat reports let readers watch a situation move. Kirk could update facts and shift his advice as news arrived. The letter shows the tempo of an embassy in a fast week. It also shows Italy's stake in Potsdam: a beaten ally of Germany, now pleading its case through men like Kirk.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d864:
American advisers at Potsdam drafted this undated working paper to suggest edits to the proposed agreement on Germany. The agreement covered the political and economic principles for the first period of Allied control. The paper responds to the text sent to the foreign secretaries by the Economic Sub-Committee.

The paper proposes new wording for paragraph 13, on treating Germany as a single economic unit. It would add finance, transport, and communications to the fields needing common policy. It also asks to strike or rewrite a clause on foreign grants and credits to Germany. Readers can watch American drafters tighten the deal line by line.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d964:
William Clayton sent the Secretary of State a joint memorandum on art objects on July 30, 1945. The enclosure, signed by Clayton and Edwin Pauley, gives their views to General Clay. It sorts looted and stored art in the American zone into three classes, from clearly stolen public works to German-owned pieces stored for safety.

Clayton and Pauley back quick return of the first two classes to their countries of origin. The third class, true German property, may be shipped to America for care by museums. They insist no final fate be promised for it now. Any such move must be announced as safekeeping only, pending later Allied decisions.
frus-1951-54Iran-d164: A 1951-1954 FRUS telegram from the State Department to the embassy in Iran. The oil nationalization crisis unfolded. This document preserves that cable. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
frus-1955-57v16-d264: A 1955-1957 FRUS editorial note from the Suez Crisis volume. The 1956 invasion's diplomacy unfolded. This note provides that context. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care.
frus-1969-76v32-d264: A 1969-1976 FRUS editorial note on the Nixon-Brezhnev talks in the SALT I volume. The arms talks. This note provides that context. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record.
gao-gaoreports-b-295764: Mathews Associates doubled its April 2005 protest — two dockets, one supply fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Paired filings get one careful answer.
gao-gaoreports-b-298864: Barnes Aerospace Group doubled its December 2006 protest — two case numbers, one aerospace fight — and GAO's combined ruling settles both. The firm challenged the awards, and the call weighs each claim. Paired filings get one careful answer. Two dockets, one fair verdict.
gao-gaoreports-b-299864: Harris Corporation triple-filed its 2007 contract protest, and GAO's combined ruling answers all three. The tech-and-defense firm said the award was flawed; the call works each claim to a close. Big-ticket bid wars like this are where protest law gets its real-world workout.
gao-gaoreports-b-305864: The Capitol Police's employee shuttle got a fiscal ruling in this January 2006 GAO call, which tests the shuttle spending. The decision reads the money law. The ruling decides whether the bus dollars were legal. The law had the final word.
gao-gaoreports-b-309964: A Government Accountability Office bid-protest ruling dated November 9, 2007, covering two filings by ITT Industries Space Systems, LLC. The defense contractor challenged an award in the space-systems arena, and the decision applies federal procurement law to the disputed competition. The case shows GAO refereeing high-stakes defense contracting, where a single award can be worth hundreds of millions of dollars.
gao-gaoreports-b-310564: This 2008 decision resolves a federal contract protest filed by Gap Solutions, Inc. Losing bidders can ask GAO to review whether an agency ran the competition fairly. Agencies almost always follow these rulings, which build the case law for federal contracts.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-264: Obsolete ships needed scrapping faster in 2005, and GAO's report says the Maritime Administration needed better program management. The review writes the disposal plan. The ghost fleet deserved the torches. The management had to improve. The ghost fleet deserved the torches.
