The team tracked reactivity to an antigen called glioma-expressed antigen 2 in patients under radiation. They found that this response rose during treatment. Signs that radiation wakes up anti-tumor immunity support efforts to pair radiation with immune-based therapies for these hard tumors.
plos-pone-0002264:
Jamie Barger and co-authors fed mice a small dose of a red-wine compound. They watched for signs of slower aging, in a study published in PLOS ONE in 2008. Resveratrol, found in grape skins, had extended lifespan in some simple animals at high doses and protected mice on a high-fat diet. Low doses over a full lifetime were untested.

The team fed mice from middle age to old age on a control diet or one with a low dose of resveratrol. The low dose partly mimicked calorie restriction, a proven way to slow aging, and delayed some aging signs. The work tests whether a gentle daily dose can borrow part of that benefit.
plos-pone-0002364:
Zhongli Luo, Xiaojun Zhao, and Shuguang Zhang studied a self-assembling peptide built from mirror-image amino acids, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Most life uses left-handed amino acids. The peptide d-EAK16 is made only of the right-handed, D forms, and it assembles itself into ordered structures in water.

The team compared its structural dynamics with its left-handed twin, l-EAK16. Using circular dichroism, which reads protein shape from light, they followed both peptides under varied temperatures. Mirror peptides resist the enzymes that chew up natural ones, so knowing how they fold guides the design of tough new biomaterials.
plos-pone-0002464:
Led by Cross, a team of researchers published its study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Alan Cross, Mark Collard, Andrew Nelson, and others. Its subject is body Segment Differences in Surface Area, Skin Temperature and 3D Displacement and the Estimation of Heat Balance during Locomotion in Hominins. The conventional method of estimating heat balance during locomotion in humans and other hominins treats the body as an undifferentiated mass.

This is problematic because the segments of the body differ with respect to several variables that can affect thermoregulation. Each part of the study builds on the part before it, in the order the team carried it out. In short, the piece gives a clear, short route into a field that can seem hard to enter from the outside.
plos-pone-0002564:
Research by Hennequin and co-authors came out in PLOS ONE in 2008. The author list runs from Martine Hennequin, Véronique Moysan, Didier Jourdan, and others. Its subject is inequalities in Oral Health for Children with Disabilities: A French National Survey in Special Schools. Despite wide recognition that children with disability often have poor oral health, few high quality, controlled results are available.

What the team did, and why they did it that way, forms the core of the piece. For science readers, it shows how a small, well framed question can add a firm piece of knowledge to a much larger field.
plos-pone-0002664:
Work by Roger Konrad and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was potential effects of oilseed rape expressing oryzacystatin-1 (OC-1) and of purified insecticidal proteins on larvae of the solitary bee osmia bicornis. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Roger Konrad, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Despite their importance as pollinators in crops and wild plants. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002764:
Work by Horst Joachim Schirra and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was altered metabolism of growth hormone receptor mutant mice: a combined NMR metabonomics and microarray study. The catalog record names Horst Joachim Schirra first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Growth hormone is an important regulator of post-natal growth and metabolism. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002864:
Work by Jingxian Yang and colleagues appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was riluzole increases the amount of latent HSF1 for an amplified heat shock response and cytoprotection. Authorship is credited in the record to Jingxian Yang and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

The opening of the abstract sets out the basis for the work. Induction of the heat shock response (HSR) and increased expression of the heat shock proteins (HSPs) provide mechanisms to ensure proper protein folding, trafficking. Its abstract frames the work for later readers, who can judge the full text against the aims stated at the start.
plos-pone-0002964:
Nina van Sorge, Celia Ebrahimi, Shauna McGillivray and co-authors studied how anthrax toxins help cause meningitis in 2008. Anthrax meningitis is the main brain complication of body-wide Bacillus anthracis infection and is nearly always fatal. Bacteria found in brain tissue at autopsy show they can breach the blood-brain barrier.

The PLOS ONE study reports that anthrax toxins inhibit signaling in neutrophils and brain endothelium, the vessel lining. Weakening those defenses could help bacteria cross into the brain. The work identifies steps in a fast, lethal infection that future treatments would need to block. Its full text, with tables and references, is openly available to any reader online.
plos-pone-0003064:
Zaruhi Khachatryan, Zhanna Ktsoyan, Gayane Manukyan and co-authors argued host genetics dominates gut microbe makeup in 2008. The human gut hosts a very diverse symbiotic microbiota. Its composition depends on host genetics and environment, but the share due to each was disputed, and no genes had been pinned down.

Their title claims a predominant role for host genetics in controlling gut microbiota composition. Published in PLOS ONE, that stance, if borne out, means family and ancestry shape internal ecology strongly. It frames later work hunting the specific genes involved. The full text gives methods, results, and references for readers who want to check each step.
plos-pone-0003164:
Alessia Galgano, Michael Forrer, Lukasz Jaskiewicz and colleagues compare the RNA targets of human PUF proteins in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Finding which messages RNA-binding proteins regulate across the genome is crucial to uncover how gene control works after transcription. The conserved PUF family proteins repress gene activity by binding to sequence elements in the tail region of messages.

Their analysis suggests extensive interaction with the microRNA regulatory system. Readers see two control systems that were often studied apart drawn together. That overlap may change how researchers model the fine tuning of gene output in human cells.
plos-pone-0003264:
Ben Buelow and Andrew M. Scharenberg characterize a widely used genetic switch in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Conditional gene targeting using the Cre-loxP system is a well established technique in numerous in vitro and in vivo systems. Ligand regulated forms of Cre have been increasingly used to gain temporal and spatial control over conditional targeting.

The authors define parameters required for effective use of tamoxifen-regulated recombination. Readers get practical limits for a tool many mouse studies depend on. Knowing dose and timing effects prevents false results where a gene seems inactive only because the switch was incomplete.
plos-pone-0003364:
Shintaro Imamura, Junzo Uchiyama, Eriko Koshimizu and colleagues study telomerase in zebrafish blood formation in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. It is clear telomerase expression is crucial for keeping telomere homeostasis. But there is growing proof the TERT protein can have roles in the body apart from this central function. The team set out to further examine the role of telomerase during early growth.

The title reports a non-canonical function of zebrafish telomerase reverse transcriptase is required for developmental hematopoiesis, the making of blood. Readers see a famous ageing enzyme do a separate job of its own. That split matters for drugs that target telomerase in cancer.
plos-pone-0003464:
Shinya Hoshikawa and co-authors studied how a nerve insulation gene is switched on in 2008. Schwann cells wrap nerves with a fatty coat called myelin. A protein named MAG appears in those cells before wrapping begins. That timing hints MAG helps start the wrapping process.

What turns the MAG gene on was unknown before this work. The team studied the gene's promoter, its start control region. A protein called RING finger protein 10 proved to regulate that switch. Naming the regulator clarifies how myelin formation gets under way. Myelin loss underlies many nerve diseases, so its first steps draw wide interest.
plos-pone-0003564:
Andrea Puhar and co-authors studied anthrax edema toxin in immune cells for this 2008 paper. The toxin is an enzyme that raises cyclic AMP inside host cells. It works near the cell nucleus, the perinuclear region. Its molecular action was still poorly understood.

The team used Jurkat T cells to track the toxin's signaling. It modulated PKA- and CREB-dependent pathways in two phases. Early and late waves hit the cell in sequence. That timed pattern helps explain how anthrax disrupts host defenses. Anthrax is also feared as a weapon, which adds weight to toxin studies.
plos-pone-0003664:
Joseph N. Brown, James J. Kohler, Carter R. Coberley, and colleagues published this immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Macrophages are long-lived immune cells where HIV-1 can hide for years. They also form a bridge between the body's first defenses and its targeted ones.

The team asked whether HIV-1 switches macrophages on through Toll-like receptors, the usual alarm sensors. They found activation that does not depend on those receptors. The result shows the virus can stir the very cells it lives in by another route, which matters for clearing hidden reservoirs.
plos-pone-0003764:
Maria Manich, Oliver Knapp, Maryse Gibert, and colleagues published this toxin study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Clostridium perfringens makes many toxins that cause severe disease in people and animals. Its delta toxin is one of three blood-cell-destroying toxins released by some strains. The team compared it with its relatives.

Delta toxin proved sequence-related to beta toxin, NetB, and pore-forming toxins of Staphylococcus. Yet it behaves differently in function from those cousins. The kinship reveals a shared pore-punching design behind diverse bacterial weapons, with each tuned to its own targets.
plos-pone-0003864:
J. Greg Doheny, Randy Mottus, and Thomas A. Grigliatti published this genetics paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Chromosomes end in telomeres, protective caps required for chromosome integrity and tied to aging and cancer. The chromatin at telomeres mixes traits of silent and active regions. Genes placed near those ends can be quieted.

The authors describe this telomeric position effect as a third silencing mechanism in eukaryotes. It works beyond the two silencing systems already established in the field. The proposal adds a distinct tool to the known ways cells hush genes by location.
plos-pone-0003964:
Laura W. Harris, Matthew Wayland, Martin Lan, and co-authors sampled tiny brain blood vessels in schizophrenia in 2008. Past studies hinted the schizophrenic brain gets too little energy. Other work found faults in the brain's smallest vessels in patients. Both clues point toward the cerebral microvasculature.

Their PLOS ONE article used laser capture to cut out those vessels precisely. Gene activity in the captured tissue could then be read cleanly. The method separates vessel signals from surrounding brain cells. Findings here may link blood flow and energy supply to schizophrenia. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004064:
Matthew C. Walsh, Gregory K. Kim, Paul L. Maurizio, and co-authors studied an immune adapter protein in 2008. TRAF6 carries signals from interleukin-1 and related receptor families. Its ring-shaped domain can build ubiquitin chains that switch signals on. Those chains were believed essential for its signaling role.

Their PLOS ONE article reports TRAF6 works without tagging itself. Activation of NF-kappaB and MAPK paths proceeded without autoubiquitination. The result separates TRAF6's adapter job from its enzyme job. Immune models must now explain signaling without the assumed chains. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004164:
William Agudelo and colleagues published this theoretical study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Adaptive immunity begins when class II MHC molecules present small protein fragments, called peptides, to immune cells. The team studied one such pairing: a class II human leukocyte antigen molecule holding a peptide from myelin basic protein, a protein of nerve insulation.

Using theory and modelling, they asked how changes in the peptide reshape the electrostatic landscape, the pattern of electric charge, across the complex. That landscape guides how immune receptors read the pairing. The work may help explain how small peptide changes can tilt the immune system toward attack, as in multiple sclerosis.
plos-pone-0004264:
Boris Shorning and colleagues published this gut study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Lkb1 is a tumour suppressor kinase involved in many processes across the body. The team examined what its loss does to intestinal homeostasis, the gut's steady state. They focused on secretory cell development, since Lkb1 is strongly expressed there.

They report that Lkb1 deficiency alters the differentiation of goblet and Paneth cells in the small intestine. These two cell types make mucus and antimicrobial defences, so their misdevelopment changes gut protection. The finding links a cancer gene to the everyday upkeep of the intestine.
plos-pone-0004364:
Mayke Oesterholt and colleagues published this malaria study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Mutations in the dhfr and dhps genes are linked to failure of sulphadoxine-pyrimethamine treatment. They are also linked to gametocyte carriage, the stage of the parasite that infects mosquitoes. This may boost the spread of drug-resistant Plasmodium falciparum, as shown before for chloroquine resistance.

The team studied gametocytes too few to see under a microscope, in western Kenya. They asked whether these hidden carriers pass on drug-resistant parasites. Invisible carriers could silently keep drug resistance spreading after treatment campaigns. A microscope misses these carriers.
plos-pone-0004464:
Stretches of DNA near a growth gene may help set how tall people grow, report Asa Johansson, Inger Jonasson, and Ulf Gyllensten in PLOS ONE in 2009. The gene makes the receptor for growth hormone releasing hormone. Broken copies of it cause a severe lack of growth hormone, yet it had not been tied to normal differences in height.

The team scanned the genomes of people from northern Sweden, a population with deep local roots. They looked for long shared stretches, called extended haplotypes, near the gene that track with height. They found such stretches linked to normal height variation, as the title reports. The result adds one more piece to the puzzle of height, which is shaped by many genes of small effect.
plos-pone-0004564:
Wild peach palm, a relative of a major Amazon crop, is being pushed out as forest falls, document Charles Clement, Ronaldo Santos, Sylvain Desmouliere, and co-authors in PLOS ONE in 2009. Southern Amazonia's Arc of Fire draws world attention each year as forests are cut and burned for farming. Those forests hold wild relatives of native South American crops, peach palm among them.

The team surveyed the wild palm's ecological adaptation and its conservation where it grows. They link deforestation to the extinction of local populations. Wild relatives hold genes for toughness that breeders may one day need. Losing them in place, before they are even cataloged, narrows the future options for the crop itself and for Amazon farming.
plos-pone-0004664:
The cystic fibrosis protein also acts as a brake on inflammation, show Neeraj Vij, Steven Mazur, and Pamela Zeitlin in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein is CFTR, a channel whose dysfunction causes cystic fibrosis. In the airways, dysfunctional CFTR is associated with elevated NF-kappaB mediated IL-8 signaling. That signal draws in neutrophils and drives the chronic lung inflammation that destroys cystic fibrosis lungs.

The mechanism by which CFTR mediates inflammatory signaling was under debate. The team tested the hypothesis that CFTR is a negative regulator of the NF-kappaB innate immune response. If the broken channel itself releases the brake on inflammation, then fixing the channel should calm the lungs, not just clear mucus. That widens what CFTR-correcting drugs could achieve.
plos-pone-0004764:
Anke Popp and colleagues systematically mapped damaged regions in a rat model of stroke, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Stroke studies first need to know the size and timing of the dead core. They also need the state of tissue around the core and in far areas touched by the event.

The team induced focal loss of blood flow in Wistar rats. They then evaluated regions by degree of impairment over time and space. A shared map helps compare drugs and recovery across labs. It also shows which tissue might still be saved. Further tests can show how widely the pattern holds beyond the cases studied here.
plos-pone-0004864:
Min-Kyoung Kim led a team that studied how sun light turns on a skin gene called MMP-1 for PLOS ONE in 2009. MMP-1 breaks down collagen, the protein that keeps skin firm. Too much of it after sun exposure can speed skin aging and may help skin cancer form over time. Chemical marks on DNA bound proteins help set how strongly the gene is read.

The team focused on a protein called p300, which adds one such mark. They asked how p300 is brought to the MMP-1 gene after UV light hits skin cells. The work links sun light, gene marks, and collagen loss in one chain. Blocking that chain could one day slow sun driven skin aging.
plos-pone-0004964:
On May 12, 2008, a huge earthquake struck Wenchuan, China. It killed tens of thousands and injured hundreds of thousands. Shu Li and colleagues surveyed survivors afterward. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. They assessed the disaster's effects on how people judged risk.

A surprising pattern emerged from the responses. People closest to the disaster felt less anxious than people farther away. The authors call this the psychological typhoon eye. Calm sits at the center, like the eye of a storm. The finding matters for relief planning. Mental-health aid after catastrophes should not assume the nearest survivors are the most fearful.
plos-pone-0005064:
Ovarian cancer is the most lethal gynecologic cancer. It lacks easily detectable early markers. Jan Rohozinski and colleagues looked for unusual flags in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied retrogenes normally active in sperm production. Those genes are called spermatogenesis associated retrogenes.

The genes turned out to be expressed in the human ovary. They were also expressed in ovarian cancers. A male-only program switches on in a female cancer. Such misplaced genes could serve as markers for the disease. They might also serve as treatment targets. Healthy tissues that lack them would be spared. The finding links gene birth in the testis to a deadly cancer in the ovary.
plos-pone-0005164:
HIV vaccine trials exclude pregnant participants. Enrolled women must use contraception to prevent pregnancy. Hannah Kibuuka and colleagues reported real-world experience from East Africa. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. The trial was a phase I/II preventive HIV vaccine study. They tracked contraceptive use among enrolled women.

Access to quality services shaped how well the requirement worked. Misconceptions about contraceptive methods also played a role. The data reveal gaps between trial rules and practice. Future trials must support women's reproductive needs better. That support protects participants and the science alike. Pregnancies during trials complicate safety data. Honest reporting of use patterns helps planners design realistic protocols.
plos-pone-0005264:
The BCG vaccine protects against tuberculosis unevenly, so better regimens are badly needed. Verreck and colleagues tested two vaccine strategies in rhesus macaques, close stand-ins for humans, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Both aimed to improve on BCG alone.

One arm boosted BCG with a modified virus vaccine called MVA.85A. The other used a weakened tuberculosis strain missing the phoP gene. Both showed protective efficacy in the monkeys. Strong animal results like these decide which candidates earn a place in human trials. Monkeys are a costly and slow test bed, so a clear win in them is the gate a new TB vaccine must pass before it can be tried in people.
plos-pone-0005364:
Protein interaction networks keep working even when parts fail, a property called fault tolerance. Brady and colleagues asked how that robustness is built in the yeast interactome in PLOS ONE in 2009, as high-throughput data on it grew.

The analysis found stable bipartite subgraphs, two-sided connection patterns, within the network. It also found redundant pathways that can perform similar jobs. Backup routes explain why single gene losses so often have mild effects, and why networks resist breakdown. Drug hunts gain from this view: a cell with two paths to one job may need two drugs at once. Not one, to shut that job down in a sick or cancerous cell.
plos-pone-0005464:
Alexander Garthe, Joachim Behr, and Gerd Kempermann studied new brain cells in adult mice for a 2009 PLOS ONE report. The adult hippocampus, a brain area tied to memory, keeps making new nerve cells through life. What those young cells add to learning was still unclear.

The team set learning tasks that called for exact use of place cues. Animals with healthy new cell growth could switch tactics in a flexible way as tasks changed. The work suggests that young brain cells help the mind adjust old knowledge to new settings, not just store more of it.
plos-pone-0005564:
Liam Morrison and co-authors reported mating in a livestock parasite in a 2009 PLOS ONE study. Trypanosoma congolense is a single-celled parasite that makes cattle sick across Africa. Sick cattle give less milk and work less, which harms the families who depend on them.

Whether this parasite could mate and swap genes was unknown, despite its importance. The team found evidence that it does mate in its life cycle. Gene swapping lets parasites mix traits such as drug resistance, so the discovery changes how control programs should watch this pest. Mating also means that traits from far apart parasite lines can meet in one offspring.
plos-pone-0005664:
Cesare Valerio Parise and Charles Spence studied cross-sense matches in people without synesthesia in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. In synesthesia, one sense triggers an extra experience in another, such as seeing colours for sounds. Only a small share of people have it.

Yet ordinary people also match sounds, shapes, and tastes in shared ways, as the saying in the title suggests. The team showed that these built-in matches change how well sight and sound are combined. Everyday perception, not just the rare condition, mixes the senses in an orderly fashion.
plos-pone-0005764:
Jose Eduardo de la Torre-Bárcena and co-authors tested in 2009 how two data choices can bend the family tree of seed plants. Genome-scale data promised clearer trees, with hundreds of genes from expressed-gene libraries. But results can hinge on which outgroup species roots the tree, and on how much data is missing.

The team varied both factors on major seed plant relationships. Some branches held firm; others moved with the choices. Their warning is practical: big data does not remove judgment calls. Plant scientists can use the findings to build trees that state their weak points honestly.
plos-pone-0005864:
Katharine Thakkar, Peter Brugger, and Sohee Park tested in 2009 whether the mental skill of taking another's viewpoint shares machinery with spatial attention. Brain scans had hinted that the parietal cortex serves both empathy tasks and visuospatial ones. The team set out to test that overlap in behavior.

Subjects performed a self-other perspective task and a line bisection task, a classic attention probe. Links between the two would suggest shared circuits for social and spatial shifts. Such links matter for conditions, like schizophrenia, where both falter. The study turns a scanning hint into a tested behavioral connection.
plos-pone-0005964:
A tree does not just grow in soil; it helps make the soil beneath it. Edward Ayres, Heidi Steltzer, Sarah Berg and colleagues showed that in high mountain forests in 2009. Their PLOS ONE study compares soil under stands of single tree species in the Southern Rocky Mountains, where one species often grows right beside another.

Soil traits differed by tree species, across physical makeup, chemistry and the small life within. A forest map is thus also a soil map, written by the trees themselves. The finding matters for anyone who plants or restores high forests, since the choice of tree will steer the ground it grows in for years to come.
plos-pone-0006064:
The flu drug Tamiflu does not end at the patient who swallows it. Hanna Söderström, Josef Järhult, Björn Olsen and colleagues went looking for it in water in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper detects oseltamivir in aquatic environments, after earlier work showed its active form passes through sewage treatment plants without breaking down.

A pandemic drug stockpiled worldwide will reach rivers wherever it is used at scale. Finding it in water raises questions about effects on wildlife and about flu in wild birds gaining drug resistance. The study is an early warning that pandemic planning should count the environment among its costs.
plos-pone-0006164:
Most plants drink nitrogen only in its processed, inorganic form, though soil is rich in the organic kind. Jim Karagatzides, Jessica Butler and Aaron Ellison showed a carnivorous plant breaking that rule in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies the purple pitcher plant, Sarracenia purpurea, and its uptake of nitrogen from the prey it traps.

The plant can directly acquire organic nitrogen, short-circuiting the inorganic nitrogen cycle, the title reports. Feeding straight from prey explains how the pitcher plant thrives in bogs where processed nitrogen is scarce. The result widens the known menu of plant nutrition and reframes what the nitrogen cycle must include.
plos-pone-0006264:
DAP12 is an adaptor protein that passes signals from immune cell surfaces inward. Nicolas Schleinitz and colleagues mapped where DAP12 appears among white blood cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. It was first found on natural killer cells, then reported in myeloid and lymphoid cells by indirect methods.

The team compared healthy people with patients who have systemic lupus erythematosus, an autoimmune disease. Direct measurement gives a firmer expression pattern than blots and arrays alone. Knowing which cells carry DAP12 guides ideas about its role in immune balance. Lupus, where that balance fails, is a natural test case.
plos-pone-0006364:
A coral's fitness emerges from three partners at once: its algae, its own genes, and its environment. Jos Mieog and colleagues teased those roles apart in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Reef corals host diverse Symbiodinium algae that differentially influence the fitness of the combined holobiont.

The relative weight of symbiont type, host genotype, and environment was the study's focus. Knowing which factor dominates guides reef restoration choices. Planting the right coral with the right algae for a site could raise survival. The work frames coral health as a three-way negotiation.
plos-pone-0006464:
Miyoung Kim and co-authors studied a protein linked to allergy signals in PLOS ONE in 2009. The protein, TCTP, was found in nose wash fluids of allergic patients. There it was named a histamine-releasing factor, since it can trigger histamine release tied to IgE. Lab-made versions of the protein acted much more weakly than the natural form, and the team asked why.

Their title gives the answer: the protein must pair up, forming dimers, for its cytokine-like activity. Single units do not send the signal well. The finding clarifies how this factor works in allergy. It may also point to ways to block its action.
plos-pone-0006564:
William Silkworth, Isaac Nardi, Lindsey Scholl, and colleagues studied chromosome errors in cancer cells in PLOS ONE in 2009. Many cancer cells display a chromosome instability phenotype. They exhibit high rates of chromosome loss or gain at each cell cycle. Over the years, a number of causes have been proposed.

Their title reports that multipolar spindle pole coalescence is a major source of kinetochore mis-attachment and chromosome mis-segregation. Cells with extra spindle poles cluster them, but the process garbles chromosome attachments. That mechanism explains a large share of segregation errors. It suggests targets for drugs that push unstable cells over the edge.
plos-pone-0006664:
Dan Li, Abbas Raza, and Jeff DeJong evaluated a frog oocyte system for gene regulation studies in PLOS ONE in 2009. They evaluate use of Xenopus laevis oocytes as a matched germ cell system. The system serves for characterizing organization and transcriptional activity of a germ cell-specific promoter, ALF. Promoters are the switches that start gene transcription.

Frog oocytes are large, hardy cells ideal for injecting test constructs. A matched germ cell system keeps the regulatory environment realistic. Their evaluation shows what the system can and cannot reveal about ALF promoter activity. Such methods papers support reproductive biology research.
plos-pone-0006764:
Anjali Bheda, Julia Shackelford, and Joseph S. Pagano studied genes controlled by a cleanup enzyme in PLOS ONE in 2009. The enzyme is ubiquitin C-terminal hydrolase L1, or UCHL1. Enzymes of its family remove ubiquitin tags from proteins. Their roles were often dismissed as minor processing jobs. Growing evidence links them to wider cellular regulation.

The team measured expression and function of genes UCHL1 regulates. Finding target genes moves UCHL1 beyond a housekeeping role. Regulated genes reveal which pathways the enzyme quietly influences. That could matter in nerve health and cancer, where UCHL1 changes appear. The study opens a functional map for a long-overlooked enzyme family.
plos-pone-0006864:
Sébastien Rodrigue and his team read the full DNA of one lone bacterial cell in PLOS ONE in 2009. Most microbes have never been grown in a lab. Reading one cell at a time could open their vast gene wealth to study. The team used Prochlorococcus, a sea microbe, as their test case. It is one of the most common microbes in the seas, and its DNA is well known.

They copied the cell's whole genome many times over. Then they built the code from scratch, with no map to guide them. One cell gives scant code, and the copies come out uneven. Clearing those bars proves the path can work. It points toward DNA reads for legions of microbes no lab can grow.
plos-pone-0006964:
Walid Maaty, Blake Wiedenheft, Pavel Tarlykov, and colleagues studied stress defense in an archaeon in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their organism was Sulfolobus solfataricus, which thrives in hot, acidic springs. All cells must repair damage caused by oxidation. Archaea live in some of the most extreme, oxidizing places known to support life.

The team exposed the archaeon to oxidative stress and tracked its response. They catalogued old, new, and borrowed defense systems at work. The mix shows how life in harsh chemistry was assembled over evolution. It also offers clues for finding life in extreme places beyond Earth.
plos-pone-0007064:
Phyllis Frisa and James Jacobberger refined protein measurement in PLOS ONE in 2009. To measure a cell protein in absolute terms, labs use purified standards on Western blots. The team had earlier counted a viral protein across cell lines this way. They correlated its amount with protein levels through the cell cycle.

Here they quantified cyclin B1, a protein that rises and falls with the cycle. Absolute counts beat relative comparisons for tracking cell states. Precise cyclin numbers can mark exactly where a cell sits in division. That precision serves cancer research, where cycle timing often goes wrong.
plos-pone-0007164:
Badara Cisse, Matthew Cairns, Ernest Faye, and colleagues ran a malaria prevention trial in children in PLOS ONE in 2009. Piperaquine stays in the body a long time, which suits it for intermittent preventive treatment. No African studies of its preventive use had been done. The team ran a cluster randomized trial in children.

They paired piperaquine with either sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine or dihydroartemisinin. The trial tested whether the combinations prevented malaria in practice. Seasonal prevention for children is a major malaria strategy in Africa. A long-acting partner drug could protect through the whole transmission season.
plos-pone-0007264:
Appolinaire Djikeng, Ryan Kuzmickas, Norman G. Anderson, and colleagues surveyed RNA viruses in a freshwater lake in 2009. Lakes and ponds sit at an interface between humans and many host organisms. They host larval insects, and they can carry viruses between species, including avian influenza A virus.

The authors use metagenomic analysis, sequencing genetic material directly from the environment. They catalog RNA viruses present in the lake water. Their PLOS ONE inventory shows the hidden viral diversity of a single freshwater site. Such surveys can warn health and wildlife researchers about viruses circulating unnoticed.
plos-pone-0007364:
Ping Hong Meng, Cécile Raynaud, Guillaume Tcherkez, and colleagues studied links between a sugar compound, cell death, and plant immunity in 2009. Programmed cell death is crucial for normal development and stress responses in plants. Its control is not fully understood, despite its importance for growth and for defense against pathogens.

The authors had earlier isolated two PCNA-binding proteins in Arabidopsis. They now examine crosstalks between myo-inositol metabolism, programmed cell death, and basal immunity. Their PLOS ONE paper connects a common metabolic compound to life-and-death decisions. Those decisions shape how plants survive infection and environmental stress.
plos-pone-0007464:
Junichi Soh and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on how cancer genes change inside tumor cells. A single mutated copy of an oncogene was widely believed to be enough to drive tumor growth. Yet tumors often show extra copies of the mutant gene, a pattern called mutant allele specific imbalance. The team measured how often these changes appear together.

Across the tumor cells they examined, the three changes frequently traveled as a set. Mutation came with copy number gains and an imbalance favoring the mutant version. That combination likely strengthens the cancer signal beyond what one mutation alone would do. Recognizing the pattern sharpens how doctors read a tumor's genetic profile. It may also affect how targeted drugs are matched to patients.
plos-pone-0007564:
Sandra Schulze and colleagues published a comparative study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on lamins, the meshwork proteins lining the inside of the nucleus. Lamins are built from a head, a central rod, and a tail with a folded motif. They come in A and B types. The team compared A-type lamins from the fruit fly with those of humans, side by side.

The comparison shows what evolution kept and what it changed. Conserved features point to jobs no nucleus can do without. Differences hint at roles tuned to each animal. Because faulty lamins cause human diseases, the fly's simpler set is a useful model. The study sharpens that model by mapping the family resemblance. It is a careful piece of comparative anatomy at the protein level.
plos-pone-0007664:
Sarah Szanton and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on schooling across generations of African-American twins. Educational opportunities for African-Americans expanded through the twentieth century. Twins are an informative group for studying that change, because twins share parents and childhood economic status. The team compared educational attainment across twin cohorts born in different eras. Each pair thus held family background constant while history moved.

Cohort differences in attainment showed up clearly in the twin data. Later-born cohorts reached further in school than earlier ones. The twin design strips away family explanations and leaves the era's effect visible. Expanding opportunity, in other words, measurably lifted attainment. Studies like this separate what families give from what societies open. The history of American education is written in such comparisons.
plos-pone-0007764:
Emile Barrias and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It tests a drug against Trypanosoma cruzi, the parasite that causes Chagas disease. The parasite lives inside host cells. To get in, it hijacks the cell's vesicle transport machinery.

The drug, dynasore, blocks a protein called dynamin that cells use to pinch off vesicles. Treated peritoneal macrophages resisted entry by the parasite. Blocking entry is a different strategy from killing the parasite later. The result points to host proteins as drug targets. Such targets may be harder for the parasite to evade.
plos-pone-0007864:
Stacie Brown and Marvin Whiteley published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It characterizes an enzyme from a bacterium tied to severe gum disease. Aggregatibacter actinomycetemcomitans lives only in the mouth, in the pocket between gums and teeth. It is the proposed cause of localized aggressive periodontitis, which destroys tissue fast in young people.

The enzyme under study is its L-lactate dehydrogenase. Such enzymes manage the cell's energy and acid balance. Describing this one in detail fills a gap in the pathogen's basic biology. Every well-mapped enzyme is a possible target for future treatment.
plos-pone-0007964:
Mahatsangy Raharijaona and colleagues studied a growth helper in thyroid tumors for PLOS ONE in 2009. The helper, called PRC, works with a known family that runs cell fuel use and builds mitochondria, the cell's power plants. The tumors in view grow extra power plants, a trait called oncocytic.

In a cell model of those tumors, PRC helped carry signals between the power plants and the nucleus, with nitric oxide as part of the chat. That two-way talk may help tumor cells grow. Learning its steps could reveal weak points in a rare and poorly served cancer.
plos-pone-0008064:
Jigang Zhang and colleagues built a gene-hunting method that scores teams, not lone genes, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Standard gene set tests ask whether each gene in a set changed on its own. Yet genes work in teams, and a team's joint shift can matter when no member shifts much alone.

Their method looks for sets where the links between genes change, a sign the team is acting as one. That view can catch disease drivers that single-gene hunts walk past. It suits cancers and other ills where whole pathways, not lone genes, go wrong.
plos-pone-0008164:
Gerardo Chowell and colleagues modeled flu vaccine choices for Mexico's 2009 pandemic in PLOS ONE in 2009. Vaccine arrived in limited amounts while the H1N1 virus was already spreading. Planners had to choose who would be first in line, by age and risk.

An age-structured spread model, tuned to Mexico's spring wave data, tested the choices head to head. Some targeting plans saved far more lives per dose than others. The work gives planners in like settings a tested way to stretch scarce vaccine when the next pandemic comes. Age proved to be the key lever in the model.
plos-pone-0008264:
Richard A. Holland and colleagues tracked oilbirds in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. The oilbird is a very unusual bird that roosts in caves by day. Huge groups share dark caves, and the birds supposedly never see daylight. At night they fly out to gather fruit and bring it back. Seeds from that fruit often sprout inside the caves.

Tracking their movements revealed more about this secret life. How far oilbirds fly shapes seed dispersal across forests. A fruit-eating night bird moves seeds in ways day birds cannot. The study adds rare data on a little-known species.
plos-pone-0008364:
Rajendra Kumar Singh and colleagues studied how HIV hides from immunity in a PLOS ONE paper from 2009. HIV's Nef protein removes MHC-I molecules from the surface of infected cells. MHC-I normally displays viral fragments so killer cells can attack. Removing it likely helps the virus evade cell-mediated immunity. That evasion contributes to pathogenesis, the way HIV causes disease.

The team showed a Nef fusion protein binds directly to a coat complex subunit. That subunit, part of the AP-1 endosomal complex, moves proteins inside cells. Direct binding pinpoints the machinery Nef hijacks. Blocking that contact could restore immune detection.
plos-pone-0008464:
Kornelis van Hateren and co-authors follow older diabetic patients in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They study type 2 diabetes and blood lipids over ten years. Lipids are fats such as cholesterol in the blood. How lipid levels relate to death risk in older patients was unclear. Guidelines built on younger adults may not fit this group.

The ZODIAC-13 study tracks lipid profiles and deaths over time. It asks which lipid measures predict who dies sooner. The answers can guide care for older patients in a more fitting way. They help weigh the gains and risks of lipid treatment at older ages.
plos-pone-0008564:
Mehregan Movassagh and co-authors link a DNA mark to heart failure in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Marks on DNA can switch genes off without changing the code. Two such mark types were already tied to bad gene control in heart failure. The role of a third mark, DNA methylation, was not known. The team study that mark in human heart failure samples. They compare it with levels of factors that grow new vessels.

Where the mark differs, those vessel factors are made at unlike levels. That link ties the mark to the gene program of the failing heart. It hints that drugs aimed at such marks could help. The work adds a new layer to heart failure research.
plos-pone-0008664:
Michiko Nakano and co-authors study promoter recognition in bacteria in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Spx is a global transcriptional regulator of the microbial stress response. It is highly conserved amongst Gram-positive bacteria. In Bacillus subtilis, Spx exerts positive and negative control of transcription. It acts through interaction with RNA polymerase, the enzyme that reads genes. The team examine recognition by a complex of Spx and the C-terminal domain of the polymerase alpha subunit.

They show how that complex recognizes stress gene promoters. Binding there switches on protective genes under stress. Bacillus is a model for many pathogenic Gram-positive relatives. Understanding Spx helps explain how those germs survive host defenses.
plos-pone-0008764:
Minerva Carrasquillo, Olivia Belbin, Fanggeng Zou, and colleagues tied a gene to Alzheimer disease from three angles. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene makes insulin-degrading enzyme, which can also break down amyloid-beta. Amyloid buildup marks Alzheimer brains. The gene sits in a region already linked to late-onset disease. That made it a strong candidate worth close testing.

The team scanned the gene and nearby DNA in cases and controls. Certain variants tracked with the gene's message levels. The same variants tracked with amyloid levels and with disease itself. Three matching links strengthen the case for this gene.
plos-pone-0008864:
Ryan Tasseff, Satyaprakash Nayak, Saniya Salim, and colleagues mapped weak and strong spots in prostate cancer's molecular networks. Their analysis appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Hormone-blocking therapy is the main treatment for spreading prostate cancer. Nearly always, the cancer eventually grows despite missing hormones. Cells rewire their networks to survive the loss. Which sub-networks bend and which break was the question.

Comparing hormone-dependent and independent cancers exposed fragile and robust subsystems. Fragile parts are candidate drug targets. Robust parts warn where single drugs will fail. Network maps can steer drug combinations toward the fragility.
plos-pone-0008964:
Maria Espinosa and co-authors gave a gene-control protein a second job in yeast, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, GCN5, adds chemical tags to the spools that wind up DNA. Those tags usually help switch genes on in baker's yeast. Evidence also hinted GCN5 touches DNA repair and other cell tasks.

The team showed GCN5 helps start DNA copying at the proper start sites. Cells lacking it fired their replication origins less effectively. So the same protein that opens genes for reading also helps launch their copying. The dual role links two of the cell's most basic routines.
plos-pone-0009064:
Manuela Pellegrini and co-authors floated young male germ cells in simulated weightlessness, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sperm formation hinges on spermatogonia entering meiosis, the dividing step that halves chromosomes. Lab culture systems for that step in mouse cells have been lacking. Progress on the whole process has suffered for it.

Under microgravity conditions, the germ cells matured more readily. More of them crossed into meiosis than in normal gravity cultures. Weightlessness acted like a developmental push rather than a stress. The trick could give reproductive biology a better lab model.
plos-pone-0009164:
Yusuke Niino, Kohji Hotta, and Kotaro Oka built a blue-glowing sensor for a key cell messenger, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cyclic GMP steers many body processes, from blood pressure to vision. It works alongside cyclic AMP and calcium signals. Watching all of them at once needs sensors in different colours.

Earlier cGMP sensors used energy-transfer pairs glowing green or yellow. A blue fluorescent sensor frees the other colours for more messengers. Cells carrying it can report cGMP live under the microscope. Multiparameter imaging can now track several signals in one cell.
plos-pone-0009264:
Gareth Williams and co-authors published this coral disease study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Coral diseases follow complicated patterns across a reef. Spread depends on the germ, the host, and the balance between them. Statistical modeling, common in other disease fields, had been little used for corals.

The authors built predictive models of disease distribution within one reef system. Their models use environmental and reef features to forecast where disease appears. A good forecast tells managers where to watch and where to act first. The study shows modeling can bring order to coral disease data that otherwise looks chaotic.
plos-pone-0009364:
Jae-Beom Kim and co-authors published this cancer imaging study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Finding tumors early can change how treatment ends. A classic question in imaging is how few cancer cells can be seen inside a living animal. The team used cancer cells engineered to glow, a trick called bioluminescence.

They pushed the light output of the cells higher to test the limits. With brighter cells, even a small number could be detected without surgery. Knowing the detection floor guides drug studies in mice, where hidden tumors must be counted. It also marks how far non-invasive imaging still has to go for human use.
plos-pone-0009464:
Angelo Livolsi and colleagues looked for a clue to sudden infant death in PLOS ONE in 2010. The syndrome, called SIDS, is the main cause of death for babies under one year. Past work had found odd brain signals in some victims. No clear fault in the rest of the body had been shown. The team studied heart tissue from infants who died of SIDS.

Hearts from these infants had too many muscarinic receptors. Those receptors slow the heart when they are switched on. Too many of them could make a baby's heart more prone to slow or stop in sleep. The finding gives a first body based lead on a long standing mystery.
plos-pone-0009564:
Marc Schwartz and co-authors studied metal detox in a tiny worm in PLOS ONE in 2010. Cadmium and other heavy metals poison soil and water. Worms of the species C. elegans can survive metals that would kill many animals. A pump protein called HMT-1 is needed for cadmium defense. Scavenger cells called coelomocytes also take up waste. The team tested how the two work together.

The pump and the scavenger cells proved to be partners in one defense system. Together they lock away several toxic metals, not just cadmium. Knowing the system in a simple animal gives a model for other species. It may guide ways to protect life in polluted places.
plos-pone-0009664:
Marc Tibber, Ayse Saygin, and Simon Grant scanned brains during prediction tasks in PLOS ONE in 2010. To catch or dodge, the brain must predict where a moving thing will be. That forward guess is called extrapolation. It happens both in perception and in eye movements, which track the moving target. The team measured brain activity while people did tasks needing each kind of prediction.

Their scans locate the networks that support both forms of extrapolation. Overlap and differences between the two maps show how prediction is shared. Understanding this machinery clarifies skills from sport to driving. It may also help design visual aids for people with prediction deficits.
plos-pone-0009764:
Simon Gengler and co-authors published a brain study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study tests learning-linked plasticity in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease. The mice carry two human gene changes and form amyloid plaques from a young age, first in the cortex and later in the hippocampus.

At four to six months, the mice matched healthy littermates on both tests, the team reports. At eight months, long-term strengthening of synapses was greatly impaired in the model mice. At fifteen months it was still weak, and a short-term measure had also fallen. The authors blame the growth of amyloid with age.
plos-pone-0009864:
Nga-Chi Lau and co-authors report a 2010 PLOS ONE yeast study on a protein called Not4p and how cells handle stress. Yeast here is Saccharomyces cerevisiae, a simple fungus used to study basic cell work. Not4p sits in a large protein group that controls gene messages.

The team found five sites where Not4p gains phosphate tags, a common on-off switch. Losing those tags did not remove a key chemical mark on gene-packaging proteins. Yet tagged Not4p helped yeast survive stress drugs, working beside a separate pathway tied to the BUR2 gene. Mutants lacking both routes fared even worse. Stress defense, the work suggests, runs on parallel lines.
plos-pone-0009964:
The bacteria that settle in a baby's gut may shape the child's allergy risk. Pei-Ying Hong and colleagues compared gut microbes in infants with and without eczema. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The study looked at babies in their first year.

Fecal microbiota are the microbes living in the gut, sampled from stool. Eczema is an itchy skin condition often tied to allergies. A comparative analysis asks which microbes differ between the two groups. Early gut differences could one day guide prevention of allergic disease. Eczema often starts in the first months of life.
plos-pone-0010064:
Anna-Karin E Svensson and co-authors examine ALS-linked protein variants in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. ALS is a fatal nerve disease. Many cases trace to SOD1, a paired protein that normally carries copper and zinc metals. Faults may raise rare, clump-prone forms of the protein.

Working with metal-free versions of five disease variants, the team measured how each fault shifts folding and pairing. Several variants greatly raised loose single units, folded or unfolded, which can seed clumps. One variant near the metal site looked near normal. Even normal SOD1 without its metals may clump, the authors warn, so metal loss itself could matter in disease.
plos-pone-0010164:
The authors were Kristen Baltgalvis, Sarah Greising, Gordon Warren, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study used mice to study estrogen and muscle. When the ovaries are removed, female mice lose muscle strength. Giving back a form of estrogen restores that strength in the mice.

The team asked how estrogen controls its own receptors in muscle. They also tracked genes that help muscle fight oxidative stress. Age raises that stress, which can weaken muscle over time. Linking hormone, receptor, and defense genes may suggest ways to keep strength in older women.
plos-pone-0010264:
The authors were Lee Wheldon, Bryan Haines, Rajit Rajappa, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study probed a protein family called FLRT. These proteins both help cells stick together and boost signaling by fibroblast growth factor, or FGF. How they achieve the boosting effect was unknown, and that gap is what the team set out to investigate.

They found that phosphorylation, a phosphate tag on FLRT1, plays a critical role. That tag links FLRT1's own function with FGF receptor signaling in an interdependent way. The link may explain how growing tissues coordinate adhesion with growth signals.
plos-pone-0010364:
Aubree Gordon and colleagues checked a rapid flu test during the 2009 H1N1 pandemic for PLOS ONE in 2010. With a new flu strain spreading, doctors needed fast and correct answers. A bedside kit promised results in minutes rather than days. The team ran a forward-looking study of how accurate that kit really was. They compared its calls against fuller lab testing.

Rapid tests trade some accuracy for speed, and the size of that trade matters. A missed case can send an infectious patient home without advice. A false alarm can waste scarce care and medicine. This study measured both error types in a real outbreak setting. Its numbers helped clinics decide when to trust the quick kit.
plos-pone-0010464:
Yoon-Dong Yu, Yoonjoo Choi and Yik-Ying Teo built math models of how bacteria swim toward food for PLOS ONE in 2010. Real biology is uneven in space, and position matters. Proteins inside cells often cluster at spots rather than spreading evenly. Randomness also rules at the tiny scale of single cells. Their models combined space and chance to capture bacterial chemotaxis, the steering of bacteria along chemical trails.

Stochastic models accept randomness as part of the answer, not noise to hide. Such models can predict patterns that smooth equations miss. Bacteria chasing food is a classic test system for cell signaling. Better models there inform fields from infection to soil ecology. The study offers tools for spatial inference in messy living systems.
plos-pone-0010564:
Mel Slater and colleagues gave people a first-person experience of body transfer into a virtual body in PLOS ONE in 2010. Touch illusions can make a fake limb feel like one's own. In the classic trick, seen and felt touch on a rubber hand create ownership. This team extended the idea to a whole virtual body viewed from inside. Participants saw the virtual body from its own viewpoint while touch was applied.

People reported feeling the virtual body as theirs. That whole-body transfer goes beyond hand tricks in scale. It matters for virtual reality design, telepresence, and studies of self-awareness. It also raises questions about how flexible bodily identity really is. The study demonstrates the effect under controlled conditions.
plos-pone-0010664:
Erik Van der Burg and colleagues studied how sound sharpens visual search, in PLOS ONE in 2010. A beep played at the same moment as a flash can make the flash easier to spot. Earlier work had cast doubt on whether the effect truly helps search.

The team varied the kind of sound and flash pairing people searched with. Search improved only when the paired events were brief, sudden changes. Steady or drawn-out signals gave no benefit. So the brain links sights and sounds by their timing, not just by overlap. The rule matters for alarms and displays that pair lights with tones.
plos-pone-0010764:
Michiro Susa and colleagues used nanoparticles to disarm drug resistance in bone cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Chemotherapy raised osteosarcoma survival greatly over thirty years. Tumors that return after treatment often resist many drugs at once. A cell pump called ABCB1 throws drugs back out before they can work.

Tiny particles carried silencing RNA into tumor cells to switch off the pump gene. With the pump reduced, standard drugs regained their punch. Delivery is the hard part of RNA medicine, and the particle design matters as much as the message. The approach offers a route for rescuing proven drugs instead of replacing them.
plos-pone-0010864:
Philippe Buchy, Sirenda Vong, Simon Chu and co-authors published this study of bird flu patients in PLOS ONE in 2010. H5N1 is a dangerous avian virus that occasionally infects people, and little was known about how their protective antibodies rise and fade. The team tracked blood samples from severely ill patients and from people exposed without symptoms.

Nearly all sick patients had measurable neutralizing antibodies within two to three weeks of falling ill. Antibody levels in severe cases ran higher than in silent infections at first, then declined over the following year in both groups. Buchy and colleagues used two lab assays that largely agreed. Knowing how long these antibodies last helps officials judge past outbreaks and plan vaccine studies for a feared pandemic strain.
plos-pone-0010964:
Irene Cervelló, Claudia Gil-Sanchis, Aymara Mas and co-authors published this stem cell study in PLOS ONE in 2010. The lining of the uterus rebuilds itself hundreds of times over a lifetime, shedding and regrowing with each cycle. Such renewal implies a resident stem cell pool, and the authors tested whether a distinctive cell fraction, the side population, is that pool.

They isolated side population cells from both layers of the tissue and checked their gene signatures, surface markers, and enzyme patterns. Under low-oxygen culture the cells formed colonies and could be coaxed toward fat and bone lineages, hallmarks of somatic stem cells. Cervelló and colleagues present converging evidence that these cells are the endometrium's regenerative reserve. Identifying them opens paths to treating uterine disorders and understanding diseases such as endometriosis.
plos-pone-0011064:
Sufang Zhang, Jianing Wei, Xiaojiao Guo and co-authors published this plant-insect study in PLOS ONE in 2010. In a three-level food chain of plant, herbivore, and the herbivore's parasitoid enemy, each partner keeps its own daily rhythm. Whether those rhythms are coordinated, and by what signals, was unknown, so the team studied lima bean, a leafminer pest, and its parasitoid wasp.

They found the rhythms correlate in both directions. Feeding by the herbivore set the rhythm of the plant's volatile emissions. Those in turn patterned the parasitoid's activity. Light acted as the synchronizing switch. Stronger volatile doses boosted wasp movement and egg laying only in the light. Experienced wasps could also exploit rhythm differences from the top down. Zhang and colleagues reveal a food chain keeping time together, an insight for timing pest control releases.
plos-pone-0011164:
Treuner-Lange catalogued signaling proteins in PLOS ONE in 2010. Two kinds of social bacteria live in groups and coordinate complex behavior, rare traits among bacteria. The author listed their full sets of proteins that add or remove phosphate tags, the main on and off switches in bacterial signaling.

Comparing those sets with other bacteria showed how rich signaling grows with social life. A wide switch set lets a germ sense and respond to many cues. That helps explain how these bacteria build group structures and hunt in packs. The catalogue is a reference for anyone studying how bacterial complexity evolved.
plos-pone-0011264:
Kojima, Gatfield, Esau and colleagues studied the mouse liver clock in PLOS ONE in 2010. A liver enzyme that trims RNA messages rises and falls on a daily rhythm. The team found a small RNA, abundant in liver, modulates that rhythm across the day night cycle.

That fine tuning links the clock to how the liver handles food and energy. Small RNAs were not thought to be central clock parts, so the role is notable. It helps explain how daily rhythms stay precise despite noisy cell conditions. The insight informs metabolism research, where clock faults and diet interact.
plos-pone-0011364:
Andrew Jefferson and co-authors examined cell nuclei from people with ICF syndrome in a 2010 study. ICF is a rare inherited disorder that weakens the immune system and alters marks on DNA. In a healthy nucleus, tightly packed DNA and loose active genes sit in set zones, and that layout helps genes work in an orderly way.

In cells from patients, the layout of packed DNA and of certain genes was disturbed. Regions that should sit at the nucleus edge or in quiet zones had shifted. The finding links the faulty DNA marks of the syndrome to a scrambled nuclear map. That connection may explain part of how the disease disrupts immunity, and it shows why the three-dimensional order inside the nucleus deserves as much attention as the DNA code itself.
plos-pone-0011464:
Alexander Kurz and co-authors studied in 2010 how a Parkinson's-linked protein variant damages brain circuits in old mice. The A53T variant of alpha-synuclein causes an inherited early form of Parkinson's disease, and mice making extra copies of it mimic parts of the illness. The team focused on dopamine signaling and on the striatum, a movement center that depends on dopamine.

In old mice, excess mutant protein crippled dopamine signaling and weakened the striatum's ability to adjust its connections, a flexibility called synaptic plasticity. Both the chemical message and the circuit's capacity to learn from it were failing together. That double breakdown maps where the disease process bites into the movement machinery. It also tells drug testers which two functions a treatment must rescue, not just one, to count as real protection.
plos-pone-0011564:
Hana Zouk, Luc Marchand, and Constantin Polychronakos zoomed in 2010 on one immune gene's local regulation. IFIH1 senses viral RNA inside cells and raises the alarm, and its variants are linked to type 1 diabetes and lupus. The team studied transcriptional effects in cis at this locus, meaning effects of nearby DNA variants on the activity of the gene copy sitting on the same chromosome.

Cis effects are the fine print of genetic risk: a variant need not change a protein at all, only how much of it is made, and in which copy. Pinning such effects at one disease locus shows how small regulatory tweaks tilt immune balance toward self-attack. The approach generalizes to hundreds of disease loci where the risk variant changes no protein. Risk, in those places, is a volume knob rather than a broken part, and this study shows how to read the knob's setting.
plos-pone-0011664:
Robert Planqué, Jan Bouwe van den Berg and Nigel Franks compared how ant colonies summon help, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Ants recruit nestmates to food or new homes by varied means, from one-to-one tandem runs to group trips and scent trails. Colony size differs hugely across species, and a loose link between size and recruitment style was already suspected.

The authors tested that link systematically across species. Their comparison shows how recruitment strategy fits colony scale, with small colonies relying on personal guidance and large ones on mass methods. The pattern reveals an organising logic for insect societies of very different sizes.
plos-pone-0011764:
Shiwen Zhao and Shao Li built a network method for finding drug targets, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Finding what a drug should hit is a key step in pharmacology. Drug effects and chemical measures had most often been studied apart from gene data, and target hunts tended to stay within a narrow set of known proteins.

Their method links drug space and gene space through networks, bridging the two fields. The bridge widens the pool of target suspects well past the usual short list. Better target picks early on can save years of failed drug work later in the pipeline.
plos-pone-0011864:
Gianfranco De Feo and co-authors measured in 2010 how long it takes to start non-profit cancer trials in Italy. Their data came from the National Cancer Institute of Naples after recent European laws changed the approval process. They tracked the activation of five multi-center trials run without commercial backing.

The record shows where the months go between a finished trial plan and the first patient enrolled. Independent trials answer questions drug companies may skip, such as comparing existing treatments, so delays carry a real cost for patients. Laying out the timeline step by step gives reformers concrete points to attack rather than a general complaint about red tape.
plos-pone-0011964:
Raphaël Ioannoni and co-workers followed in 2010 how a fission yeast moves its copper import machinery as copper levels change. Copper is essential but toxic in excess, so cells meter it carefully. In Schizosaccharomyces pombe, uptake runs through a two-protein complex, Ctr4 and Ctr5, sitting at the cell surface.

The team tracked the complex's location and found copper-dependent trafficking: the importers are repositioned as copper availability shifts. Moving the doorway rather than rebuilding it lets the cell fine-tune how many importers sit at the surface at any moment. That design is a general lesson in how cells handle nutrients that are also poisons.
plos-pone-0012064:
Verónica Di Stilio and co-workers adapted in 2010 a virus-based trick to switch off genes in meadow-rue plants, genus Thalictrum. These woodland herbs show wide variety in flower shape and run four breeding systems and two pollination systems. Their position near the base of the eudicot family tree makes them prime material for studying how flowers evolved.

Virus-induced gene silencing infects a plant with a modified virus that shuts down a chosen gene, revealing what that gene does. Applying the tool in a non-model genus like Thalictrum opens comparative functional studies that were previously limited to a few lab plants. Flower diversity finally gets a direct experimental handle.
plos-pone-0012164:
Sunil Sazawal, Usha Dhingra, Girish Hiremath, and co-authors ran a community trial of fortified milk for young children, reported in PLOS ONE in 2010. Infections still kill many preschool children in poorer countries, and cheap ways to cut that toll are a pressing public health need. The team gave children milk fortified with helpful live bacteria and the food that feeds them, and compared illness rates with a control group.

A large trial run in real neighborhoods, with treatments and dummy versions assigned by chance and hidden from families, gives answers a clinic study cannot. If fortified milk cuts illness, it is a strategy markets can deliver daily without doctors. The results feed directly into child health policy where the burden is highest.
plos-pone-0012264:
Koen Verhoeven, George Casella, and Lauren McIntyre asked whether gene interactions help or hinder the mapping of complex traits, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Most gene hunts scan one marker at a time, yet evidence keeps growing that genes interact, with one gene's effect depending on another's state. Those interactions, called epistasis, are often treated as a nuisance that clouds the simple signals.

The authors weigh the opposite case: interactions can be an advantage, revealing trait genes that single scans miss entirely. Complex traits from crop yield to human disease may hide much of their genetics in such interplay. How a field treats epistasis decides how much of that hidden inheritance it will ever find.
plos-pone-0012364:
Srabanti Chaudhury and Oleg Igoshin explored the noisy inner life of enzymes in a 2010 PLOS ONE theory paper. An enzyme's shape and speed flicker over time, sometimes fast and sometimes slow. In some cases the average speed still obeys the classic Michaelis-Menten rule taught in textbooks, but the flicker can change how reactions behave.

The authors worked out when the classic rule holds for near-equilibrium enzyme systems and when random flicker, called dynamic disorder, bends the outcome. Their math gives chemists a clearer guide for reading enzyme data. It matters for designing drugs and industrial enzymes, where small speed changes can shift yields and side effects.
plos-pone-0012464:
Anmaar Abdul-Nabi, Enas Yassin, Nobish Varghese and colleagues transformed human blood stem cells in a dish with leukemia fusion genes, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Acute myeloid leukemia often starts when two genes fuse into an abnormal one. Each fusion gives the disease its own look and course, suggesting each transforms cells its own way.

By adding fusions to primary human CD34 cells and reading early gene changes, the team found candidate drug targets among the first switches thrown. Early changes are the closest to the root cause, before secondary chaos sets in. The dish model lets scientists test fusion-specific drugs without waiting for rare patient samples.
plos-pone-0012564:
Chun Hei Cheung, Su-Ying Wu, Tian-Ren Lee and colleagues studied how cancer cells learn to dodge anti-mitotic drugs, in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Drugs like vincristine and vinblastine jam the microtubule ropes that pull chromosomes apart, and they cure many cancers — until resistance emerges. Microtubules are built from tubulin, including the beta I form the team examined.

Mutations in beta I tubulin and shifts in which tubulin types the cell used gave cells drug resistance during division. Knowing the exact escape changes lets chemists design next-generation blockers that grip differently. It also suggests tests to predict which patients' tumors already carry the escape.
plos-pone-0012664:
Boue, Paramonov, Barrero and co-authors reviewed how lab-made stem cells are produced in humans and mice. Two decades of debate over embryo stem cells changed when, in 2006, ordinary body cells were reprogrammed into induced pluripotent stem cells. Their 2010 paper takes stock of what sits in the culture dish during that change.

They compare methods, cell quality and the gaps between mouse and human work. Careful stock-taking keeps a fast, hopeful field honest about what its cells can and cannot do. The review helps labs judge which cell batches deserve trust.
plos-pone-0012764:
Diallo, Remoue, Gaayeb and co-authors studied how one parasite infection shapes a child's defence against another. In the tropics, malaria and schistosomiasis often infect the same children at the same time. Their 2010 study asked whether carrying the water-borne Schistosoma parasite changes antibody answers to the malaria parasite.

They measured children's antibodies against malaria antigens with and without the second infection. Coinfection effects matter because vaccine trials usually assume one disease at a time. If a second parasite bends immunity, malaria vaccine results need reading with that in mind.
plos-pone-0328664:
Arturo Franco-Andrés and colleagues follow a squad of semi-professional women volleyball players across the days around one match, tracking jump power and felt recovery. The countermovement jump is a quick, painless check on leg freshness. A dozen players were tested before the match and at set hours after it. Jump measures were split by how much court time each player saw. Recovery and well-being ratings were taken too.

Jump height and related measures dipped most clearly around the second day after the match. Patterns differed by playing time. Players were expected back at baseline by then, but they were not always there. Felt recovery, by contrast, barely moved. Franco-Andrés and colleagues caution coaches not to trust feelings alone when judging whether legs are ready.
plos-pone-0332164:
Jiao Wu and colleagues improved a fast image analysis model so it can outline the figures in Thangka paintings, the intricate sacred scrolls of Tibetan Buddhism. In these images, deities blend into busy backgrounds filled with ritual objects and ornament, blurring the edges that computer vision needs. Their upgrades sharpen attention on informative details and blend local and global features while keeping the model quick.

On a custom Thangka dataset the model labelled regions with solid accuracy while running at more than one hundred frames per second, fast enough for live use. It also generalised well on a standard city-scene benchmark, beating its baseline there too. The authors offer the tool for digital preservation and restoration work, where scholars must map damaged or crowded paintings quickly and reliably.
plos-pone-0333564:
Sarvenaz Heirani Moghaddam, Erin Krista Cressman, and Gerome Aleandro Manson asked whether people learn mirror reversed reaching without knowing it. Forty two right handed adults reached with a robot arm to targets beside the body. Half saw their cursor rotated, half saw it flipped like a mirror, both by a small amount. No cursor test reaches then probed hidden, automatic learning.

Everyone mastered the rotation, but only about half mastered the mirror flip. Rotation learners showed clear automatic learning on test reaches. Mirror learners showed none, even those who managed the task. Mirror reaching seems learned by conscious strategy alone, a useful warning for rehab and training design with flipped feedback.
plos-pone-0333864:
Shyun Ping Tiong and colleagues used artificial intelligence to sift the outcome lists that neurology trials are told to measure, hunting for the structure beneath them. Core outcome sets exist to make trials comparable, but neurology, which touches three billion people, has built few of them. The team mined a global database of such sets, let the AI cluster their domains, and had experts review the groupings.

Common patterns emerged across very different brain disorders, enough to draft a reference framework, called COS-Neuro, describing the domain families future sets tend to need. Trial designers starting a set for an unlisted condition can begin from this skeleton instead of a blank page. The authors present it as a descriptive aid, not a mandate, and the expert pass over the machine's clusters is part of the method's honesty.
plos-pone-0336064:
Zahra Asadollahi Seyedabadi and co-authors examined how feed ferments inside the stomachs of cattle and sheep, using lab glassware that traps the gas released. Their 2026 PLOS One study compared mixed rations with different shares of roughage and concentrate feed, some with added buffers that keep acidity steady.

Four curve-fitting formulas were tried against the gas readings, and none won in every case. S-shaped curves matched buffered feeds best, while simpler rising curves suited rich, unbuffered feeds. Added buffers steadied acidity, raised total gas, and changed the mix of acids formed. The lesson is practical: pick the math model that fits the diet being tested.
plos-pone-0341564:
Yue Luo and co-workers test whether a very low-carbohydrate ketogenic diet can ease autoimmune thyroid disease in mice. In this disease, the immune system attacks the thyroid gland, and few diet options are proven. Their 2026 study triggers the disease with iodine in a prone mouse strain, then feeds some animals the special diet for four weeks.

Diet-fed mice showed less thyroid damage, fewer attack antibodies, and calmer swelling signals than diseased mice on normal food. A key alarm pathway quieted, and the balance between attacking and calming immune cells swung back toward normal. Signs of chemical stress in tissue also eased. The mouse results support testing the diet carefully as a helper beside standard thyroid care.
plos-pone-0341764:
Ruya Fan, Yan Chen, and Bo Shan present this 2026 PLOS One methods paper on matching donated organs to patients fairly and stably. The matching problem has three sides: donors, recipients, and the hospitals involved, each with their own preferences and uncertain information. The authors build a model that handles fuzzy preference data, the random timing of donor arrivals, and the risk that recipients might misreport their situation.

They prove their matching approach is stable, meaning no group would rather break away and re-match on its own. An improved optimization algorithm searches for good matchings, and simulations in a transplant setting showed steadier results and better use of scarce organs. The work is a contribution to allocation theory, aimed at systems where a poor match wastes a life-saving resource.
plos-pone-0342964:
Christopher Freeman simulates workplace fraud inside computer-model organisations to ask how fraud behaves as companies grow, in this exploratory 2026 PLOS ONE study. Real fraud data show only detected cases, so the underlying patterns stay hidden. His simulated employees influenced each other across networks, in nine thousand runs spanning tiny firms to organisations of several thousand people, with varying peer pressure and connectedness.

Average and peak fraud grew in simple proportion to size. But fraud's volatility — how wildly it swings — grew much faster: doubling the workforce roughly multiplied swinginess by two and a half. Peer influence and connectedness fed the swings, not the average. Big organisations, Freeman argues, face a fraud-risk shape that headcounts of past cases cannot reveal.
plos-pone-0344264:
Aber Sharon Kagwa and colleagues interviewed thirteen Swedish social care professionals about why families from non-European backgrounds caring for a relative with dementia so rarely use the support offered to them. Sweden's municipalities are charged with helping family caregivers, yet uptake gaps persist. The professionals described the obstacles and openings they meet in daily work.

Eight themes emerged, led by mistrust of the system, the sheer difficulty of reaching these families, mismatched expectations, and the stigma dementia carries in some communities. Contact early, speaking through the younger generation, and adapting the offer rather than repeating it all helped, as did coordinating with community groups. The authors conclude that culturally shaped, trust-building support, delivered through many channels, is the route to closing the gap.
plos-pone-0345964:
Jack W Wheelahan, Michael Lynch, and co-authors investigated a deadly herpesvirus outbreak in a captive herd of Asian elephants in Australia. The virus, known as EEHV1B, can kill young elephants within days through severe bleeding. Their 2026 study followed one nine-year-old elephant that died, testing herd samples collected before and after the illness and reading the virus's full genome from infected tissue.

Blood virus levels peaked the day after signs appeared, showing how fast the disease moves. Among storage methods, samples kept in transport medium gave the best DNA recovery, though frozen tissue without medium still worked.
