The genome proved close to a known 1B strain yet carried signs of mixing with the 1A type. Such mixing between virus types could affect how the disease behaves and how tests detect it.
plos-pone-0346164:
Humberto Pereira and colleagues introduce in 2026 an updated code system for giving biological sequences a short, unique fingerprint. Fingerprints help labs check that a DNA or protein file has not changed and find its notes quickly. The older system could not handle circular DNA or DNA with two strands, both common in plasmids used worldwide.

The new version gives the same fingerprint no matter where a circular sequence starts or which strand is read first. Packages for several common programming languages were released openly, plus an online calculator. Custom alphabets extend the idea beyond standard DNA and RNA as well.
plos-pone-0346464:
Marilyn Reese and colleagues fed tobacco hornworm larvae extra iron to test whether it helps the microbes that infect them. Iron is essential for insects and bacteria alike, and germs must steal it from their host. The team's 2026 experiment combined iron-rich diets, with or without antibiotics, and two kinds of bacteria.

Iron feeding raised blood iron greatly, yet bacterial loads did not rise for either microbe. Survival effects were mixed and depended on antibiotics. With a harmful bacterium and no antibiotics, iron actually helped larvae live longer; with antibiotics, it shortened survival. The results reject the simple idea that dietary iron fuels infection in this insect, and point to a more tangled role.
plos-pone-0346564:
Laura Drew and colleagues ask whether racist attitudes in a state track with high blood pressure in pregnancy, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. They paired United States birth certificate records from 2016 to 2021, covering more than twenty-two million single births, with a sample of tweets scored for negative feeling toward racial and ethnic minorities.

People living in states with the most hostile scores had clearly higher rates of blood pressure problems both before and during pregnancy. The authors also compared the years before 2020 with the pandemic and protest years that followed. The work adds area-level attitudes to the list of forces that may shape unequal birth outcomes.
plos-pone-0346664:
Yusheng Zhang and Adrian Collins model how the environmental footprint of intensive farming in England changed over time, in this 2026 PLOS ONE paper. Using a process-based model, they calculated footprints for 2010, 2016, and 2021 for every water management catchment, the units English policy uses for reporting.

They tracked warming impact over short and long horizons, plus pollution that overfeeds waterways and pollution that acidifies soil and rain. By 2021, shifts such as fewer cattle and less dairy land had cut the typical warming footprint by about a fifth compared with 2010, though some catchments barely improved. The authors caution that modeled trends are hard to check against real monitoring data.
plos-pone-0346864:
Hyeongcheol Kim and his team read the DNA of four dogs buried long ago in Korea. Three came from a site at Neuk-do, from about the third century BCE. One came from a site at Gimhae, a few hundred years younger. The 2026 study asks where these dogs fit in the dog family tree.

The old Korean dogs were close kin to the dingo and the New Guinea Singing Dog. Yet they were not the same, and they form their own branch in East Asia. They also carried genes from dogs far to the west. That mix had already begun before the third century BCE, and it grew in later years.
plos-pone-0347664:
Pratibha Bhandari and colleagues surveyed three hundred and forty-three ninth and tenth graders in Tokha municipality, Nepal, about how their parents raise them and how they feel about themselves. Standard scales sorted parenting into warm and structured, strict, or lax styles, and measured each teenager's self-esteem. About one adolescent in six scored low on self-esteem.

Warm, structured parenting tracked with higher self-esteem, while strict and lax styles both tracked with lower scores. Older students were somewhat protected. Students at private schools, and those whose fathers had little schooling, faced higher odds of low self-esteem. The authors urge schools and parent programmes in Nepal to promote the warm, structured style, noting that family habits formed at home echo through a teenager's confidence at school and beyond.
plos-pone-0347764:
Rayane Barcelos Bisi, Ute Albrecht, Randall P. Niedz, and Kim D. Bowman tuned LED lighting recipes for young grafted citrus trees growing through short winter days. Nurseries lose growth in winter light, and modern lamps let growers choose colour and brightness precisely. Two rootstocks budded with navel orange received daylight stretched to sixteen hours, topped up with lamp light in many colour blends.

Blue and white light woke buds and built chlorophyll in the two rootstocks, most when turned up bright. Red light and far-red light alone held budbreak back. The fullest shoot growth came from mixing red, blue, and white at top intensity. Far-red helped only in combination. The recipes can raise winter propagation efficiency for nurseries.
plos-pone-0348064:
Juliet Rowe, Theresa Gaughan, and Shaun Boe survey how researchers have studied motor imagery with qualitative methods, in this 2026 PLOS ONE scoping review. Motor imagery means mentally rehearsing a movement without doing it, a technique used by athletes and in rehabilitation, and most research on it uses numbers rather than interviews or open accounts.

Thirty-nine studies qualified. Well over half came from sport psychology and most studied athletes, usually asking how a group uses imagery. Over half named no specific research design, and only one study looked at learning through imagery. The authors say the field knows much about athletes' habits but little about how imagery is experienced or learned, and they call for clearer designs.
plos-pone-0348264:
María Pía Peláez Caro and colleagues mine a huge goat-breeding data set. Their paper appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The breed is the Murciano-Granadina dairy goat of Spain. The question is whether chasing more milk trades off against breeding success. Records held nearly thirty-three thousand inseminations. They covered more than twenty-one thousand goats.

Fresh or chilled semen beat frozen semen by a wide margin. Milk output swung hugely between animals. Milk makeup stayed fairly steady, though. Math tools that hunt shared patterns found a compact result. A small set of pathways links milk traits to fertility traits. Breeders can use that map. They can pick goats that milk well and still breed well.
plos-pone-0348364:
Asim Shoaib and co-authors present a method for picking out buildings in high-resolution satellite and aerial images, a basic step for city planning and land records. Buildings blend easily with roads and trees, and simple methods chop regions wrongly or miss small structures. Their approach first over-splits the image into small patches, then merges patches using deep features learned by a neural network, with thresholds that adjust themselves.

Guiding merges by learned features rather than colour alone keeps building edges cleaner and reduces the misalignment that plagues older merging methods. On a standard benchmark set of city images, the method outperformed the alternatives the team tested. The authors aim the technique at mapping tasks where fast, accurate building outlines matter for fast-growing urban areas.
plos-pone-0348764:
Ashenafi Miresa and a large team analysed the natural mineral springs, called hora, and surrounding soils that Ethiopian herders use as free mineral supplements for cattle. Samples from several districts in the southwest were tested for water quality measures and for a dozen minerals, then compared against what cattle can safely take in.

Many values sat within safe ranges, and the springs genuinely carry useful minerals. But some samples ran very salty, with high dissolved solids and ammonia that raise doubts, and the soils held iron, molybdenum, and manganese above the maximum levels cattle tolerate. The authors conclude that these traditional sources can help fill mineral gaps, yet unsupervised grazing on the soils risks poisoning, so herders need guidance on how much access is safe.
plos-pone-0348864:
Muhammad Rashid Majeed and colleagues propose OracleTrust, a security scheme for blockchains that rely on outside data feeds called oracles. If the data attached to a transaction can be quietly altered, attackers can double-spend or corrupt records. Earlier fixes each covered part of the problem but none bound the oracle's data to the transaction itself.

OracleTrust works in two layers. First, each transaction is encoded into a verifiable record of where its data came from. Then a smart contract checks that record before the transaction joins the chain. Binding origin proof to every transaction aims to close the malleability gap that oracle-driven systems still face in lending and other finance uses.
plos-pone-0349064:
Liton Chandra Sen and co-workers study whether short health lessons can ease painful periods among female university students in Bangladesh. Painful periods are the most common menstrual problem for young women and often spoil study and daily life. Their 2026 study compares students who attended three behavior-change sessions with matched students who did not.

In matched pairs, painful periods were less common among students who attended the sessions. The gap was large, about twenty-three points in percentage terms, and held across several ways of checking the math. Students in the lesson group also reported habits such as regular exercise more often. The results suggest low-cost talks on campus could help many students, though the study design cannot prove cause on its own.
plos-pone-0349164:
Zhenxing Li and colleagues asked whether integrative neuromuscular training, a mix of strength, balance, and movement drills, could lift the fitness of elite Sanda fighters. Sanda is a Chinese combat sport built on kicks, punches, and throws. Twenty-six top male athletes were split at random between the new training and a standard conditioning programme for twelve weeks.

Fighters on the new programme improved across nearly every test, from bench press and squat strength to sprint speed, jumping, reaction agility, and balance. The standard group barely moved. The gains were large and consistent, which suggests that varied neuromuscular work fills gaps that routine conditioning misses in a sport that demands power and quick reactions at once.
plos-pone-0349564:
Mikhail Y Kartashov and co-authors surveyed tick borne phleboviruses across Asian Russia in 2026. These emerging viruses can infect people, yet their spread in the region's taiga ticks was poorly charted.

More than a thousand ticks from over a hundred forty sites were screened in summer 2023, and positive samples were sequenced and modelled. Four virus types turned up at low rates, with one the most common. Family trees suggested one virus sits inside another's species complex, and its shell protein resembles that of two known fever viruses. Baseline maps like this let health agencies judge a little known risk.
plos-pone-0349664:
Nader Iskandar Hamwi and Hamam Adib Altajer fed African catfish five diets for twelve weeks to test cheaper replacements for fishmeal, the costly protein in fish feed. Four balanced diets swapped in poultry by-product meal and brewer's yeast at different levels. A fifth diet was deliberately unbalanced: poultry meal alone, with no added fats, carbohydrates, or micronutrients, mimicking risky low-cost feeding.

A middle mix, with moderate fishmeal, the most poultry meal among balanced diets, and some yeast, gave the fastest growth, the best feed efficiency, and the healthiest liver and blood readings. The unbalanced diet left fish in visible metabolic stress. The pairing of a winning recipe and a warning case gives small fish farmers practical guidance on cutting costs safely.
plos-pone-0349764:
Naif Taleb Ali, Mansour Abdulnabia H Mehdi, and Radfan Saleh Abdullah tracked the children of related parents in Yemen over twenty-six years to measure how survival differs by disorder. Marriages between relatives are common in Yemen and raise the chance of recessive genetic conditions. Their 2026 review covered more than three thousand offspring from over a thousand families, verifying deaths and their causes from multiple sources.

Survival to age five ranged starkly: lowest for blood disorders at about forty-two percent, and highest for sensory impairments above ninety percent. Children of first cousins faced close to three times the adjusted death risk of unrelated parents' children. Different disorders killed at different ages, with structural birth defects dominating infancy. The authors say the patterns can guide counseling and early care for the highest-risk conditions.
plos-pone-0349864:
Xiao Xiao, Deyu Liu, and Hai Qin designed a vision-guided grasping system to help robots pick recyclable bottles out of kitchen waste without fumbling. Dirty, slippery bottles cause missed and failed grabs in automated sorting. Their 2026 method first detects and locates bottles, then a generative network reads color and depth images to propose the best grasp points and grip boxes.

On a standard public grasping dataset the method inferred grasps accurately and quickly for single objects. On the team's own kitchen waste images it generated grasp boxes and named object categories at the same time, scoring above ninety-four percent on their accuracy measures. The authors present the framework as a step toward robots that can handle messy real-world waste, not just clean lab objects.
plos-pone-0350264:
Amril Nazir and six colleagues forecast COVID-19 case counts with a neural network and phone movement data. Their 2026 study tests a model called N-BEATS in four large countries: Brazil, Russia, Britain, and the United States. The virus spreads mainly through human contact. How people move should therefore foreshadow case curves. Mobility records from Google and Apple supplied that signal. Case data came from a public global dashboard.

N-BEATS beat the benchmark model everywhere. Its errors came out lower on both standard measures, across all datasets and countries. Adding mobility data improved it further. The same model without movement inputs performed worse, confirming the data's real value. Interpretability improved alongside accuracy, which matters when officials must explain forecasts. Epidemic planners gain a tool that reads tomorrow's case pressure partly from today's journeys, buying hospitals and governments precious days of warning.
plos-pone-0350664:
Jens Abraham and seven colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One process evaluation of COFRAIL, a German trial program for frail older people living at home. The program centered on family conferences where patients, relatives, and family doctors set health priorities and reviewed whether medicines could be safely stopped. The evaluation, running from 2019 to 2021, asked whether the program was delivered as planned and how participants experienced it.

Nearly all doctors completed their training, most patients attended at least two of the three conferences, and families said they felt genuinely involved in decisions. Few patients objected when medicines were discontinued, and doctors rarely found the format impractical, though a medication advice hotline went mostly unused. The main trial missed its primary goals, but the authors find no major delivery barriers and draw lessons for similar programs.
plos-pone-0351064:
Krittaphas Kangwanrattanakul, working alone, built a translation table between two health questionnaires widely used in Thailand. The short SF-12 survey is cheap to run but yields no utility score, the single number health economists need to compare treatments. Using a national sample of two thousand Thais, he fit a battery of statistical models, direct and indirect, to predict the utility-yielding EQ-5D answers from SF-12 responses.

A mixture model using age and selected SF-12 answers predicted best, with the smallest errors under cross-checking, while the indirect route lagged. The author warns the table was built on a mostly healthy sample and may drift for sicker groups. For Thai studies that collected only the short survey, the algorithm rescues economic analysis that would otherwise be impossible, provided users heed that warning.
plos-pone-0351164:
Hibeb Alejandra Silvestre Tuch and five colleagues report Guatemala's first national survey of what tuberculosis costs its patients, conducted in 2023 and published in 2026. Treatment itself is free, but travel, lost work, and extra food drain households. Interviewers reached five hundred thirty patients through forty-two facility clusters and counted costs against the threshold of catastrophe, spending above a fifth of yearly household income.

About thirty-six percent of households crossed that line. Poverty sharpened the blow: in adjusted sensitivity analyses two thirds of the poorest fifth faced catastrophic costs, against half of the richest fifth, a reminder that even the better-off were not safe. Younger adults were hit hardest, while larger households and lower-level facilities offered some protection. Coping strategies and social fallout tracked disadvantage closely. The authors map policy routes toward the national goal of zero catastrophic costs.
plos-pone-0351464:
Yanli Zhao led a team of eight authors on this 2026 poultry diagnostics study. A Mycoplasma bacterium sickens chickens, and flocks are vaccinated with a weakened strain that ordinary tests cannot tell apart from wild infection. Borrowing an enzyme from a heat-loving microbe that can spot a single letter change in DNA, the team paired it with standard amplification.

On twelve real samples the method correctly separated three vaccine strains from nine wild ones, at high sensitivity. Zhao offers poultry vets a reliable tool for watching disease spread after vaccination campaigns.
plos-pone-0351564:
A year after catching the Omicron variant of COVID-19, some people still feel unwell. Gunnhild Helmsdal and colleagues studied such long COVID cases in the Faroe Islands, comparing them with people verified never to have been infected, in this 2026 PLOS One clinical study.

Scores from a twenty-four item symptom list tracked strongly with belonging to the long COVID group. Tiredness, cloudy thinking, nerve symptoms, and chest and muscle complaints stood out most. Mental strain and fatigue each predicted the condition on their own. The authors say the pattern can help doctors recognize long COVID and plan follow-up care for those still struggling.
plos-pone-0351664:
Sei-Woong Choi and colleagues compared the genes of two moth species between mainland Mount Jirisan and island Mount Hallasan in South Korea, testing the textbook expectation that island populations lose genetic diversity. A hundred fifty-five moths were sequenced at a standard mitochondrial marker and sorted into family lines, with elevation gradients sampled on both mountains.

The two species refused to share a story. One held equally high diversity on island and mainland. The other, less diverse overall, was actually richer on the island. Both showed real mainland-island divergence yet free mixing within each mountain. Island erosion of diversity, it turns out, is a possibility, not a law: each species' history writes its own outcome, a warning against managing island wildlife by slogan.
plos-pone-0351764:
Sebastiano Cinetto and three colleagues preregister a test of whether breathing steers the numbers we invent. Their 2026 registered study grows from embodied cognition, the idea that bodily states shape thought. Volunteers will write random digits on a tablet at their own pace. A belt around the abdomen records each breath's phase and depth. Thirty participants give the design strong power for effects of the size reported before. Three hypotheses are fixed in advance.

Breathing in, the first predicts, will bias people toward larger numbers. Deeper abdominal expansion should also predict larger numbers on its own. Written digits themselves may grow bigger on inhaled, fuller breaths. The design's rigour is the point. Preregistration and a stringent setup mean a positive result would support body-to-mind influence. A null would bite as hard. Either way, the study sharpens a live debate about how abstract thought stays tethered to the body.
plos-pone-0351864:
Halid Worku Jemil and co-authors studied young children in Mali who suffer from anemia and poor nutrition at the same time. Using a recent national health survey, they looked for family and community traits linked to having both problems together. About one child in four in the survey had the combined condition, which makes it a heavy burden.

Risk ran higher when mothers had little or no schooling, lacked health insurance, lived in rural areas, or were short in stature. Taller mothers and slightly older toddlers were linked with lower odds of the combined condition. Because the two problems together raise the risk of death and lasting harm, the authors point to mothers' schooling, insurance cover, and rural services as places where help could matter most.
plos-pone-0351964:
Tebelay Dilnessa and four colleagues hunt for drug-resistant tuberculosis in Ethiopia's Amhara region. Their 2026 study enrols people suspected of pulmonary tuberculosis at the region's big hospitals. Rifampicin resistance is the warning flag for multidrug-resistant disease. It brings longer, harder treatment and more spread. Sputum samples were tested with a rapid gene machine. It detects the TB germ and rifampicin resistance in one run. Questionnaires captured patients' backgrounds and risk factors.

The study ran prospectively from April 2023 to May 2025 across several hospitals. Its design lets the team estimate how common resistance is among suspects, not only confirmed cases. Logistic models then connect resistance to patient characteristics. Ethiopia sits on the global high-burden list for tuberculosis. Regional numbers like these steer real decisions. They show where to place testing machines and which patients to watch closest. They also help keep first-line treatment working for everyone else.
plos-pone-0352164:
Ashraf Mahmoud Emara and three colleagues report this 2026 PLOS One cohort study on how much the body recovers during a three-week inpatient alcohol detoxification program. Fifty men with alcohol use disorder were compared with twenty-five healthy men, with blood, heart, and oxidative stress measures taken before and after the twenty-one-day program of medication and nutritional support.

Before treatment, patients differed from controls on several lipids, blood counts, blood pressure, and oxidative markers. After detox, red blood cell measures, one protective cholesterol, and cell counts rose, while heart rate, systolic pressure, a heart injury marker, and oxidative stress indicators fell. Some measures, including weight and one antioxidant enzyme, did not change. The authors describe the outcome as real but partial short-term recovery.
plos-pone-0352264:
Rahaf Zyad Attar and seven colleagues introduce this 2026 PLOS One report on a new Canadian registry for psoriatic arthritis, a chronic inflammatory disease affecting joints, skin, tendons, and nails. Registries capture the messy reality of everyday care that trials miss. The team describes how the registry recruits patients starting new therapy and presents the first eighteen months of results from its first hundred or so enrollees.

Most patients had arthritis in many joints plus skin psoriasis, and about half had tendon inflammation. Over eighteen months, reported outcomes improved, yet only a third of patients reached minimal disease activity, and tendon symptoms responded worst. Most patients stayed on their first therapy despite ongoing symptoms. The authors read this as evidence of unmet need that the growing registry will help characterize.
plos-pone-0352464:
Myo Oo, Soe Tint, and Somdeth Bodhisane present a plan, published in 2026, for a review of how depression links to clustered heart and metabolic disease. Living with several such ills at once is increasingly common and deadly. Depression's part in that clustering has never been pulled together. The plan is logged publicly and follows standard reporting rules. Searches will cover three databases from their start.

Studies that count are ones that observe rather than test treatments: cohort, case-control, and cross-sectional designs. All involve adults. Depression must be measured by proven tests, screening tools, or clinical codes. The cluster counts two or more heart or metabolic ills, with both kinds present. The review will weigh the link and estimate how often such clusters occur among adults with depression. As a plan, it fixes the questions and methods before answers are known. That guards the pooling from cherry-picking.
plos-pone-0352564:
Yadong Wang and coauthors published a study in PLOS ONE on the violent shaking that wears out coal-cutting machines, and on predicting when housings will crack from fatigue. In thin coal seams, the shearer's spiral drum meets rock bands of varying hardness, and field tests cannot separate the causes. The team built a coupled computer model of drum and rock, validated it against cutting tests, then varied rock hardness, blade angle, and speeds.

Rock hardness dominated everything, explaining most of the variation in vibration and raising peak shaking by roughly a third as it increased. A cross-type pick layout trimmed vibration noticeably. Feeding the validated loads through standard fatigue methods located the weak spots: lug transitions, the drum connection, and gear holes. Even in the worst condition, the shortest predicted fatigue life met service requirements. The workflow lets designers screen vibration and fatigue before building hardware.
plos-pone-0352664:
Haotian Han and five colleagues analyse traffic stability in a 2026 modelling study. Future roads will mix human-driven cars with connected automated vehicles. The automated cars drive best when they can share information with each other. The study asks what happens when that communication weakens or fails.

Their frequency-based framework tracks how small speed disturbances grow or fade along a line of traffic. When automated cars lost their shared information, they fell back on simpler solo control. The share of automated cars needed for stable flow then jumped sharply. Human drivers' varied styles mainly shrank the safe speed ranges rather than moving that threshold. Even a small loss of communication reliability could push the required share near total, a warning for engineers designing mixed traffic systems.
plos-pone-0352764:
Mohammad-Reza Esmaeili and four colleagues published this 2026 re-analysis of kidney filter cell injury in mice. Podocytes, the cells that wrap the kidney's filters, fail early in many kidney diseases. The team combined two public gene data sets from mice injured with a targeted toxin, comparing gene activity a few days apart.

A shared pattern emerged: early on, cells mounted an inflamed but adaptive response, then slid into a damaging state with scar-like rebuilding and failing protein cleanup. Well over a thousand genes moved together at each stage. Esmaeili frames the two-phase signature as a guide for timing future treatments.
plos-pone-0352864:
JianMei Wu, ChunYun Pu, and Li Zhang study why heart patients move less than they should. Their 2026 survey covers five hundred thirty-three people with atrial fibrillation in Chongqing, China. Heavy symptoms plainly discourage physical activity. The authors test two psychological links in between. One is exercise sensitivity, anxiety about bodily sensations during exertion. The other is kinesiophobia, fear that movement will cause harm.

Symptoms reduced activity directly, accounting for about a third of the total effect. The rest travelled through the psychological chain. Exercise sensitivity alone carried over a quarter of the effect. Fear of movement carried a further share, and the two in sequence carried more. Altogether, nearly two-thirds of the effect was indirect. Treating symptoms alone will not restore activity. Clinicians must also calm exertion anxiety and rebuild confidence in safe movement.
plos-pone-0352964:
Lucca Passow Carpinelli and seven colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One systematic review of sleep problems among refugees and asylum seekers. Pooling sixty-six studies covering nearly forty-three thousand people, the authors combined scores from standard insomnia and sleep-quality questionnaires and calculated how common sleep adversity is in these displaced populations.

Average scores sat at the edge of clinical insomnia and clearly past the threshold for poor sleep quality. Roughly forty-three percent of adults and thirty-six percent of children experienced sleep adversity, with long times to fall asleep and frequent nightmares common. Results varied a lot between studies, limiting firm subgroup conclusions. The authors urge that standardized sleep assessment and treatment become a routine part of refugee health care.
plos-pone-0353064:
Wenjie Li and five colleagues present this 2026 PLOS One study on adding farm waste to constructed wetlands so the wetlands clean polluted water better. Constructed wetlands often struggle when incoming water lacks enough carbon. The team combined a statistical meta-analysis of published experiments with machine learning models trained on a larger set of observations, and used explanation tools to see what drives performance.

Bamboo charcoal added to wetlands lifted removal of organic pollution substantially, and lotus leaf charcoal did the same for nitrogen. The machine learning models predicted removal rates well, and both pointed to wetland volume as a lever that improves both targets at once. The authors offer the combined approach as a design framework for turning agricultural residues into cleaner water.
plos-pone-0353164:
Killingmo and colleagues gathered research priorities for back pain in Norway in a 2026 study. Back pain research has many gaps, and patients rarely get to set the agenda. Using a partnership method built for that purpose, people living with back pain and clinicians raised questions in group talks, then narrowed hundreds of questions by survey.

A final workshop picked the top ten questions the group judged most urgent. Two hundred thirty questions entered the process, showing how wide the uncertainty runs. Publishing patient-led priorities gives funders a check against studies that answer questions nobody with back pain is asking. The list can steer Norwegian research money toward daily-life concerns.
plos-pone-0353264:
Yan Wang and co-authors mine in 2026 tens of millions of United States drug harm reports for links between a common stomach acid drug and thinning bones. The drug class has long been tied to bone loss, but the pathways remain unclear. Four signal methods scanned the reports, and computer toxicology then hunted for genes and pathways the drug might affect.

The studied drug held the largest share among its class and was the only one positive on all four signal checks. Age, sex, and low body weight also linked to bone reports. Network work flagged a few hub genes and bone related pathways as early, unproven leads for lab study.
plos-pone-0353364:
Ploensil and colleagues, in a 2026 laboratory study, test a protein borrowed from a parasitic flatworm against leukemia cells. The protein, called stefin-1, normally helps the worm deal with its host. Leukemia is hard to treat, in part because many drugs harm healthy cells along with cancer cells, so selective agents are prized.

The team made the worm protein and applied it to a leukemia cell line grown in dishes. Treated cancer cells died in greater numbers as dose and time rose. Normal blood cells from healthy donors, by contrast, barely changed under the same treatment. Inside the dying cells, signs pointed to the classic self-destruct program: a key execution protein was switched on, and the balance of guard proteins tipped toward death. The authors stress that this is early, dish-based work. More models and animal tests must follow before any treatment claims can be made.
plos-pone-0353464:
Grunfeld and colleagues studied stress-built structures inside cancer cells in a 2026 paper. When stressed, cells form dense bodies that gather proteins and RNA, and similar clumping appears in tumors. The team developed staining methods and a semi-automated counting pipeline to find these bodies in human tumor tissue.

Bodies appeared across tumor types, grades, and stages, and rarer bodies matched faster cell growth marks. In a mouse breast cancer model, silencing the RNA that helps build the bodies sped tumor growth. That suggests the bodies may restrain tumors rather than help them, a twist that could reshape how stress structures in cancer are viewed.
plos-pone-0353564:
Fonny Cokro and seven colleagues follow patients with type 2 diabetes in Indonesia who were taking a modern class of glucose-lowering drugs, in this 2026 PLOS ONE real-world study. The drugs, which make the kidneys spill sugar into urine, have strong trial evidence behind them, but Indonesian patients differ from trial populations in diet, body type, and care access. Six hundred and thirty-eight patients across several centres were tracked for a year.

Those on the drugs improved in blood sugar control, weight, blood pressure, and cholesterol, and their calculated heart-attack risk fell. Compared with patients on other regimens, sugar and weight fell further. No major safety problems appeared. The authors read the results as reassurance that trial benefits survive contact with everyday Indonesian practice.
plos-pone-0353664:
Langenbucher and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask how alike a person's two eyes are, using measurements from more than thirteen thousand cataract patients. Surgeons measure eyes before lens surgery, and when one eye's data are missing or doubtful, the other eye could serve as a check, if eyes truly mirror each other. Both eyes were measured with the same optical device.

Most measures matched closely between eyes: eye length, corneal thickness, chamber depth, lens thickness, and corneal width all tracked strongly. Corneal curvature matched too. The cornea's astigmatism, its ovalness, followed mirror symmetry rather than direct symmetry: tilt it as in a mirror and the two eyes align, with axes far closer under mirroring than under matching. Rare patients broke the pattern with large gaps between eyes. The authors say the fellow eye is a sound stand-in and sanity check, with mirror logic for astigmatism.
plos-pone-0353764:
Sunhee Park and co-authors asked whether government money lifts flu vaccination rates in South Korea, and for whom. Flu shots prevent illness, yet coverage stays uneven. Their 2026 study used a national health survey from 2020 covering several thousand adults, comparing people eligible for financial support with those who pay themselves.

Supported people vaccinated at nearly double the rate of unsupported people. After adjustment, support still came with about twice the coverage. Inside the supported group, lower schooling and economic inactivity came with higher rates. In the paying group, women, higher income, and employee insurance predicted vaccination. Park and colleagues say subsidy design should account for these differing patterns.
plos-pone-0353964:
Winfred Nazziwa and four colleagues published this 2026 interview study in Uganda about research that infects volunteers on purpose with germs to test treatments. Such challenge studies raise sharp ethical questions where poverty is common. Twenty-seven researchers, ethicists, and regulators described how local communities should properly be brought into these projects.

Those interviewed favored building engagement from the community upward, as an ongoing partnership grounded in respect and fairness, not a formality for approval. Nazziwa argues that real engagement from the start decides whether such studies are accepted and succeed.
plos-pone-0354164:
Xu and colleagues, in a 2026 analysis, trace whooping cough in children across China and the world from 1990 to 2023. They draw on the Global Burden of Disease project, which estimates illness and death by country and age. Measures include deaths, years of healthy life lost, and case counts.

Across those decades, all four measures fell sharply, both worldwide and in China. The heaviest burden sat with babies aged one to five months, too young to be fully vaccinated, and rates eased as children grew older. In China, that infant group saw rates fall in several stretches but rise in others, including the early 2020s. The team's forecast for the next decade is mixed: death and lost-health rates may climb even as case rates keep falling, and infant rates may edge up. They urge that prevention be aimed hardest at the youngest babies.
plos-pone-0354264:
Fernanda Castro Monteiro led a team of eight authors on this 2026 study of what drives exercise in Brazilian clinic patients with bipolar disorder. Forty-three patients wore movement trackers that recorded real activity and answered a survey on why they exercise, plus mania and depression scales.

Patients who moved enough were driven far more by fun and personal value than inactive patients, and inner drive predicted a fifth of movement levels. Inactive patients carried heavier depression. Monteiro suggests programs for bipolar patients should build real fun, not just issue orders to move more.
plos-pone-0354364:
Qingqing Kang, Zhuang Min, and Lei Li report a new source of high-purity quartz in China's North Qinling mountains, in this 2026 geology study. Quartz pure enough for semiconductors and solar panels is a strategic material. Yet where it forms and why it stays clean are poorly understood for the dense vein deposits of the East Qinling region. The team combined field surveys, close study of mineralized veins, and chemical analyses around Shangnan County.

The purest quartz sat in highly evolved pegmatite veins rich in lithium, cesium, and tantalum. Intense alteration and late fluid flow had scrubbed impurity elements out of the quartz. Mineralized veins differed clearly from barren ones in structure, mineral mix, and fluid history. The authors lay out the formation mechanism and give exploration criteria for finding similar deposits across the region.
plos-pone-0354464:
Cristina Costa-Santos and five colleagues published this 2026 study of people in Portugal who feed and care for feral cat colonies without pay. Such caregivers face animal suffering and loss almost daily, yet they are rarely studied. Structured phone interviews with well over a hundred caregivers measured resilience, spiritual well-being, social support, and colony workload.

Costa-Santos found that stress from others' trauma eased when caregivers felt supported and coped well inside, and rose with heavier outside burdens. Help with food and vet bills mattered alongside emotional support. Pairing psychosocial aid with trap-neuter-return work could protect both the volunteers and the cats they serve.
plos-pone-0354664:
Luke Marney and colleagues present in 2026 a faster pipeline for finding helpful plant chemicals in a traditional herb used for brain and skin health. The old route, testing fraction after fraction, is slow and often rediscovers known compounds. Their pipeline mixes lab separation and activity testing with advanced mass measurement and learning methods that group related signals first.

Grouping cut the data down and made the models clearer. Applied to a water extract of the herb, the method flagged signals tied to known active features plus rare new signals worth study. The authors offer the pipeline as a way to join traditional medicine with evidence based checks.
plos-pone-0354964:
Mirthe Muilwijk and seven colleagues map how obesity clusters with other disadvantages across Dutch neighborhoods in this 2026 study. Using nationwide data for more than twelve thousand neighborhoods, they combined health outcomes, features of the food and movement environment, and socioeconomic position, then clustered neighborhoods into profiles. Their lens, an ecosyndemic framework, treats these burdens as joint products of place rather than separate problems.

Five profiles emerged. The worst-off cluster, over a thousand neighborhoods, carried the highest obesity, chronic disease, and anxiety and depression risk, alongside poor food surroundings and low income. A large privileged cluster covering half the country fared best on nearly everything. A psychosocial cluster stood out for high mental health risk despite modest obesity. The authors argue such maps let policy target places where burdens pile up, instead of lecturing people.
plos-pone-0355164:
Muhammad Saad Ansari is first author on a 2026 PLOS ONE national survey study of immune-suppressing treatment and stroke in United States adults. Such drugs treat autoimmune, inflammatory, cancer, and transplant conditions that may carry high stroke burden. National evidence linking current use to lifetime stroke history was limited.

Pooling two years of a national health interview survey gave sixty thousand adults, representing about two hundred and fifty million people. Stroke history was reported by six percent of those on immune-weakening drugs, against under three percent of others. The link held after adjusting for age, blood pressure, diabetes, and other factors. The authors stress the design shows association, not cause.
plos-pone-0355464:
Osama Elsabagh and colleagues test in 2026 whether an extract from a tropical tree can protect rat livers against cadmium, a toxic metal. The tree has a folk history for liver complaints, but how it might help was unclear. Chemical profiling found dozens of compounds, mainly plant pigments and acids with protective reputations.

Cadmium raised liver harm markers and weakened defences against oxidation, while the extract lowered metal build up in the liver and eased inflammation. Tissue looked nearly normal at the higher dose, and many disturbed blood chemicals moved back toward normal. The authors read the pattern as broad, multi path protection.
plos-pone-0355864:
Md Faruqul Islam leads a team of eight measuring back pain among postmenopausal women in Bangladesh, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Back pain disables more people worldwide than almost any other complaint, and women after menopause are especially exposed, yet South Asian data are thin. Five hundred sixty-six women attending two rehab centers answered structured questions on health, lifestyle, and circumstances. The team then trained learning models on their data, alongside standard models.

Just under half, about forty-seven percent, reported low back pain within the past year, a heavy burden in a group already attending for rehabilitation. The analysis weighed which social, clinical, and daily habit factors traveled with the pain. The learning models were cross checked twice, with an explainer showing which inputs drove each call. The authors aim the results at targeted prevention and at clinics deciding which patients need early, intensive support.
plos-pone-0355964:
Ravear Zhiqiang Wang, Fang Yang, and Jianhua Sui published a cancer immunology study in PLOS ONE in 2026. They studied two proteins, Galectin-9 and B7-H4, both linked to how tumors quiet the immune system. The team asked whether the two proteins bind to each other and work as partners.

Wang and his co-authors confirmed that binding and described how sugar chains on the proteins shape it. The paired proteins affect signals that T cells, key immune attackers, rely on. A partnership like this is of interest because blocking it might release the brakes on immune cells in cancer treatment. The work adds one more defined target to a crowded but promising field.
plos-pone-0356064:
Nataly Lobos-Parra and colleagues analyzed in 2026 which genes switch on or off in the livers of zebrafish exposed to sediments from the Loa River in Chile. Zebrafish are a standard laboratory stand-in for how pollution affects vertebrate animals, and the liver is where many poisons are processed. A transcriptomic analysis reads the activity of thousands of genes at once, revealing the biological pathways a contaminant disturbs.

River sediments gather whatever washes off mines, farms, and towns upstream, so fish living in them carry a record of that pollution. Gene level evidence can flag harm before whole populations visibly decline. Studies of this kind support environmental monitoring and arguments over who must clean up a working river.
plos-pone-0356264:
Kaige Xu and fellow surgeons examine blood loss that stays hidden inside the body after knee replacement surgery. Some blood seeps into tissues and never shows in drains, yet it can slow recovery. Their 2026 study reviews patients who had one knee replaced for worn joints at a university hospital in Qingdao during a single year, split by how much hidden loss each person had.

Two traits stood out in the final analysis. Higher body weight for height was the strongest warning sign, with a clear cutoff value that separated most high-loss patients. A history of high blood pressure also raised the odds. Xu and colleagues suggest that checking weight before surgery can flag patients who need closer blood care and tailored plans.
plos-pone-0356364:
Claire-Marie Pilard and colleagues tested whether blocking a cell-to-cell communication channel, connexin 43, could protect premature lungs from the damage high oxygen causes, the root of bronchopulmonary dysplasia. Their 2026 study exposed newborn rats to very high oxygen for two weeks with or without a targeted blocker drug, and ran parallel tests on human fetal lung vessel cells.

The blocker lowered the channel's excess and partly rescued the lung's air sac development. Almost everything else refused to improve: lung function, surfactant protein, scarring markers, vessel pressure disease, and survival all stayed on their damaged course, and some epithelial markers fell. The authors read the channel as a bit player, not the master switch, in oxygen lung injury.
plos-pone-0356464:
Merron Woodbury and colleagues published a 2026 developmental study in PLOS ONE on how related memories interfere with each other in children versus adults. Both groups learned object locations on maps, then learned new locations that either fit into a map they already knew or stood apart. Because learning happened on the same day, the team could see whether old memories got in the way while new ones formed, or later, when the first map was recalled.

Adults were slowed while learning new locations inside a familiar map, as if their recent memories crowded the new ones. Children showed no such slowdown during learning. At recall, the pattern flipped: children remembered the first map worse after adding new memories to it, while adults recalled it fine. The authors conclude that memory interference strikes at different stages by age: during learning for adults, during later retrieval for children.
plos-pone-0356764:
Hijrah Nasir and coauthors published a 2026 international study in PLOS ONE, from the COVISTRESS project, on how working from home affects sitting time. Earlier work hinted teleworkers sit more, but no study had modeled sitting against the full range of social, job, and lifestyle factors at this scale. More than six and a half thousand respondents reported their habits, and the authors used layered statistical models to isolate telework's contribution.

Average sitting ran near six hours a day, but it climbed steadily with telework share: Full-time home workers averaged over nine hours. One in ten of them sat more than fourteen hours daily. After adjustment, heavy telework multiplied the risk of extreme sitting many times over, beyond any other factor measured. Telework, they conclude, is the strongest driver of sedentary days, and home-office routines should be treated as a sitting hazard in their own right.
plos-pone-0357264:
Changgui Wu designs a steering controller that keeps self-driving vehicles on their path despite uncertain mechanics and outside pushes such as wind or road tilt. Classic robust controllers learn the car's unknowns only from tracking error, which demands demanding conditions to learn well. The new scheme builds a second estimate of the unknowns and blends both errors into its learning rule, relaxing what the road must provide.

A specially shaped sliding surface guarantees the car settles onto its path within a set time without mathematical blow-ups, and a disturbance watcher cancels leftover pushes in real time. In heavy simulated tests, the controller tracked more accurately and settled faster than three established rivals. Wu supports the claims with a formal stability proof, though road trials remain future work.
plos-pone-0357364:
Arzu Peker and colleagues sort pet clinics in Ankara, Türkiye, into types by their money and service profiles, looking for what separates thriving practices from struggling ones. Clinics face rising costs, stiff competition, and changing owner expectations, yet clinic performance itself is rarely studied. Owners or managers of several dozen clinics answered a long survey covering dozens of financial and social indicators, which the team compressed and clustered.

Four types emerged. Broad multi-service clinics earned and spent the most. A steady middle group ran moderate, efficient practices. Cat-focused lean clinics, spending least, actually banked the highest profit. Exotic-animal specialists earned least and struggled to stay regularly profitable. Peker and colleagues say strategy, not effort alone, separates the winners.
plos-pone-0357464:
Mariam Moarefi and colleagues explore whether changes in the eye's tiny vessels and cell-energy markers track changes in thinking after a long yoga program for older adults. The retina offers a window on the brain's small vessels, so eye scans might mirror cognitive health. Thirty healthy older adults practiced one of two yoga styles several times a week for about half a year, with eye imaging and thinking tests before and after.

Several eye–mind pairings moved together in the raw counts, linking blood flow and tissue supply in the eye with attention, memory, and sorting tasks. None of the pairings survived a strict correction for multiple testing. Moarefi and colleagues label the study a pilot and say the hints justify a larger trial, not firm claims about yoga and the brain.
plos-pone-0357564: Sumner and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE interview study on heart attack care in Tanzania. They asked stakeholders how they feel about a planned program to raise uptake of proven emergency care for myocardial infarction. Views came from people who would give, receive, or fund the care. Early views on acceptability can make or break a program once it reaches busy hospitals.
plos-pone-0357664:
Dhirendra Prasad Yadav and fellow engineers present a computer vision system that sorts growths in the colon from medical images. Finding these lesions early matters because bowel cancer ranks among the most common cancers worldwide, yet expert review takes time and skill. Their network mixes two designs: one that reads fine local detail and one that weighs the whole image at once, with a bridge part that lets the two share what they learn.

Tested on two public image sets, the combined system scored high on precision, recall, and agreement measures, missing few true cases. Yadav and colleagues argue that joining local and global views helps a model notice both small surface changes and wider shape cues. Hospitals short on specialists could use such tools as a first reader.
plos-pone-0357764:
Alonso Espinoza, Eric Goles, and Marco Montalva-Medel modeled drug resistance in lung cancer as a logic network, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Drug resistance in this common form of lung cancer is a network problem, not a single-gene fault. The team used Boolean networks, where genes act as on-off switches, then simplified the network and fitted its rules.

Espinoza's simplified logic maps reveal the molecular switches that flip tumors from drug-sensitive to drug-proof. A readable map is more useful than a huge tangle: it shows which switch combinations matter and which might be druggable. Boolean models suit biology where genes mostly act as switches. This work gives experimental teams a short list of control points to test in real cancer cells.
plos-pone-0357964: Solouki and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on spotting fibromyalgia, a long-term pain condition, with brain scans. Volunteers did a task involving feelings while inside an fMRI scanner. The team fed the brain network maps into machine learning built on graph theory. A scan-based aid could one day support diagnosis of a condition that now rests mostly on self-reported pain.
plos-pone-0358264:
Michael E. J. Stouthandel and coauthors published a 2026 engineering paper in PLOS ONE describing a rig they built for injecting fluid into the body's tiniest lymph vessels in anatomical research. Better three-dimensional maps of the lymphatic system could sharpen cancer treatment, but the vessels are thinner than a millimeter, so threading them by hand across a whole body is extremely hard. Their rig hangs an aluminum frame over the dissection table, carrying a micromanipulator on a sliding, double-jointed arm.

The setup allows many approach angles, and it can also hold fluid pressure controllers and a surgical microscope. In trials, the team completed full-body micro-cannulations with the rig, and after brief practice it beat careful hand work on success and ease. The authors recommend the design to other microvascular researchers, noting that lymph maps still rest on centuries-old atlases that modern imaging could refresh.
plos-pone-0358364:
John David Johnson II, Michael Hales, and Joshua Pitts studied Major League Soccer in a PLOS ONE paper from 2026. They asked whether the playing surface, grass or artificial turf, shapes match results and the formations coaches choose. Many MLS stadiums use turf, so the question affects a large share of games.

Johnson and his co-authors compared outcomes and team shapes across surfaces. Patterns of that kind tell whether turf quietly aids home teams or pushes coaches toward certain lineups. Clubs deciding on stadium surfaces, and leagues weighing fairness, can use such evidence instead of anecdote. Players, too, have a stake in how surface affects play and injury risk.
plos-pone-0358464:
Adrien Le Guillou leads a team of five with a lesson for everyone training image models on small maps, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their task was spotting invasive cordgrass in aerial photographs of tidal marsh, where labeled examples are inherently scarce. Three respected segmentation architectures were each trained under twelve configurations, varying how the training itself was run, for many runs judged by cross validation.

Training strategy crushed architecture. The spread between the best and worst training recipes was about ten points of overlap accuracy; the spread between the three architectures was under one point. Two popular tricks, freezing the encoder and a fashionable loss function, hurt every architecture they touched. The winning recipe mapped the whole Bay of Brest, estimating some forty-four hectares of cordgrass. Elevation data, assumed precious, contributed little beside the color imagery. Data scarce fields should tune their teaching before shopping for bigger models.
plos-pone-0358764: Hussain and four co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on measuring how body weight spreads across the feet. Their setup uses a grid of force-sensitive resistors, thin sensors that react to pressure, plus foot data analysis. The goal was a shared standard way to record and read such maps. Standard foot pressure records help shoe design, sports science, and care for people with foot risk.
plos-pone-0358864:
Jun Chen, Xun Wan, and Yu Zhou follow three trainee teachers through a year of change in PLOS ONE in 2026. Rural schools in China struggle to recruit and keep teachers, and a beginner's professional identity, how they see themselves as a teacher, shapes whether they stay. The case study examines an English teaching course at a university in western China that wove theory, practice teaching in miniature, and guided reflection into one design.

At the start, the three trainees doubted themselves and pictured teaching as drilling grammar and vocabulary. By year's end their outlook had widened to whole lesson design, and fear had given way to confidence and commitment. Interviews and reflective journals traced the shift to discussion rich practice, where rehearsing, talking, and belonging to a learning community rebuilt identity. The study offers teacher programs a concrete model for growing rural teachers who intend to remain.
plos-pone-0358964:
Jae Shin Song and Min Seok Kim ask whether smoking changes the thickness of the choroid, the blood vessel layer feeding the retina, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their data come from a national Korean health survey spanning 2017 to 2021. Over twenty-two thousand adults with clean eye scans and no eye disease were divided into never, former, and current smokers, and the layer under the central retina was measured for each group.

Thickness rose in steps across the three groups in both eyes. Never smokers measured thinnest, former smokers sat in the middle, and current smokers measured thickest, a gap that survived adjustment for age, sex, eye length, and heart disease. The authors read the pattern as a fingerprint of smoking on the eye's circulation, visible in ordinary population data. Whether the thickening harms or merely marks exposure is a question they leave for follow up studies.
plos-pone-0359164:
Shuai Yan, Qingzhi Yu, Wenfeng Dai, and Xiang Cheng published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It presents a dual-head transformer model, called GP-DHT, for single-cell gene regulatory network prediction, mapping which genes switch others on and off in individual cells. Pretraining uses shared genes and supervised contrastive learning.

Gene regulatory networks explain how the same DNA produces many cell types. Predicting them from single-cell data is a central problem in genomics, and pretraining on shared genes aims to make the model work across datasets. Computational biologists building cell atlases are the readers who would test this model's predictions.
plos-pone-0359564:
Abdullah Shaker and Muawia Dafalla characterized in 2026 the expansive soils of a region and how their mineral makeup governs their swelling when treated with lime. Expansive soils swell when wet and shrink when dry, cracking roads, pipelines, and building foundations. Adding lime is a standard treatment that tames the swelling, but how well it works depends on the minerals in the soil.

The authors describe the region's soils and test how mineralogy influences the swelling of the treated ground. Regional characterization matters because soil recipes do not travel: what works on one clay may fail on another. Engineers planning foundations and highways in such terrain need exactly this local evidence before they build.
plos-pone-0359864:
Pizhao Hu and five colleagues published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It studies how people look at book covers, using atlas covers as the test case. The authors connect aesthetic preference, which designs people like, with gaze-based visual attention, where the eyes actually go.

The evidence comes from an eye-tracking study, which records eye movements as people view the covers. Comparing what people say they like with where they look can reveal gaps between taste and attention. Cover designers and publishers can use that pairing to make designs that both attract the eye and please it.
plos-pone-0359964:
Solène Neyret, Julien Pellet, Julien Ryard, Mickaël Campo, and Jean-Rémy Chardonnet wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article about professional rugby players. The players were immersed in an interactive virtual environment. The authors work on inducing and measuring identity levels, how strongly players feel merged with their virtual presence.

Virtual training and analysis tools only work if athletes take the simulation seriously as themselves. Measuring identity inside the environment tells designers whether players engage as competitors or as detached viewers. Sports scientists building virtual reality training for contact sports are the audience for methods that create and verify that sense of presence.
plos-pone-0360164:
Mohamed El-Tanani and colleagues reported in 2026 a two front strategy against lung cancers that have learned to resist the drug gefitinib. The cancer type is non-small cell lung cancer, and gefitinib works by blocking EGFR, a growth signal receptor many of these tumors depend on. Resistance to it is a common and deadly turning point.

The team combined EGFR blockade with a second attack on microtubules, the cell's internal scaffolding needed for division. Together, the two pressures raised the stress tied to copying DNA and suppressed tumor growth in their models. Combination strategies of this kind try to close the escape routes that single drugs leave open, and this study tests one pairing in detail.
pmc-13196964:
Zhe Jing and Zhengguo Yan present a 2026 model called RPINet for labeling city scenes in three dimensions. Point clouds are sets of measured points that map streets and buildings. Labeling them is hard because points are sparse and uneven, and photos alone miss depth.

RPINet runs two branches side by side. One branch reads the three-dimensional points, while the other reads flat aerial images for texture and edges. An attention unit blends both streams, weighing each part by its value. On a large city test set, the model beat prior methods on overlap scores. It also held up on new data it had not seen. The approach may aid city planning and mapping.
pmc-13197564:
Yumeng Zhang and colleagues built a 2026 AI framework to read rectal cancer scans. Doctors must judge whether cancer has entered nearby veins or reached the sheet that bounds the rectum. Eye reads vary by reader and hospital, so an automated read could steady care choices.

The team gathered 331 scans from three European hospitals. A signal tuning step cut scanner-to-scanner drift. Three classifiers were trained on most scans and tested on the rest. The best vein-invasion score came from blending two scan angles with a pre-trained medical model. The best sheet-invasion score came from one angle after tuning. Heat maps showed the models looked at the right zones. Results beat a prior contest benchmark.
pmc-13198364:
Colin Baker and colleagues present SCOT+, a 2026 software suite for aligning single-cell data. Modern tests can read several layers of cell biology, but measuring all layers in one cell is costly or impossible. Optimal transport, a math method for matching two sets at least cost, can align cells across separate datasets with no known pairs.

The suite unifies four earlier alignment methods under one framework. Its flexible design also yields a new matching formula and solver. The package runs in Python and ships with tutorials and a friendly website. It is free on public code and package sites. Better alignment should sharpen downstream study of how cells are regulated across data types.
pmc-13199564:
Amany Tarek and colleagues derive exact wave solutions for light pulses in magnetic-optic channels in a 2026 theory study. Solitons are self-holding light pulses prized for fast data links. Standard models gloss over how magnetism and strong nonlinear effects interact, so the team solved a fuller paired equation system.

Using an improved equation method, they found a fresh set of exact solutions. Shapes include kink and anti-kink fronts, which flip between two levels, plus sharp singular profiles. Tuning key nonlinear settings gave precise control over pulse stability and front steepness. The math may guide high-capacity optical links and all-optical switches, devices that route light with light.
pmc-13202164:
Living with several chronic diseases at once complicates self-care, and a 2026 protocol headed by Ana Lúcia Junger sets out a systematic review on how patients' beliefs shape their behavior. The protocol examines illness perception and self-management in adults with multimorbidity, an area where evidence from single diseases may not transfer.

Grounded in the Common-Sense Model of self-regulation, the review will search seven databases for observational studies using validated perception measures. Two reviewers will select studies, extract data, and judge quality with established scales, and a meta-analysis will be run where the data allow. The goal is to link beliefs about causes, control, and consequences to adherence and self-care.
pmc-13209764:
A tracking tag that folds like paper and shrugs off acid is presented in a 2026 engineering study led by Meng Zeng. The research article designs a miniature radio-frequency identification antenna from graphene film on a flexible plastic sheet, folding one arm behind the tag instead of adding connectors through the material.

The finished tag measures only twenty-four by thirteen millimeters yet tunes into the standard UHF identification band. Adjusting the folded arm shifts its resonance, and a stepped arm plus matching network achieved near-perfect power transfer to the chip in testing. Performance held after corrosive soaks and a thousand bends, with a read range beyond a meter.
pmc-13236164:

pmc-13238664:

pmc-13240864:

pmc-13241464:

pmc-13241564:

One figure reference in the text was adjusted as well.
pmc-13242464:

pmc-13242664:

pmc-13243764:

pmc-13245064:

pmc-13246064:

pmc-13248764:

pmc-13248964:

pmc-13249164:

pmc-13250164:

pmc-13250464:

pmc-13250764:

pmc-13250864:

pmc-13251064:

pmc-13251764:

pmc-13253064:

pmc-13253364:

pmc-13253664:

pmc-13254264:

pmc-13258064:

pmc-13262364:

pmc-13262864:

pmc-13275064:

pmc-13276764:

pmc-13277664:

pmc-13277764:

pmc-13279264:

pmc-13279664:

pmc-13280464:

Their patient was a thirteen year old girl with congenital stenosis and a secundum defect. She was lost to follow up for ten years.

Worse stenosis and a larger hole drove major left to right shunting of blood. Severe right heart overload, pulmonary hypertension and severe tricuspid regurgitation, a leaky valve, followed. Cath tests showed low cardiac output and high lung pressures. Surgery held mechanical mitral valve replacement, hole closure and tricuspid annuloplasty, a valve repair. Left heart weakness after surgery eased with drugs. At two years, both sides of her heart worked well and failure signs had fully cleared.
pmc-13280664:
Ziwei Wang and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on protecting the brain after a bleed inside it. A bleed harms brain cells at once and then keeps harming them for days. The review links three topics that are often treated apart. They are cell death, the birth of new brain cells, and stem cell therapy, meaning care that uses young cells that can grow.

The authors explain how blood, iron, and swelling set off more cell death after the bleed. New cells do form, but few live or link up well. Stem cells may help by sending signals that calm harm and aid repair. The review lists blocks to human use, such as poor cell survival and safety risks.
pmc-13281164:
Md Borhan Uddin and colleagues applied queue math to a heart ward in a 2026 study from Bangladesh. The Sylhet hospital serves a poor region where heart care is often delayed. The team used records for more than six thousand patients treated in 2023. They tracked arrivals, stays, and beds in four units, from standard care to the heart lab and two intensive units. Queue models show where flow jams when demand nears capacity.

Two intensive units jammed worst, with bed shortages that hurt care quality. The heart lab, by contrast, had beds to spare. The authors advise moving spare beds and growing the small intensive unit from eight beds to fifteen. The larger intensive unit would grow from ten beds to twenty-five. They also warn against piling extra beds into standard wards, which crowds care and hides the true shortage.
pmc-13281464:
Ameer Hohlfeld and colleagues surveyed trial leaders in sub-Saharan Africa on publishing results in a 2026 study. Trials that never reach print can skew what doctors think works. The team emailed more than six thousand leaders found in a global trial registry. Four hundred nine took part in the web survey. They were asked about duty to publish, delays, and blocks they had met.

Most agreed trial leaders must publish all results, and most within two years. Bias in what gets printed was rated high for the region. Close to two thirds had printed at least one trial within two years. Yet about one in four had a finished trial they could not print. Top blocks were journal rejection, lack of time, and dull results. Three in four had no training in writing trial papers. The authors urge training and support for African teams.
pmc-13281764:
Emanuela Foglia and colleagues assessed full automation in an Italian germ lab in a 2026 study. Germ labs face rising sample counts with flat staffing. Machines that run the whole chain, from check-in to plate reading, promise relief. The team took a broad health technology view at one hospital lab. They compared hand work and machine work on urine samples and on blood cultures that had turned positive. Costs, staff time, and staff views were all weighed.

Automation cut check-in time by about two thirds. Seeding plates by hand all but vanished, and plate reading time fell steeply. Yearly staff costs for the tracked work fell by about two thirds too. Total handling time dropped by a like share. Staff reported safer work and a lighter load. The authors say the case rests on more than speed: freed hands can shift to harder tasks.
pmc-13281864:
Jun Zou and colleagues published a 2026 case report on a woman with a deadly fungal infection. She was thirty-nine and had just learned she carried both HIV and hepatitis C. The fungus spreads through the body in people with weak immunity and kills up to three in ten treated patients. Blood tests and cultures confirmed it had spread widely. She began a strong fungal drug at once. Her liver and kidneys then failed, and confusion set in as the liver faltered.

She was moved to intensive care in grave shape. Teams added a machine that does the liver's cleaning work from outside. A second machine took over the kidneys' filtering. The authors present the paired support as a rescue that pulled her through. They note that organ failure often caps drug doses in such cases. Their report adds rare guidance for this exact crisis.
pmc-13282164:
Taifu Huang and co-authors published a 2026 study modelling how climate change is shrinking habitat for the dhole in China. The dhole is a wild dog and top predator, listed as endangered worldwide and given the highest protection class in China. The team combined sighting records with climate projections in an ensemble model, a blend of several models, to map suitable habitat in past, current, and future periods.

Suitable habitat now covers about one million four hundred thousand square kilometres, mainly around the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau. That area has fallen by nearly half since the past period studied. Future climate scenarios project a further fall of roughly twelve to thirteen percent. Cold-month temperature, height above sea level, and slope shaped past habitat most. The authors name mountain ranges, including the Qilian and Hengduan ranges, as future refuges, and call for larger protected areas.
pmc-13282264:
Mojtaba Aghaei and co-authors wrote a 2026 narrative review on two small genetic variants in a gene linked to leukaemia. Leukaemia is a group of blood cancers shaped by both genes and environment. The gene, BMI1, helps blood stem cells renew themselves and is tied to cancer growth. The review examines two single-letter DNA changes, named rs1042059 and rs11591377, and their possible effect on leukaemia risk.

The authors gathered case-control studies, large genome scans, and lab studies of how the gene works. Some reported that these variants raised leukaemia risk, perhaps by changing gene activity and growth signals. Other studies, in other populations, found no such link. The review judges the evidence inconclusive overall. It calls for larger population studies and clearer work on the mechanism. If confirmed, the variants could help refine risk checks and personal treatment choices in future.
pmc-13282864:
Can extra calcium help control blood pressure after menopause? Ahmed Farouk Alaarag and fellow clinicians tested that idea in 2026. The study enrolled women who had both low blood calcium and hypertension. Low calcium after menopause may raise blood pressure by affecting blood vessel tone.

A total of 300 women received calcium carbonate at 1,000 mg per day plus usual blood pressure drugs. Staff measured blood pressure and calcium at the start and after three months. Women whose calcium returned to normal showed better blood pressure control. More of them reached target levels. The authors suggest that fixing low calcium may aid standard treatment.
pmc-13283164:
An adult bleeding-risk score for brain vessel tangles falters in children, Frankfurt records analyzed by Sepide Kashefiolasl show in 2026. Such tangles are a top cause of brain bleeding in young patients. The VALE score was built for adults, so its value in children was unknown.

Hospital records in Frankfurt covered 52 patients aged 18 years or younger from 2005 to 2023. A total of 31 patients arrived with bleeding at first care. Only one score part, a vein bulge near the tangle, stayed linked to bleeding after full adjustment. The full score sorted risk poorly in children by standard tests. The authors advise against direct use of the adult score for child patients.
pmc-13283264:
Nanoparticles that kill germs by fresh routes headline Akmal Zubair's 2026 survey of superbug countermeasures. Germs that resist many drugs are a rising global health threat. Few new antibiotics are emerging, and old drugs keep losing strength.

The review explains how bacteria resist drugs, from pumping drugs out to shielding targets. Tiny particles can kill germs by new routes or carry drugs past defenses. Metal, organic, carbon-based, and hybrid particles all showed strong germ killing. Pairing particles with plant compounds is also under active study in the field. The authors weigh safety and scale-up needs for clinical use. Nano tools may revive options against hard infections.
pmc-13283364:
Five bedside factors combine into the Base-C score for spotting collapsed-lung treatment failure, Xiangli Shao's hospital team reports in 2026. Collapsed lung from air leaks often fails non-surgical care. Early spotting of high-risk patients can speed the right intervention.

Records came from two large hospitals for score building and testing. The main cohort held 1,378 patients, and the check cohort held 506 patients. Five factors formed the Base-C score: air blisters, age, smoking, emphysema, and collapse size. The score sorted failure risk well in both cohorts by standard tests. Fit checks also looked good in the validation work. The tool can help tailor care plans early.
pmc-13285364:
Forecasting who will still hurt a year after knee replacement stays hard, even for smart algorithms, Anni Rajamäki and co-authors show in a 2026 cohort study. Between ten and twenty percent of patients end up unhappy after surgery, so a good forecast could steer counseling and spare needless operations. The team fed 751 patient traits into boosted-tree models for 11,755 patients.

About seven percent still had lasting pain at one year. Model accuracy landed in the poor range for pain and for the paired score outcomes. Low starting knee scores, younger age, and higher body weight ranked among the top signals. The authors conclude pain after this surgery resists prediction with current data.
pmc-13285564:
A helpful fungus may rein in the anthracnose blight that rots crops worldwide, Rendra Adhitya and co-authors review in a 2026 article. Colletotrichum fungi hit over three thousand plant kinds and swap between quiet and killing growth phases, which foils control. Chemical sprays bring resistance, pollution, and food safety worries.

Lab, greenhouse, field, and storage trials show Trichoderma can curb the blight, best under controlled terms. Weather, strain pick, product shelf life, and spray style all sway results in the works surveyed here. The authors urge gene-wide studies, strain tuning, and better formulas so farm results hold steady, letting growers cut chemical use while crops resist disease better.
pmc-13286164:
Julia Döge and colleagues link hearing loss with planning skill in a 2026 population cohort study from Mainz, Germany. Straining to hear may drain the mental budget that planning draws on, but proof on single thinking skills has stayed scarce. Volunteers took tone tests, a speech-in-noise test, and a tower puzzle that grades how well a person plans ahead.

Records held 4,458 adults aged 40 to 80 with full hearing and puzzle data. People with measured hearing loss scored lower on planning overall, though loss alone did not push them into the clinical danger zone. Stronger planners, in turn, showed lower odds of hearing loss and picked speech out of noise more cleanly. The two-way pattern fits the idea that hearing effort taxes shared brain resources, and the authors call for long-term studies to sort cause from effect.
pmc-13286864:
M Kodeeswaran and a multinational team describe repairing a giant torn artery bulge inside the skull in their 2026 case report. The patient, a 48-year-old woman, endured two months of dull left-sided headache, then a week of blurred vision and a weakening right arm. Imaging revealed a dissecting pseudoaneurysm of the left internal carotid artery just above its bony canal, pressing on nearby brain with mild midline shift.

Surgeons reached the lesion through the leg artery rather than open surgery. A flow-diverting stent bridged the diseased stretch from the carotid into the middle cerebral artery, and soft platinum coils packed the sac to spur clotting. Final angiography showed the bulge nearly shut out of circulation while the parent artery and its branches stayed open. The report pairs the case with a literature review favoring this combined route for high-risk lesions.
pmc-13287164:
Luísa dos Santos Conceição and co-authors reviewed fifteen years of work in 2026 on quixabeira, a thorny medicinal tree known to rural communities in Brazil. Their aim was to gather what is known about each plant part and where useful products or treatments might realistically come from.

Leaf extracts were studied most, often made with methanol or ethanol, and showed antioxidant and microbe-fighting activity in laboratory tests. Fruit work is thinner, though pigments and flavonoids were measured. Local uses span food, medicine, animal care, and building. The reviewers say safety and dosing work is still missing, so claimed benefits should be treated as early leads awaiting stronger checks.
