pmc-13287464:
Faxin Zhou and colleagues recorded brain activity in 2026 from electrodes placed inside the skulls of 19 people watching a short film in several languages. The aim was to see how the frontal cortex handles sound and picture together during lifelike viewing, rather than in stripped-down lab tasks.

A clear gradient appeared: lower frontal areas leaned toward sound, upper areas toward vision. That layout shifted as film scenes changed, suggesting flexible sharing of work. Behaviour ratings pointed to the frontal cortex as the main site sorting out which sense leads. The authors read the pattern as a flexible system that builds one story from two input streams.
pmc-13287564:
Dong Won Kwack and Dong Wook Kim piloted slow-release melatonin in 2026 in adults who live with both epilepsy and insomnia. Thirty-four patients enrolled between March 2024 and February 2025, and 25 finished twelve weeks of nightly tablets. Sleep and mood scales were taken before and after.

Sleep scores improved clearly over the twelve weeks. Depression scores fell by a smaller but real margin. Seizure patterns did not change, and nobody stopped the tablets because seizures worsened. Most finishers had focal seizures. The authors present the hormone tablet as a candidate add-on for sleep and mood in epilepsy, while noting the small, uncontrolled design.
pmc-13288864:
Jae-Woo Song, Sunhee Yoon, Sunghoon Jung, and Wang-Hee Lee refresh climate data for species models in 2026. Many forecasts still use old climate averages. Those averages run from 1961 to 1990. The team built a global database for 1992 to 2021. It was shaped for the CLIMEX system.

Three species were modeled as a test. Both CLIMEX and MaxEnt were used. Old and new baselines were compared. Overall skill barely moved. Broad niche overlap barely moved either. Local fit shifted clearly in places. Occurrence chances shifted there too. Matching climate years to sighting years should cut error. Pest risk and biosecurity work stand to gain.
pmc-13289064:
Leopold Hentschel and colleagues study strain on family caregivers in Germany. Their 2026 study deals with home palliative care. One clinic team ran the study. Recruitment ran from April 2021 to August 2022. The team logged illness and home facts.

Of 250 patients screened, 152 pairs joined. Low mood topped the mark in 31 percent of caregivers. Worry topped it in 33 percent. Broad distress hit 82 percent of them. More care hours per day tied to low mood. COVID strain also tied to low mood. Oddly, COVID strain tied to less worry. The models left most strain unexplained.
pmc-13289364:
Junho Kang, Jinhyeon An, and Jung Kyoon Choi built a 2026 atlas comparing immune side effects of cancer checkpoint drugs with chronic inflammatory diseases. Both can look alike in symptoms and treatment, yet their cell-level drivers may differ. The team merged gene data from millions of cells to map where the two kinds of inflammation truly diverge.

The compendium held over 4.3 million cells from 1137 samples plus spatial maps and blood data before and after treatment. Side-effect tissues showed a distinct mix rich in certain phagocytes, dendritic cells, and chemical signals, plus special regulatory and tired T cells in tight niches. Severe side effects tied to higher CXCL10 signaling after treatment and to a specific HLA type in carriers.
pmc-13289464:
Caroline Cohrdes and coauthors present a 2026 population study on mental paths linking hard life events to later well-being in young adults. Potentially traumatic events include not only classic trauma but also social harms such as exclusion and discrimination. The authors test shared mental processes that cut across diagnoses, rather than one disorder at a time.

Data covered 3,051 emerging adults in a population sample, modeled with structural equations for indirect links. Three broad process groups emerged: thought-focused, emotion-focused, and social-focused paths between events and outcomes. Emotion-focused paths carried the largest share of indirect links overall. Social exclusion showed the strongest and steadiest ties to mental health, and models explained inner distress better than outer behavior or positive health.
pmc-13289764:
Rapeepong Suphanchaimat headed a 2026 study on whether public insurance cuts out-of-pocket costs for mental health care among migrants who cross borders into Thailand. Migrant insurance schemes exist, yet mental health care is not clearly listed as covered, and cost evidence was scarce. Routine service data from public hospitals nationwide covered 2018 to 2022 for the analysis.

A total of 4,559 patients made 13,744 visits, and 84.1 percent were uninsured at care. Mean spending per visit was 449 Baht, with a very wide range up to over one hundred thousand Baht as reported. A two-part model with machine learning found insurance cut the chance of any payment by about half. Mean cost per visit also ran lower for insured patients.
pmc-13290164:
Reddit talk during the 2022 mpox outbreak is analyzed by Xi Ning Luo and colleagues in a 2026 observational study. Health emergencies tend to stir uncertainty, stigma, and rumor online, and the authors wanted to see how sentiment, topics, and engagement interacted on one platform.

They gathered 1,169 posts and 6,571 comments from four mpox subreddits and sorted them with sentiment analysis and topic modeling into nine themes. Most posts were neutral in tone, about a third negative, and a smaller share positive. Negative posts drew higher engagement scores than positive ones, and comments tended to echo the tone of the post they answered. Luo and colleagues say communicators should expect emotional narratives to spread fastest and plan responses accordingly.
pmc-13290564:
Acupuncture alongside IVF may lift pregnancy rates for women with diminished ovarian reserve, Liangliang Xu and colleagues conclude in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Low egg supply is a stubborn cause of infertility, and earlier trials of needling disagreed.

Searching eight databases, the team pooled 11 randomized trials covering 885 women undergoing IVF or ICSI. The pooled results favored acupuncture: clinical pregnancy (risk difference 0.25), live birth (0.22), and implantation (0.30) all ran higher with treatment, with more eggs retrieved and more top-quality embryos too. Subgroup checks held up, but the graded certainty of evidence ranged only from very low to moderate. Xu and colleagues call the signal promising and ask for stricter trials to confirm it.
pmc-13290864:
Alzheimer's blood markers track brain shrinkage and thinking problems inside Parkinson's disease, Eleonora Fiorenzato and colleagues report in a biomarker study from 2026. Alzheimer co-pathology may speed decline in Parkinson's, and cheap plasma tests now allow staging it, but their meaning for Parkinson's types was unclear.

Fifty-eight Parkinson's patients across the cognitive spectrum and 76 dementia-free older adults gave blood, MRI scans, and cognitive testing. The Alzheimer markers p-tau217 and the amyloid ratio beat the nerve-damage and inflammation markers: higher p-tau217 meant more Alzheimer-like MRI change and worse cognition in both groups. In Parkinson's it also mapped onto memory and executive problems, and mood symptoms tracked the Alzheimer markers too. Fiorenzato and colleagues back p-tau217 especially for sorting Parkinson's patients by biology.
pmc-13290964:
Junjie Cao leads a 2026 landscape study of clinical trials testing immune checkpoint inhibitors for hepatocellular carcinoma, the main form of primary liver cancer. Rather than testing a drug, the team mapped how this research area is organized around the world.

Four international trial databases were searched through February 14, 2026, leaving 132 trials that met the study rules. China accounted for 95 trials and the United States for 16, while most work targeted PD-1 or PD-L1 and few trials targeted CTLA-4. Phase II work was most common, with 59 trials listed. Very few results had been published, so the authors urge better reporting and wider collaboration.
pmc-13291264:
Trees that learn can stay small and clear. Sabino Francesco Roselli and Eibe Frank test best-possible model trees in a 2026 study. Normal tree methods grow greedily, split by split. Each split looks good alone but may miss the best whole tree.

Model trees put math formulas in their leaves. Optimal versions were built with mixed integer planning. Leaves held linear support vector machines. Tests used standard benchmark data sets. Rivals included greedy trees, forests, and support machines. Optimal trees matched strong accuracy with tiny size. Slanted splits boosted accuracy but blurred clarity. The trade-off between clear and sharp is made plain.
pmc-13291564:
Virtual reality may make colon checks calmer and less painful. Yijie Sun leads a 2026 randomized trial of VR during colonoscopy. Adults aged 18 to 70 took part without sedation. Pain and anxiety are common barriers to screening.

Patients were split into VR and control groups. Pain, anxiety, and vital signs were tracked live. VR users felt less pain and less anxiety. Their heart rate and blood pressure also ran lower. Procedure time and success matched the control group. More VR users would accept a future colon check. That gain could lift screening rates over time. Comfort care need not slow the procedure down.
pmc-13291764:
Crone and co-authors map the worldwide use of gut stimulating drugs in intensive care in this 2026 PATIENCE study. Feeding intolerance is common in critically ill patients, and prokinetic agents are given to move the gut along. Evidence for them is thin, so practice varies. The team followed newly admitted patients in 56 intensive care units across 11 countries.

Among 1440 patients, 187 received a prokinetic agent during their stay, roughly one patient in eight. Metoclopramide was the drug used most often. Patients who had undergone abdominal surgery before were more likely to receive one. Use of these drugs came with a higher hazard of serious adverse events and fewer days alive out of intensive care and hospital, though not with higher 90 day mortality. Crone presents the figures as a baseline for future trials.
pmc-13292264:
Karim Qayumi and a large team evaluate a 2026 digital medical school built for Afghan women shut out of university classrooms. The Canadian Virtual Medical University Initiative delivers an online, competency-based curriculum built around five entrustable professional activities across body systems. Lectures came through Lecturio, and CyberPatient supplied simulated clinical practice.

Ninety-two former Afghan medical students with strong English and reliable internet joined the first term, studying from November 2024 to July 2025. Level I students gained 52 to 58 points on knowledge tests across every system taught, with strong statistical significance. Level II students also improved in knowledge and in virtual clinical exam performance. The authors present the model as a workable lifeline where campuses, faculty, and women's access have collapsed.
pmc-13292464:
Ellainy Maria Conceição Silva and co-authors use a 2026 shellfish survey to test whether Maranhão Island's bivalves carry Toxoplasma gondii, the parasite behind toxoplasmosis. Oysters, mussels, and clams came from natural mangrove beds around four island municipalities through 2022, in both rainy and dry seasons. Gill tissue pools underwent DNA extraction and gene testing targeting SAG1, with deeper marker panels for positives.

Three mussel pools, 1.8 percent of the sixty tested, came back positive, all from rainy-season collections in Raposa and São José de Ribamar. Sequence matching confirmed 98 to 100 percent similarity with known Toxoplasma sequences, though extra markers failed to amplify, limiting genotype claims. Tree analysis grouped the finds with classical genotype references. The authors recommend monitoring shellfish grounds as a food safety measure.
pmc-13292664:
Lara Hamzeh Hamzeh and a large team pool a 2026 meta-analysis on magnetic brain stimulation for freezing of gait, the sudden stepping stall that makes Parkinson's patients fall. Searching four databases through January 2026 under PRISMA 2020 rules, they kept randomized trials only. The main outcome was freezing severity on the standard questionnaire.

Twelve trials with 293 participants qualified. Stimulation improved freezing scores by a standardized mean difference of 0.97 in the pooled estimate, a solid effect. Motor ratings, Timed Up and Go times, walking speed, stride length, and turning measures all improved too, while cadence alone stayed flat. No serious adverse events appeared in any trial. The authors call the therapy a safe, promising add-on for gait problems that resist drugs, while asking for bigger trials with shared protocols.
pmc-13292764: Penelope Banchi and co-authors issued this brief correction in 2026 to their review on early-life gut microbes in dogs and cats. The notice fixes one label in Figure 1 and states that the review itself has been updated. The figure had shown weaning for puppies and kittens with a wrong age note, and the correct wording is more than 2 months of age. No findings or advice in the review change. Readers who need the timeline for feeding and weaning should use the corrected figure.
pmc-13293364:
Ericka Stoor-Burning leads a 2026 Army study comparing three prototype sensor suits that record battlefield casualty care without adding hands-on work. Medics in combat zones have little time to chart care, so passive recording could fill the gap.

Testing ran in three stages: bench review, practice use, and a full simulation event under varied lighting. All three suits passed basic checks, and simpler layouts scored best on capturing and exporting raw data. In practice runs, usability scores ran from 60 to 85 out of 100, a spread the authors report. Display lag for vital signs raised trust concerns among users.
pmc-13293464:
Muzafar Riyaz and co-authors compare, in a 2026 field study, insect pollinators in sprayed apple orchards and nearby unsprayed graveyards in Shopian, Kashmir. Heavy spray schedules may do more than poison insects directly; they may also warp how insects choose flowers.

Eight orchards held far fewer insects and species than paired graveyards, with hoverflies and lone bees hit hardest. Visiting networks in orchards grew sparser and less nested, and insects fed on fewer flower types. One common flower drew most visits during peak spraying, acting as a trap with no clean option nearby. Long-tongued insects fell sharply, flattening the pollinator mix.
pmc-13293564:
Arun Dahil and co-authors set out, in a 2026 protocol, a planned review of clot complications from cardiac myxoma, the most common benign heart tumor. Though benign, these tumors can shed fragments that cause stroke, heart attack, or limb and organ damage.

The review will search six databases for large case series, cohort studies, and registries with confirmed tumors. Pairs of reviewers will screen and extract data, with bias checked by standard tools. Planned outputs cover how often clots occur, where they land, how patients present, and how care is managed. The protocol aims to fill a gap in pooled knowledge; no results are given yet.
pmc-13293664:
Shireen Dogar and colleagues combine, in a 2026 paper, a literature review and hospital cohort on wrist tissue biopsy as an early test for heart amyloidosis. A wrist operation for carpal tunnel release offers a chance to spot the protein buildup before heart failure starts.

The review of 22 studies from 2017 to 2025 found amyloid in 10% to 30% of wrist specimens, a range the authors report. At their center, 89 patients had biopsy during release surgery from 2021 to 2025, over half of them African American. No specimen showed amyloid on staining. Better patient picking and sampling rules are needed, the authors conclude.
pmc-13294064:
Zongxin Ling and coauthors compare gut microbes and inflammation in older adults with high blood pressure, with and without memory-type mild cognitive impairment, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Groups held 52 healthy controls, 83 hypertensive adults with normal cognition, and 70 hypertensive adults with impairment. Stool sequencing and a 27-marker blood panel were combined.

The impaired group showed richer but clearly separate gut communities, with fewer short-chain fatty acid makers like Roseburia and Faecalibacterium and more opportunistic genera. Inflammatory signals including IL-6 and IL-8 ran higher. Blautia levels tracked with lower inflammation and better cognition, while pathobiont levels tracked the opposite way.
pmc-13294164:
Meriem El Karoui, Ignacio Madrid, and Sylvie Méléard model a bacterial survival trade-off in a 2026 math study. Under low antibiotic stress, E. coli cells can randomly switch on the SOS response, which helps them endure damage but slows division. Their two-type, age-structured model splits cells into fast but fragile growers and slow but tolerant responders, in steady and pulsing stress.

Two fitness lenses disagreed: chance of survival from one cell versus long-run growth rate reacted differently to switch settings. Under periodic stress, best growth needed joint tuning of response triggering and repair speed. Single-metric lab screens may thus misjudge which strategy truly wins.
pmc-13294264:
Ryota Nomura and colleagues build a machine learning soft sensor for polyvinyl alcohol viscosity in a 2026 process study. Viscosity mirrors chain length and decides whether a lot can ship, yet lab readings lag production and batches drift. Models using squared terms, cross terms, and time-series data learned to predict viscosity from plant conditions.

Prediction accuracy improved with the richer inputs. A case study then searched for settings that pull off-target lots back into the goal range, and the designed conditions succeeded. Virtual sensing plus condition design could cut waste in plants where direct measurement arrives too late to steer the batch.
pmc-13294364:
Ehab A Okba, Hend Mansour, and Shaban Y Shaban compare dye-cleaning nanomaterials in a 2026 adsorption study. A lanthanum-zinc-iron oxide powder was made by coprecipitation, alone and coated with chitosan from natural polymer. Seven lab methods confirmed crystal phases and texture, then two anionic dyes, indigo carmine and Acid Blue 25, were soaked under acidic conditions.

Bare powder removed 97.7% and 92% of the two dyes, beating the coated version in the reported tests. Uptake followed second-order kinetics and released heat. Bare powder fit single-layer math, while coated powder fit multilayer math. Both held up over five reuse cycles, supporting low-cost wastewater use.
pmc-13294464:
Chloe Braun and a large team interview staff about fluid overload in sick children for a 2026 qualitative study. Extra fluid harms critically ill kids, yet spotting and cutting it varies wildly. Thirty-eight interviews across four pediatric intensive care units from August to October 2025 covered 19 nurses, 12 physicians, 4 advanced providers, and 3 trainees, coded rapidly by two analysts.

Three themes emerged. Bedside data are noisy, subjective, and measured with shaky tools. Teams pay too little heed to simply giving less fluid up front. Culture blocks change through training gaps, missing standards, habit, and poor communication. Fixing overload needs better data plus habit change.
pmc-13294764:
Yu Zhou and co-authors track deaths among people with schizophrenia in one Shanghai district in a 2026 cohort study. People with schizophrenia die earlier than the wider population, yet how risk changed over recent years needed clearer figures. Data came from the official city database for severe mental disorders.

Altogether 5,234 people were followed from April 2021 to March 2023, with 370 deaths recorded across the period. Deaths rose sharply in the later year, peaking in December 2022 and January 2023. Older age, male sex, later illness onset, longer illness, and being unmarried, divorced, or widowed each raised the risk of dying.
pmc-13294964:
Hassarutai Yangthong and a large team test palm oil as a greener processing aid for natural rubber in a 2026 study. Rubber makers usually soften compounds with petroleum based aromatic oil. Palm oil was tried instead, using a latex route that mixes ingredients before the rubber sets.

Curing speed stayed much the same after the swap, and filler interaction measures were close between the two oils. Palm oil compounds proved stiffer and showed the lowest rolling resistance signal, a useful trait for tyres. A life cycle review also favoured palm oil and the latex route on fossil fuel use, human toxicity, and ozone harm.
pmc-13295164:
Jarett E Prince and colleagues review two centuries of penetrating wounds to a major brain vein in a 2026 article. Injuries to the superior sagittal sinus are rare but can bleed massively and raise pressure inside the skull. Guidance has stayed scattered across old and new case reports.

Searches of four databases gathered 39 articles covering 51 cases from 1826 to 2025. Nearly all patients were men, and military harm, accidents, and suicide attempts led the causes, with nails and bone pieces as common objects. Repair choices ranged from clotting agents and grafts to tying off the vein. About one quarter of patients died.
pmc-13295464:
Jie Wang and colleagues re-examine biodegradable mulch film and soil life in a 2026 review. Such films promise an escape from the white pollution left by ordinary plastic mulch in farm soils. Beyond breaking down itself, the material may reshape soil microbes and nutrient flows in lasting ways.

Common film ingredients include starch, cellulose, and several made polymers that soil microbes can eventually turn into carbon dioxide, water, and living matter. Gains in warmth, moisture holding, and weed control mirror plastic film benefits. The authors argue that judging these films only on waste reduction misses deeper effects on soil community structure and nutrient availability.
pmc-13295564:
Khemrutai Sripath and Teerasak E-kobon hunt vaccine parts against the acne bacterium by computer in a 2026 study. Acne affects most teenagers, and resistant Cutibacterium acnes strains weaken antibiotic control. Genome data offer a wide, mostly untapped pool of possible vaccine ingredients.

Across 609 bacterial genomes, 972 shared core genes were found and screened for immune visibility. Chosen fragments predicted to stir both antibody and cell defences were stitched into four multi-part peptide candidates. Docking tests suggested friendly binding to two immune sensors, and simulated immune runs behaved as hoped. The candidates now await bench testing to confirm the computer predictions.
pmc-13295764:
George A Karpouzas and colleagues ask how two blood markers change heart risk reading in arthritis in a 2026 study. Rheumatoid factor and anti-citrullinated protein antibodies mark rheumatoid arthritis type, while joint inflammation itself raises heart event risk. Whether marker status bends that link was the question.

Records covered 3,952 patients without heart disease across an international group, followed for first major heart events. Disease activity predicted events overall, with 184 events logged over the follow-up years. The activity link appeared in marker-negative and double-positive patients but not in single-positive ones. The authors argue risk reading should weigh activity and marker pattern together.
pmc-13296764:
Shaoli Li and co-authors pool, in 2026, evidence on preventive brain radiation for limited-stage small-cell lung cancer carefully staged with MRI scans. Brain spread is common in this cancer, but modern imaging raised doubts about whether blasting a clear brain still helps.

Across 1,894 patients, preventive radiation cut death risk by about a third and added a clear survival gain at two years. The benefit held against active scan surveillance alone. Thinking side effects were mostly brief and overall quality of life held up. The authors reinforce preventive radiation as a real option after first treatment.
pmc-13297164:
Oscar Fraile-Martinez and a large team review, in 2026, how drug use in pregnancy damages the placenta, the organ feeding the fetus. Alcohol, tobacco, cannabis, cocaine and opioids, plus synthetic drugs, can cross it and distort its vessels, chemistry and gene settings.

Consequences range from stunted growth and early birth to lasting brain effects in the child. Placental examination can also reveal exposure and its timing, giving forensic as well as clinical value. The authors favour using that evidence to support care rather than punishment, and to shape public health responses.
pmc-13298964:
Gene scans of a drug-proof gut bug across five Dutch care sites found spread that one site alone could not see. Djamayl L H H Engelen and his team report the work in 2026. For one year they read the full gene code of each VRE strain found in sick or screened patients, then set the codes next to ward stay logs.

Of 57 strains, 38, or 66.7%, matched at least one other strain. Near all matched sets traced spread inside one site, but three crossed from site to site. The scan net caught one wide outbreak and two small ones. The team back shared, region-wide gene watch as a core tool for care-site safety.
pmc-13299064:
A panel of blood proteins can flag brain amyloid without a brain scan, suggest Stelios Lamprou and colleagues in a 2026 machine learning study of the Bio-Hermes cohort. They profiled 295 plasma proteins in 988 participants and trained classifiers to separate amyloid PET-positive from negative individuals.

Thirty-one proteins differed between groups, and five survived strict correction. Tree-based models performed most steadily, reaching AUC values of 0.79 to 0.81. Eight proteins kept surfacing as important, including APOE4, complement C3, and CRP. The authors present multi-protein signatures as a complement to single-analyte Alzheimer blood tests, adding information about which biological pathways are active.
pmc-13299564:
A cell catch long cast as a mere decoy in fact puts a brake on muscle cell growth. Mitsutoshi Kurosaka and Kazuhisa Kohda show that in a 2026 cell study. They hushed the catch, IL-13Rα2, in mouse C2C12 muscle cells and watched growth and ripe change.

The cells still ripened into muscle strands as they should, and genes for cell fuse held steady. Growth, though, leapt: more cells took up a growth mark, and cell counts rose. A growth path through Akt woke up, which raised cyclin D1 and its mate CDK4. When the team blocked Akt, the growth leap died. The catch, they say, reins in muscle cell spread through that path and plays no part in ripe change.
pmc-13300964:
Using only arteries for bypass grafts sounds better, but Albaraa Al-Holy and colleagues found no survival edge in a 2026 cohort study of patients with moderately weak hearts. The retrospective review covered 1,866 people with ejection fractions of 30 to 49 percent who had isolated bypass surgery. Propensity matching produced 640 balanced patients for the head-to-head test.

Ten-year survival read 85.8 percent with total arterial grafting against 81.7 percent with a single artery, and fifteen-year figures kept the same small gap. Neither difference reached significance, and graft strategy dropped out as a mortality predictor after adjustment. Age, symptom class, prior surgery, and off-pump technique mattered instead, the authors report.
pmc-13304664:
Laura García-Quintanilla and colleagues track one-year results of eye injections for wet age-related macular degeneration in a 2026 prospective study. Ranibizumab helps many patients, but response varies and blood clues to that spread are lacking.

Forty-four patients new to treatment received monthly shots at first, then a stretch-as-needed plan. Vision, retinal thickness, and scans were checked at start and one year, alongside blood immune signals and small RNA markers. Retinal thickness fell clearly and vision held steady overall. Good and poor responders split by combined sight and anatomy rules, guiding marker hunts.
pmc-13305664:
Peter-Jon Williams reported a 2026 case of a 43-year-old man who survived cardiac arrest linked to severe mitral annular disjunction. The man had collapsed at work, received chest compressions from colleagues, and recovered after one shock from a defibrillator.

Heart scans showed leaking of the mitral valve with both leaflets prolapsing and suspected separation at the valve ring. Doctors fitted an implantable defibrillator to guard against repeat arrest, then later completed robotic valve repair as an outpatient plan. The authors stress early recognition and advanced imaging, since both shape device choices and surgical planning after arrest or fainting.
pmc-13305964:
Junqing Huang grew upright nickel cobalt sulfide sheets on nickel foam for alkaline zinc batteries in a 2026 study. The open, layered array was formed in place through a solvent heat step followed by sulfur treatment, without added alkali.

Its linked pores shorten ion paths, expose many reaction sites and speed electron flow in the authors' account. The best electrode stored 323 mAh g−1 at 0.5 A g−1 in reported tests, and a full cell with a zinc anode kept strong capacity after 500 cycles. High energy and power figures support use for large-scale storage, pending wider validation.
pmc-13306364:
Olamilekan Banjo built a spiking neural chip design for live heartbeat classification in a 2026 study. Wearable monitors need on-device answers across several rhythm classes without cloud delay, yet low-power spiking models face skewed class counts.

A two-head network first separates normal from abnormal beats, then sends only abnormal beats to a four-class stage to save computing effort. Tests compared two training losses under four ways of adding beat-interval features. Focal loss helped when interval features were absent, gaining about 2.3 to 2.5 percent in reported macro scores, while the edge vanished once interval data joined.
pmc-13306464:
Hao Cheng boosted a water-channel gene in poplar to speed root formation in a 2026 plant study. The gene PtrPIP2:4 sits in cell membranes and is active mainly in roots, yet its role in new root growth from cuttings was unclear.

Cuttings carrying extra copies rooted faster than normal plants, grew longer new roots and formed many more side roots, though total new root count barely changed in reported results. Gene activity scans found 4204 changed genes, with hormone auxin pathways and flavonoid making strongly represented. Nine auxin-linked genes were confirmed by targeted checks.
pmc-13307164:
Aphelele Taliwe reviewed daisy-family plants against inflammation and cancer in a 2026 survey of work from 2022 to 2026. Asteraceae ranks among the largest medicinal plant families, long used in traditional care and now probed for drug leads.

Lab, animal and computer studies tie extracts to antioxidant action, cytokine calming, enzyme blocking and gene control in the gathered evidence. Key pathways covered include NF-κB, MAPK, PI3K/Akt and COX-2, plus death regulators such as Bax, Bcl-2 and caspases. The synthesis supports careful development of family compounds into tested therapies. The team notes most proof is still early, so firm dose and safety work must come next.
pmc-13307764:
Thatiana Corrêa de Melo and co-authors trace in 2026 how the power units of lung cells shift shape and defence work during SARS-CoV-2 infection over four days. They used imaging, gene reads, protein maps, and fluid checks in infected cells at 48 and 96 hours after entry.

Early on, the units showed stress and split more, with one fusion protein down and a splitting protein up in that phase. Later they stretched into long nets near the nucleus and raised fusion and growth marks again. Defence genes stayed on, yet release of a key alarm protein stayed low. A tag system called SUMO moved with the changes, which hints at shared control of shape and defence.
pmc-13309464:
Adib Al-Haj Husain and colleagues compare two scan methods for checking face and jaw fracture repair in a 2026 study. One method takes cone-beam scans during surgery, while the other uses magnetic scans soon after surgery with special settings that cut metal glare. Both aim to show whether bones sit right and plates and screws lie well.

Fifteen patients with acute face fractures had surgery with the in-room scan, then a magnetic scan within 36 hours. Two surgeons scored image quality and measured implant position. Certain magnetic sequences gave sharp, CT-like views of bone and hardware. The authors weigh whether the later scan can match or beat the during-surgery scan for repair checks.
pmc-13309564:
Sherin A M Ali and colleagues test a new chemical guard against acid corrosion of low-carbon steel in a 2026 study. Steel in acid baths needs additives that cling to the surface and block attack. The new compound, shortened to SHIB, joins a sulfur-bearing acid group with a rich ring structure suited to surface binding.

Weight loss, electric, and imaging tests all showed protection rising with dose, reaching about 92 percent blocked attack at 300 ppm in strong acid. Protection held across a useful heat range but weakened as heat rose. Surface data fit a single-layer binding model with spontaneous attachment. Computer modeling backed the binding picture, and the authors propose the compound for acid cleaning use.
pmc-13309664:
Na Zheng and co-authors chart the features of a rare inherited movement disorder in Chinese patients in a 2026 study. The disorder, dentatorubral-pallidoluysian atrophy, stems from a repeated DNA stretch in the ATN1 gene and varies widely in age and symptoms. Chinese case data had stayed scattered across local reports.

Three related patients at one hospital were joined with 42 published Chinese cases, giving 45 patients in total. Repeat counts centered on a median of 62, and illness began at a mean age near 28 years across the group. Seizures and unsteady walking were the most common first signs, with thinking problems frequent later. Brain scan patterns were also reviewed. The authors offer the summary to speed recognition.
pmc-13309964:
Nicole Fritz-Silva and co-authors relate body makeup to bone strength in older adults in Chile in a 2026 study. Low bone density drives frailty and fracture risk in later life. Muscle mass loads bone through movement and direct tissue links, yet Latin American scan-based evidence, split by sex, stays limited.

A community sample of 274 adults aged 65 and older in Puerto Montt, four in five of them women, received full body scans. Total lean mass linked moderately and positively with whole-body bone density in those with complete data. Fat amount and placement were also weighed, with models adjusting for age, body size, and sex. The authors argue that keeping muscle may help guard bone in this population.
pmc-13310664:
Qianwen Wang and co-authors review gene profiling of liver echinococcosis in a 2026 article. The disease is a parasitic cyst or infiltrating growth in the liver, driven by tapeworm larvae in farming regions. Lesions persist for years through a stalemate of immune control, vessel growth, and scarring, whose cell-level drivers stay fuzzy.

Bulk gene studies mapped broad shifts in immune, vessel, and matrix programs but averaged signals across mixed tissue. Single-cell and spatial methods now resolve which cells do what and where they sit. Early cell studies flag expanding macrophage types, tired T cells, and vessel-friendly myeloid cells near lesions. The authors set standards for future cell-level work and warn where bulk habits mislead.
pmc-13310864:
Myles Murphy and a large team co created a plan to cut injuries in police recruits in a 2026 concept mapping study. Recruits face a high burden of muscle and joint injury, which costs money and drives dropouts. Views from recruits, staff, clinicians, and experts were pooled to rank what matters and what can be done.

Forty eight people brainstormed, sorted, and rated ideas, yielding 96 distinct strategies in eight groups. Clear sharing of training demands ranked highest for importance. Other groups covered load control, best injury care, staff teaching, and a supportive setting. Forty two ideas scored above average on both importance and ease.
pmc-13311164:
Athanasios Feidakis and colleagues test a heart strain marker in tricuspid valve catheter care in a 2026 study. NT-proBNP sorts risk in heart failure well, yet its value before and after tricuspid valve intervention was unclear. Patients with severe valve leak were grouped by starting marker levels and by early change.

Higher starting levels linked on their own to higher long term death rates. Patients whose marker rose by four weeks fared far worse, whatever the procedure result. Rising marker patients also held larger right heart chambers and higher pressures at start. Starting level did not foretell symptom gain at four weeks.
pmc-13311364:
Dóra Biskup and co-authors compare four small drug candidates that switch on the somatostatin 4 receptor in a 2026 study. The receptor is a target for nerve pain, where current drugs often fall short or harm.

The team checked the compounds against natural somatostatin and a known strong activator using computer docking, drug-likeness screens, cell tests of a signaling molecule, and a mouse nerve injury model. All four compounds gripped the same key spot on the receptor in the docking work. Cell tests confirmed they switch the receptor on. The results rank the candidates for later pain drug work.
pmc-13311764:
Davide Viggiano and co-authors set out the VIRTUAL trial protocol in a 2026 article. The trial tests virtual reality thinking training for adults on dialysis, among whom thinking problems are common and drag on daily life.

Sixty adults aged 18 to 75 on regular dialysis for at least 90 days will join across several centers. Half get standard care; half add a twelve-week program of game-like memory, attention, and speed tasks during dialysis sessions. Main checks cover recruitment, retention, session completion, and how patients view the process. A feasible design would open the way to a full outcome trial.
pmc-13311964:
Bee O'Shea and Joanna Smith comment in a 2025 article on a study of bedtime screen use and sleep in young people. The discussed study measured both screen habits and sleep directly rather than by recall.

Brosnan and colleagues tracked 79 youths aged 11 to 15 over four nights in a week, using wrist sensors for sleep and a wearable camera approach for screens. Passive viewing, such as television, seemed relaxing yet still delayed sleep onset, while interactive use cut into sleep more. The commentators note hospital relevance, where evening screens are common. Type of activity, not just minutes, shapes the sleep cost.
pmc-13312164:
Jiaying Chen and co-authors examine, in a 2026 study, how teacher feedback shapes student motivation and reading results, using situated expectancy-value theory as their lens. Feedback is often praised as a strong teaching tool, yet studies disagree on whether it helps, does nothing, or even hurts achievement.

The team modeled links among feedback, students' expectancy and value beliefs, and performance in data from 569,311 students across 80 countries. The direct link between feedback and reading performance was negative. Through beliefs, though, feedback worked the other way, partly lifting performance by raising students' confidence and sense that reading matters. The authors argue feedback pays off only when it builds motivation, helping students believe they can succeed and enjoy what they learn.
pmc-13312264:
Wenjie Meng and colleagues analyze, in a 2026 study, how local public-place smoking bans changed smoking behavior across China. Tobacco control there is run city by city. The team used the China Family Panel Studies from 2010 to 2020 to compare residents of 37 cities with differing local rules over a decade.

The regulations showed no significant overall effect on whether people smoked. They were, however, linked to how much smokers consumed, and the direction swung by city. In Hangzhou both smoking likelihood and daily cigarette counts rose after the local policy. In Tianjin both fell clearly, and Guangzhou saw lower daily consumption without a change in smoking probability. The authors conclude that local bans produce sharply uneven results, an argument for national standards adapted to local conditions rather than a patchwork of city rules.
pmc-13313264:
Laura Haag and a large team follow preterm babies in a 2026 study of whether early antibiotics blunt vaccine responses. Babies born too soon face high sepsis risk, so many get antibiotics in their first days, but how that shapes their young immune systems stays unclear.

The team studied 69 preterm infants born before 32 weeks, with 35 given antibiotics in the first week and 34 not given them. Blood and stool were taken at day 14 and again at four months of corrected age. They measured antibody levels raised by vaccines against whooping cough and Haemophilus influenzae, among other targets named in the report. The design also allows a check for unlike effects in boys and girls, a point the title flags as a focus of the work.
pmc-13314464:
Demy van Gilst and co-workers check whether breast milk for very early babies still carries day-night hormone rhythms, in a study from 2026. Milk holds hormones that guide brain and clock growth, but preterm babies in intensive care get pooled milk by tube, with no time-of-day match.

The team studied mothers of babies born before 30 weeks, across stages of lactation. Each milk series held 13 to 17 samples, with a median of 15 as stated in the report, gathered over three straight days. Cortisol and melatonin were measured with kit assays, and rhythm was judged by curve fitting. Knowing whether the clock signals survive in preterm milk can shape how units store and time feeds, a field called chrononutrition that is gaining ground in newborn care.
pmc-13314564:
Edoardo Beatrici leads a large expert panel that agreed rules for a fast tissue imaging method in prostate surgery, in a 2026 paper. Leaving cancer at the cut edge after robot-assisted prostate removal raises relapse risk and can force extra treatment that harms recovery.

Frozen section checks can catch those positive margins, but most centers cannot run them as routine. Ex vivo fluorescence confocal microscopy offers a quick, live-time swap, reading fresh tissue without freezing. The Delphi process gathered surgeons and allied experts to settle when and how to use the method during robot-assisted radical prostatectomy, as the report has it. Shared rules may spread a tool that helps surgeons clear cancer while sparing function.
pmc-13315664:
SARA FIGLIOMENI and a large team report in 2026 a rare adult case of meningitis caused by Neisseria lactamica, a harmless throat germ found mostly in children. The germ shares much of its genome with its dangerous relative but lacks the tools to cross into the brain, so disease in adults is almost unheard of.

Their patient was a 58-year-old woman with a past head injury who arrived with sudden headache, nausea, vomiting, and light sensitivity. Spinal fluid fit bacterial meningitis, standard gene tests were negative, yet cultures grew the germ from fluid and blood. Scans revealed a skull base defect linked to a spinal fluid leak near the nose.
pmc-13315764:
Lingling Dai and co-authors review in 2026 how microbes and the fish's own enzymes work together in fermented fish to shape flavor, texture, and safety. Salt-tolerant microbe groups and inner enzymes break down proteins and fats, freeing amino acids, peptides, and fatty acids that become aroma and taste compounds.

Acid formation, protein cutting, and matrix change balance enzyme softening against acid firming to set texture. Risks center on biogenic amines and nitrosamines, which careful process control and chosen starter cultures can limit. Multi-omics tools paired with artificial intelligence may reveal quality markers and allow advance monitoring of batches.
pmc-13315964:
Frank Ssedyabane and a large team reviewed six years of treatment results in 2026 for cervical precancer lesions at Mbarara Regional Referral Hospital in southwestern Uganda. Real-world outcome data from such settings are scarce, so records were gathered for women treated from January 2020 to July 2025.

Among 184 women, with mean age 43.3 years, 150 cases, or 81.5 percent, were recorded as cured, while 34 cases, or 18.5 percent, had lesions that persisted. Age, home district, HIV status, HPV test results, treatment type, and year were all extracted. The split shows where follow-up care needs strengthening.
pmc-13316364:
Gregor Massoth and colleagues describe a 2026 project report from University Hospital Bonn on joint training for final-year medical students alongside anaesthesia assistant trainees. The IPAPA program teaches both groups together, using practice runs of anaesthesia induction, because teamwork in that moment guards patient safety.

Design followed a six-step curriculum method and drew goals from national rulebooks for both professions, shaped around the TeamSTEPPS teamwork system. The finished course holds eight teaching units and now runs as a required part of both training paths. Early feedback praised the hands-on practice and clear team talk, and learners said working side by side felt true to real care. The report gives other schools a working model to copy.
pmc-13316564:
Roman O Kowalchuk leads a 2026 case series on spatially fractionated radiation for children, a method that places small spheres of very high dose inside a tumor rather than spreading dose evenly. Adults had shown promise, but no data existed for young patients before this report.

Charts covered five patients treated from 2019 to 2025, with a median age of 15.7 years in the group. No tumor growth and no serious side effects appeared at treated sites during follow-up, and three children were alive at last check. Two pelvic bone cancers stayed controlled locally, though spread elsewhere remained. The authors call the early control encouraging and ask for more study in stubborn or returning tumors.
pmc-13318764:
Jiahui Fu and co-authors offer a 2026 scoping review of tools that measure family caregivers' ability. Their focus is relatives caring for disabled older adults at home. Good measurement helps nurses target support. The review followed standard scoping guidance and searched nine databases through October 19, 2025.

Twenty-five articles covered 21 assessment tools. Four were generic and seventeen were built for specific diseases. Tools have moved from single-score impressions to multi-part structures. Common domains include disease knowledge, hands-on skills, psychosocial strength, and use of resources. Most tools are self-report scales with decent consistency. Reporting of structural validity and measurement error is often thin. The authors suggest modular designs and tiered testing for wider use.
pmc-13318864:
Yaxuan Hao and colleagues present a 2026 mouse study of a traditional Chinese compound, Yin Huang Ge, for Alzheimer's disease. Early treatment matters because amyloid changes begin decades before symptoms. The team used APP/PS1 mice, a standard disease model. Treatment ran for 30 days by stomach tube.

Behaviour tests covered mazes and object recognition. Model mice learned and remembered poorly, with high amyloid protein in the brain. Two amyloid-clearing enzymes, IDE and NEP, were reduced in those animals. Treated mice performed better on the cognitive tests. Their clearing enzymes rose in amount and activity, while harmful enzymes fell. Growth factors BDNF and NT-3 also increased. The authors credit a two-way effect on amyloid build-up and damage.
pmc-13318964:
Florian Grafl and Florian Steger present a 2026 historical study of venereal disease practice under Spain's Franco dictatorship. Their focus is the Patronato de Protección a la Mujer in Catalonia. That state Catholic body was created to discipline teenage girls. The authors ask whether its medical work served ideology rather than care.

Sources came from national and provincial archives in Catalonia. At the Barcelona board headquarters, examinations were performed against patients' will. Women with venereal disease were forcibly admitted to a closed hospital ward until it shut in 1959. From 1963, girls were isolated in an observation centre for extensive medical checks. The authors conclude the examinations rested on doubtful medical grounds. They functioned mainly as social control over girls who broke regime norms.
pmc-13319064:
Xuejiao Pan and co-authors present a 2026 surveillance analysis of reactions reported after MMR vaccination in Zhejiang Province, China. Reports covering January 2020 through December 2025 came from the national reporting system. The team classed events as common reactions, rare reactions, or coincidental. Patterns by age, dose, season, and region were examined.

In total, 12,597 events were reported, a rate of 213.15 per 100,000 doses in their figures. Most cases involved children aged one year or younger, at 76.49 percent of the reports. Fever led the symptoms at 70.75 percent, followed by rash and irritability. Sixty-eight severe events occurred, and 95.49 percent of all cases improved without treatment. Giving MMR alongside other vaccines raised high fever and rash rates. The authors judge the safety profile sound.
pmc-13319864:
Pedro Giorgetti Montagner and co-authors fire dental ceramic discs again and again in a 2026 lab study of crown materials. Machine made crowns often need extra firings to fix shade or shape, yet heat rounds may change surface feel and strength. Two glass ceramic types in wide use were fired two, three, or five times and then tested side by side.

Sixty discs were split evenly between the two materials and across the firing counts. One type grew smoother and stronger with more firings, while the other grew weaker at five firings. Hardness fell at five firings for both, and one type showed tiny surface flaws at that count. Extra firings help one material more than the other, so lab plans should differ by type.
pmc-13320664:
Jan Hojný and colleagues write a 2026 letter on the mixed nature of high-grade womb stromal sarcomas. They respond to a study by Hartwich and others that used whole genome, exome, and RNA reading on 80 such tumours and flagged a gene gain tied to worse survival. These cancers are aggressive, hard to classify, and short on treatment options.

The writers note that similar looking tumours can stem from quite different gene faults. Some are driven by gene fusions, with fairly few added mutations, while tumours lacking fusions more often show a mutation driven pattern. Sorting those groups apart matters for prognosis and for finding drug targets, including rare repair fault cases.
pmc-13322864:
Manar Abdelazeem Gomaa and colleagues report real-world use of anti-CGRP drugs for migraine in Egypt, in a 2026 study of patients prescribed these newer treatments. Clinicians followed headache diaries and disability scores at the start of care and again at one and three months.

The cohort held 80 patients, 62 with chronic migraine and 18 with episodic migraine, treated with erenumab, galcanezumab or rimegepant. About two thirds reached at least a halving of migraine burden, with gains in monthly migraine days, pain level, attack length and disability scores. Stopping treatment, seen in 35 patients, often reflected cost, good improvement or poor response, and relapse followed in a large share of those who stopped.
pmc-13323164:
Robert N D'Angelo and Natalia C Berry argue in a 2026 commentary that care for the left atrial appendage in atrial fibrillation needs one joined strategy. The appendage triggers rhythm trouble and supplies most clots in this disease, so isolating it electrically and closing it mechanically are often discussed apart.

Trials pull in mixed directions: isolation cut recurrence in the BELIEF trial, device closure matched drug care in OPTION and CHAMPION-AF, yet CLOSURE-AF missed its target in older, higher-risk patients. Stroke risk after isolation, from weak appendage contraction, pushes many clinicians toward closure anyway. The authors weigh why results differ, including leftover patency, and propose treating isolation and closure as one planned package.
pmc-13323464:
Yang Wu leads a review of CRISPR tools for tracking mosquito-borne viruses, published in 2026, across detection, tracing and discovery support. Surveillance must catch many co-circulating pathogens, types and lineages quickly at clinics and mosquito sampling sites.

Detection is the most mature use, with Cas12 and Cas13 assays for Zika, dengue, West Nile virus, chikungunya, Japanese encephalitis and kin reporting sub-hour runs and portable readouts. Tracing still leans on portable sequencing, while CRISPR sample preparation tricks remain transferable ideas rather than field standards. Multiplex systems such as CARMEN can screen known viruses, but finding truly new ones still needs metagenomic sequencing. Field proof in pooled mosquito samples stays thin.
pmc-13324664:
Fei Ye and co-authors test whether a yellowing step can soften the bitter taste of Qianlin cha in a 2026 food study. The herbal tea comes from Camellia cuspidata and is valued for health uses, yet its harsh flavor limits appeal.

Sensory panels, color checks, and two gas chromatography methods compared plain and yellowed tea. Yellowing lifted panel scores, moved color toward yellow, and raised amino acids and soluble sugars for a sweeter sip. Bitter ester catechins fell at the same time. Four scent-active compounds stood out: linalool, nonanal, sulcatone, and (E,E)-2,4-heptadienal. The shift from herbal and bitter toward sweet and floral gives makers a route to premium products.
pmc-13325364:
Cándida Pastor-Ramírez and co-authors build copper cluster compounds with three, four, and eight metal centers in a 2026 chemistry study. One product holds the first cubane-like core built from a Cu4O3N unit.

A Schiff base ligand, sodium azide, and copper salts combined into three structures read by X-ray diffraction. The four-copper compound forms a distorted cube, the eight-copper one a double cube with azide bridges, and the third a chain polymer. Magnetic tests from 2.9 to 300 K showed mixed friendly and opposed spin coupling in the first compound. The larger two showed opposed coupling throughout, tied to their wide copper-oxygen-copper angles.
pmc-13326064:
Fernán González Bernaldo de Quirós and Alejandro Macchia question a national dengue estimate built from blood donors in a 2026 letter. The study under discussion found rising dengue antibodies in donors and virus RNA during the 2022-23 outbreak in Argentina.

From those data came a claim of about 10.2 million new infections nationwide. The letter argues donors from 12 urban centers cannot stand in for the whole country without calibration by age, sex, and region. Reweighting to an older donor mix fixes survey comparability, not population reach. A Buenos Aires household study with careful weights found adult rates of 8.1 percent before and 18.6 percent after a later outbreak, on a stated base.
pmc-13326464:
Ramazan Başaran and co-authors follow blood pressure around the clock in adults over 80 during Ramadan fasting in a 2026 study. Daytime fasting shifts fluid and meal timing, and evidence in the oldest old was thin.

Sixty-nine community-dwelling adults were checked in fasting and non-fasting periods with 24-hour monitors and function tests. Average pressure rose slightly while fasting, to 132.5 over 70.2 mmHg from 129.8 over 68.0 mmHg in the comparison period. Hydration markers and mobility scores did not shift. Fall risk scores, though, rose by a mean of 0.44 points during fasting. The afternoon near 15:00 showed the widest gap between periods. Careful fall watchfulness seems wise.
pmc-13327164:
Marie-Joelle Beaudoin and co-authors published a 2026 study on spotting dementia in adults with intellectual disability. Early signs are hard to judge when thinking skills were already limited, so carers often complete a screening questionnaire. The team checked how questionnaire scores related to age, background, and thinking test results.

Data came from 322 adults, including 55 people with Down syndrome, who also took tests of severe impairment, practical skills, and word fluency. Older age and Down syndrome both went with higher questionnaire scores, while disability severity did not. Higher scores also tracked with stronger verbal fluency, hinting that carers notice change more easily in people who speak well. Closer watching is urged for adults with weaker speech.
pmc-13328364:
Sharmake Gaiye Bashir and a large team review artificial intelligence for forecasting pregnancy complications in a 2026 article. Models now predict preeclampsia, preterm birth, gestational diabetes, and growth restriction, yet reported accuracy swings widely, with AUC values from about 0.73 to 0.97 across studies. The authors focus on bias and the road to clinic.

Eight bias routes are named, from sampling and measurement bias to deployment and access bias, each able to warp performance and widen gaps in maternal care, above all in poorer countries. Outside validation, real impact trials, and cost studies remain scarce, and rules for accountability are still forming. Careful bias control must precede bedside use, they argue.
pmc-13328464:
Julie Toby Thomas and co-authors test saliva markers in prediabetes with gum disease in a 2026 study. Eighty-four adults aged 25 to 55 were split into four groups crossing prediabetes and periodontitis status, and saliva was assayed for three molecules: total MMP-8, adiponectin, and resistin. Clinical, body, and metabolic measures accompanied the sampling.

Total MMP-8 ran highest in prediabetic patients with periodontitis, while adiponectin ran lower in prediabetic groups than in healthy controls, and MMP-8 rose alongside body mass, HbA1c, pocket depth, and attachment loss. A combined profile separated the groups in pattern analysis. A spit test joining metabolic and gum signals could flag patients needing joint medical and dental care.
pmc-13329564:
Robert Lundberg and co-authors detail a method for gathering airborne chemicals over time in a 2026 article. Metal discs coated with sorbent collect volatile compounds, which are then moved onto a fibre for gas chromatography and mass checks. Steps cover disc making, cleaning, exposure, heating, and transfer in a repeatable routine.

Each disc of 3.6 cm held about 0.2 g of sorbent, and sampling lasted 60 minutes in the described setup. Across standard tests, discs gave larger signals than direct fibre sampling for most compounds, though very volatile ones such as acetone gave lower signals. The authors explain the pattern with a model that weighs trapped mass against transfer success. The routine uses no solvents and discs can be reused.
pmc-13333364:
Amr El-Nile and co-authors tested a trace mineral cocktail in drinking water for growing rabbits in a 2026 feeding study, asking whether it improves organ health, immunity, antioxidant defenses, and gut bacteria. Minerals such as iron, zinc, and copper run many enzymes, and shortfalls quietly cap farm animal performance.

Seventy-two seven-week-old male V-line rabbits were split into four groups of 18: plain water or water carrying the mineral mix at 0.5, 1.0, or 1.5 mL per liter. At the two higher doses, the liver enzyme alkaline phosphatase rose while alanine aminotransferase fell, hinting at friendlier liver readings, and blood antioxidant capacity increased across treated groups. Total gut bacterial counts dropped with supplementation, and the top dose cut E. coli counts below every other group. The authors conclude the mix benefits liver and kidney markers, antioxidant and immune status, and gut balance, most clearly at 1 and 1.5 mL per liter.
pmc-13333764:
Hamid Ullah, Muhammad Adil, and Chong Zhang wrote a 2026 lab study of Fingerhuthia africana, a perennial grass used in folk healing for gut disorders and wound care. Its chemistry and safety had barely been studied.

Gas chromatography with mass spectrometry profiled the methanol extract and found 35 metabolites, while atomic absorption measured minerals such as calcium at 12.4 mg per gram and potassium at 9.8 mg per gram in the plant matter. The extract scavenged DPPH radicals in step with dose, reaching 79.5 percent at the top strength tested. A comet assay in human white blood cells probed gene damage risk, and a charcoal meal test in mice measured effects on gut transit. The package gives this folk remedy its first broad chemical and safety profile.
pmc-13336364:
Keyi Chen and co-authors found a new antibiotic candidate by predicting it from a genome and then building it in the lab in a 2026 natural products study. Most microbes resist culturing and many antibiotic genes stay silent, so the team used a synthetic gene-data approach instead of growing the producer.

A gene cluster from Rhodococcus erythropolis D-1 pointed to a nonribosomal peptide scaffold, which the chemists built and refined through four rounds of structure-activity work, yielding 37 analogs. One, ZURJC28, killed multiple Gram-positive bacteria, among them two drug-resistant strains. Mechanism studies and metabolomics showed it disrupts membranes rich in phosphatidylglycerol, wrecking cell chemistry along the way. The pipeline shows genome mining plus lab building can surface antibiotics that fermentation never reveals.
pmc-13336564:
Lina Gao and co-authors link copper imbalance to depression in a 2026 study spanning patients and stressed mice. Copper was high in the blood of people with major depression and in a mood-related brain area of the mice. Inside star-shaped support cells called astrocytes, the protein FDX1 rose as copper built up.

Extra FDX1 in astrocytes tracked with fewer, simpler support cells, weaker calcium signals, and faulty excitatory connections between neurons. Targeted cell changes and recordings showed FDX1 carried much of the harm. Exercise in mice restored copper balance, calmed FDX1, and eased depression-like behavior. The work names a cell-level path that lifestyle steps might help correct.
pmc-13336764:
Qiaoli Wu and colleagues map how a brain lymphoma feeds in a 2026 single-cell study. Primary central nervous system lymphoma grows in a setting low in oxygen and short on glucose in spinal fluid. Starved of glucose, tumor cells instead leaned on fructose, imported through a carrier called SLC2A5.

Low oxygen also switched on that carrier in macrophages that support the tumor, through a HIF-driven route. Blocking fructose uptake, by gene or drug means, sharply slowed lymphoma growth in lab and animal tests. Because both tumor cells and their helper macrophages share the habit, fructose handling stands out as a weak point worth targeting in this hard-to-treat cancer.
pmc-13336864:
Abin Nas Nalakath and a large team test an ultrathin chiral layer for spin-selective electronics in a 2026 study. When electrons pass through twisted molecules, their spin tends to align with the twist, an effect called chiral-induced spin selectivity. Most test systems use long, fragile biomolecules, so the team tried a small, sturdy acid instead.

A layer only about 1 nm thick on nickel oxide gave a strong spin effect, with magnetoresistance of 50%–80% in microscope measurements across the reported runs. Depending on handedness, one spin direction faced a barrier 80% higher or 40% lower than the other above 0.5 V in the fitted model. Small, shelf-available molecules on oxides suit real spintronic devices.
pmc-13336964:
David Kiwic, Linard Räz, Elena Tervoort, and Markus Niederberger heat a catalyst with light to turn carbon dioxide into carbon monoxide in a 2026 study. Their support is zirconia aerogel, a feather-light solid that lets light in deep and holds heat in. Palladium particles spread evenly across the granules by a scalable wet method.

Under strong white LED light at 4.8 W per square centimeter, the catalyst hit 300°C and converted CO2 with about 96% selectivity toward carbon monoxide in the reported runs. Adding indium steadied activity and pushed selectivity above 99% during testing. Aerogel spheres made about four times more CO than powders of the same makeup. Light-heated aerogels could replace fossil-fired reactors.
pmc-13337364:
Maciej Walkiewicz examines whether two mental resources protect medical students steadily over time in a 2026 multi-cohort study. Sense of coherence and emotional intelligence are both cast as buffers against training stress. Data came from the Medical University of Gdańsk, drawn from six cohorts of second-year students between 2014 and 2024.

The sample held 1,595 students, 64% of them female, with a mean age of 20.97 years at entry to the analysis. Sense of coherence tracked quality of life clearly only in the 2014 group, while emotional intelligence peaked in the 2024 cohort and linked to adaptation in several groups. Because the resources behave differently across cohorts, mentoring should build specific skills rather than one global shield, the author argues.
pmc-13337464:
Le Huang, Yi Wang, and Shi Huang examine why teens with allergic rhinitis withdraw socially in a 2026 survey study. Lasting nose symptoms disturb sleep, social life, and mood, and deep life distress may deepen isolation. The team recruited 425 teen patients from three top-tier hospitals in Sichuan Province between December 2025 and February 2026 and gave them five standard scales.

Existential distress correlated with social alienation at r = 0.479 in the survey data, a solid link. Two habits carried the effect in a chain: mental inflexibility and avoiding hard inner experiences. Their chained indirect path was small but firm in the model. The authors point to acceptance-based therapy that loosens avoidance as a practical direction for care.
pmc-13340664:
Repeat surgery without radiation for a returning skin sarcoma is reported by Ehsanollah Rahimi-Movaghar and colleagues in 2026. Their 41-year-old patient had dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans come back after an earlier wide removal that reportedly cleared the margins.

Mohs re-excision with 3-cm margins down to the fascia achieved microscopically clear edges, confirmed during surgery, and a flap closed the wound. No radiation or drug therapy followed. Four years of checks, including repeated MRI scans, showed no new growth or spread. The case suggests careful re-excision alone can control selected recurrences, sparing patients radiation side effects while a flap preserves appearance and function.
pmc-13341564:
Teen stress and alcohol leave lasting molecular fingerprints, in a 2026 mouse study by Dina Medina-Vera and colleagues. Young mice, normal or lacking the fractalkine receptor CX3CR1, faced restraint stress, alcohol at 2 g/kg for 14 days, or both during adolescence.

As adults, the animals were tested for anxiety-like behavior while blood markers and heart gene activity were profiled. Losing or blocking CX3CR1 raised anxiety measures and cut open-arm exploration, and a receptor-blocking drug in normal mice backed the genetic result. Heart tissue showed shifts in chemokine, hormone receptor, and blood pressure system genes, tying early adversity to later cardiac signatures.
pmc-13341664:
Access to specialist ataxia centers varies across Europe, in a 2026 survey study by Suzanne Booth and colleagues. Responses from 550 people in the United Kingdom, Italy, and Germany were harmonized to examine who reaches these centers and who stops going.

People with genetic diagnoses, especially Friedreich's ataxia, appeared more in Italian and German centers than British ones, and idiopathic cases were referred less in the UK. Fewer other illnesses, being employed, and shorter travel all favored attendance, while worsening mobility predicted dropping out. For rare, complex conditions, geography and life circumstances gatekeep expert care as much as medicine does.
pmc-13343464:
Charlene Harriswangler and co-authors test a tweak to a lead and bismuth chelator in 2026, swapping acid arms of the macropa scaffold for picolinamide pendants. Matched lead and bismuth isotopes power scan-and-treat medicine, so chelators must grip both metals tightly, and the team asked whether amide donors help or hurt.

Crystal structures and bonding analysis showed the metal lone pair behaves more actively in bismuth complexes, and that activity faded as amides entered. The bismuth complex also flexed between shapes very fast in solution, flipping on a microsecond timescale. Radiolabeling trials settled the question: amide versions performed worse, so the charged acid donors suit these borderline metals better.
pmc-13346264:
Guy Dabby and co-authors introduce a lab system, published in 2026, that stretches cow mammary cells in cycles much like the pulses felt during milking. Bovine mammary epithelial cells grew inside stretchable silicone chambers, and image tools tracked thousands of cells before and after each stretching routine.

Cells stayed alive, kept growing, and still formed fat globules under the pulses, which supports the setup as a way to study function under force. Under some routines cells became rounder yet stayed attached, and milking-like cycles kept shape and lipid output steady. On collagen with a special medium, pulses seemed to boost release of fat globules outside the cells.
pmc-13347364:
Md Arif Mahmud and colleagues add starch to light-cured resin networks that contain no water, in a materials study from 2026. Mixes paired starch with varied methacrylate and friendlier polymer bases, with and without coupling agents. A wide test set measured strength, bending, heat behaviour, bonding, and gel share across each blend.

The all-methacrylate mix with 40 percent starch reached the highest tensile strength, at 17.0 MPa in the reported tests. While the best bending value came at lower starch loading with weaker pull strength. Friendlier bases and coupling agents lowered strength overall, and stiffer networks formed where mixing was less even, showing that base chemistry governs whether starch helps or hurts.
pmc-13348064:
Matías Goddard and colleagues report draft genomes from Chile. Their announcement was published in 2026. It covers two strains of a likely new Bartonella species. Blood came from rodents and their fleas. The place was Laguna Verde. Bartonella-like colonies grew from the blood. Gene tests confirmed the colonies. The strains were then grown for sequencing. Chilean surveys had hinted at unknown species before. Live isolates were missing, though.

Similarity scores fell below both species cutoffs. The two scales capped at 95 percent and 70 percent. That result backs a new species claim. Rodents host many Bartonella kinds. Some kinds tie to human illness. Named isolates therefore sharpen regional risk maps.
pmc-13348164:
Divesh Nazar and colleagues wrap flat semiconductor sheets around cube scaffolds to make packable light emitters, in a study from 2026. Flat cadmium selenide sheets hold fine light physics yet stack poorly in device films. So sheets were grown on all six faces of cadmium sulfide cubes, then capped with a second shell to form quantum wells on each face.

Cube films packed tightly with better electric contact than loose sheets. While the capped cubes showed repelling exciton pairs that split faces into near-separate emitters in the reported light tests. That split curbed wasteful Auger loss, lengthened multi-exciton life, and gave broad light gain, a promising mix for solution-made lasers and screens.
pmc-13349764:
Yang Li and Kazuyuki Aihara chart energy valleys and noise-driven jumps in a frustrated oscillator network, in a modelling study from 2026. A Stuart-Landau network on a ring-shaped grid mixes local coupling with global frustration. A shortcut approximation plus path-following maths tracked steady states into the full model as frustration strength varied, with special handling for flat critical lines.

Lower starting energies tended to land on lower, stabler end states, while mid frustration opened many valleys holding one deep pit plus long troughs in the reported maps. Simulations then showed noise flipping the network between sync and drift and hopping among shared states, a picture for how restless systems settle and switch.
pmc-13349964:
Wenjin Lin and co-authors checked a standard ultrasound scoring system for children's ovarian-area lumps in a 2026 multicentre study. The O-RADS system was built for adults, and its accuracy in children was unproven.

Records covered 301 lumps from three centres to tune the approach and 95 from a fourth to test it, all confirmed by tissue results; 44 of 396 were malignant. The adult system performed strongly in children, and the team built a simpler four-feature framework, C-CAS, from the strongest predictors. A child-specific shortcut that keeps accuracy could help smaller hospitals triage these uncommon but worrying lumps faster.
pmc-13350064:
Miguel Vera-Vega and fellow authors charted genetic variety inside a single native Peruvian maize race in a 2026 study. Cabanita maize supports food security in southern Andean communities, yet diversity within one race had never been measured.

They sampled 48 collections from two provinces of Arequipa, using seven DNA markers plus measurements of total DNA content, and explored links to visible plant traits. Variety proved low overall, but cluster patterns still matched province of origin, and collections from Castilla were slightly richer. A few markers carried most of the signal. Knowing how much variety a heritage crop holds guides efforts to conserve it.
pmc-13350164:
Sertaç Ayçiçek and Berçem Ayçiçek compared mental distress and stress hormones in women with unexplained infertility in a 2026 case-control study at a Turkish clinic. Fifty patients and 52 fertile controls of similar age completed anxiety and depression questionnaires.

Blood cortisol and DHEAS were drawn once, in the morning, under standard conditions early in the cycle. Distress scores were tied to infertility status, while the single hormone readings did not mirror the emotional burden well. The authors argue that a one-off hormone snapshot cannot stand in for how a woman actually feels, and clinics should ask directly about distress rather than rely on blood markers.
pmc-13350264:
Xiao Deng and co-authors silenced the SOX18 gene in colorectal cancer cells in a 2026 laboratory study. SOX18 is overproduced in several cancers, and patient data linked high levels to poorer survival in bowel cancer.

Turning the gene down in two cancer cell lines slowed growth, movement, and invasion, raised cell death, and reduced the growth of new blood vessels in supporting cells. Two major signalling routes quietened as well, and switching one back on with a drug partly rescued the cells, while blocking the other confirmed its role. SOX18 looks like a driver worth targeting to curb spread and vessel growth.
pmc-13351164:
Martin H Lundqvist and co-authors compared stress hormone responses between men and women in a 2026 clamp study. It probed why men develop type 2 diabetes more often. Twenty-two men and 28 women took part. Some had diabetes. All had controlled low and high blood sugar tests.

During low sugar, men mounted bigger hormone responses. Their glucagon, cortisol, and growth hormone all rose more. But their heart rhythm adapted less well. Menopause changed growth hormone and rhythm measures somewhat. Sex hormones themselves correlated weakly. Body shape and insulin sensitivity were the strongest predictors of hormone responses. Defence systems against low sugar may be wired differently by sex.
pmc-13354464:
Muhammad Asif and co-authors report intensive care for Kala Pathar hair dye poisoning in a teen patient in 2026. The dye's paraphenylenediamine is cheap and easy to buy across the subcontinent, yet swallowing it poisons the whole body with no known antidote. A 16-year-old female developed swelling of the airway tissues plus uncommon heart and liver complications after ingestion.

Dark brown urine and airway swelling can flag the poisoning where lab tests are absent. Dose drives outcomes, and dangers span liver necrosis, muscle breakdown, blood cell rupture, sudden kidney failure, and heart inflammation or fatal rhythms. Supportive intensive care succeeded in her case. Public awareness and tighter product rules are urged.
pmc-13355264:
Shuai Tang and co-authors sorted bladder cancers in 2026 by genes tied to pyroptosis, a fiery form of cell death that shapes the tumor's immune setting. Bladder cancer outcomes vary widely, and cell death patterns may help predict them. Using large cancer datasets plus two outside cohorts, the team found tumor groups and built a risk score.

Two tumor subtypes emerged, with distinct survival and immune traits. A six-gene score split patients into high and low risk groups that held up across cohorts and after other factors were weighed. High scores linked to worse grade and stage and to distinct immune signals. The authors say the score may guide immune and drug choices, pending more tests.
pmc-13359464:
Zimeng Li and co-authors explore why obesity hits the sexes differently in a 2026 mouse study. They focused on selenoprotein F, a protein that helps cells keep their protein folding in order. Female mice lacking it were fed a high-fat diet and compared with normal mice and with males.

The females without the protein gained more weight and fat, with worse blood lipids and higher levels of leptin, the fullness hormone. Their brain weight-control center showed signs of cell stress, and heat-making pathways in brown fat ran low. Males were barely affected. The findings suggest this protein links brain control and fat burning in females.
pmc-13359764:
Grigorios A. Moschos and co-authors present a deep learning tool for protein mapping in a 2026 paper. Many key proteins sit in cell membranes or carry a short address tag that sends them out of the cell. The two features look alike in the protein's code, so older tools often confuse them. Their tool, PRED-TMSdeep, predicts both in a single pass.

Trained on carefully checked reference sets, the tool matches leading rivals at mapping membrane crossings. It does better at telling the three kinds of secretion tags apart and at finding the exact spot where the tag is cut off. A free web server puts the method within any lab's reach.
pmc-13361064:
Masahiro Komeno and co-authors show that a gold drug can curb cancer spread in a 2026 study. The target is heparanase-1, the only enzyme of its kind that cuts a sugar chain helping cancers invade tissue. Past drugs aimed at the enzyme's cutting action alone fell short, since the protein has other jobs. The team screened for drugs that stop the protein being made at all.

Auranofin, a gold drug long used for rheumatoid arthritis by mouth, proved a strong blocker of the gene's start switch. The search revealed the signal path that drives the gene, running through two named proteins. Treated cancer cells made far less of the enzyme and lost much of their power to invade. Reusing a known drug this way could speed a new anti-spread therapy.
pmc-13361664:
