Çalık Veli Koçak and co-authors tested water exercise for boys with autism in a 2026 trial. Autism affects social communication and brings repetitive behaviors, and motor skills often lag as well. Exercise is known to help both behavior and movement. The team enrolled 35 boys with mild autism, around eight years old, and split them by chance into two groups.

Seventeen boys took part in a 16-week adapted water exercise program, meeting twice a week for 50 minutes. Eighteen boys kept their usual care. The team measured autism-related behaviors, flexibility, and handgrip strength, all tied to daily functioning. Water exercise is gentle and fun, which may suit children who resist land sports. The trial tests whether it earns a place in therapy plans.
pmc-13361864:
Panpan Wang and co-authors fed zebrafish a cooking contaminant to test gut harm in a 2026 study. PhIP forms when protein-rich foods are heated hard, as in grilling, and it is a major heat-born contaminant in such foods. Its effects on the gut barrier and gut microbes were poorly defined. Adult zebrafish ate the compound for 90 days at three dose levels.

Exposure slowed growth and caused growing gut lesions. The mucus layer thinned, mucus-making cells fell, and the genes and proteins that seal gut cells together weakened. Blood signs of leaked gut germs and gut inflammation signals rose. Gut microbe balance also shifted, with Proteobacteria patterns tied to the upset. The study warns that a common cooking chemical can erode the gut's defenses.
pmc-13362364:
Matvey M Murashko and colleagues describe a 2026 lab study on how a cancer-linked gene fusion forms. They built a reporter in human lung cancer cells that glows red when the EML4-ALK fusion appears. The tool let them count fusion events cell by cell and test which DNA repair factors change the rate.

When they lowered the APEX1 gene, which makes the APE1 repair protein, fusion levels rose in both the reporter cells and the parent cells. That makes APE1 a brake on this harmful swap of gene parts. The glowing reporter gives other labs a fast, clear way to hunt for more factors that raise or lower fusion rates.
pmc-13362564:
Virginia Boldrini and a large team report a 2026 physics study on whether strong electric fields can shift the decay rate of beryllium-7 atoms. They built silicon carbide diodes, planted the atoms inside, and held a high reverse voltage for more than 100 days, long enough to time the decay with care. The setup tests the Stark effect, where an electric field distorts atoms.

Tests before and after planting showed the diodes kept a stable field and near-normal blocking behavior, even though the planting added some defects and raised leakage a bit. Control devices with stable beryllium showed decay itself caused no clear damage. The team concludes these diodes are fit for the planned decay measurements.
pmc-13363164:
Ting Pan and colleagues present a 2026 study on smuggling antibiotics inside cells, where some bacteria hide from drugs that cannot cross cell membranes. Their platform pairs a common carrier protein, albumin, with a tiny cell-penetrating protein that can slip out of the cell's sorting bubbles. They loaded the carrier with the antibiotic ceftriaxone and tested the system in lab infection models with Staphylococcus aureus.

The penetrating partner raised protein entry into cells more than five-fold, and the cargo spread through the cell body rather than staying trapped in waste bubbles. Bacterial counts confirmed the delivered drug killed germs hiding inside cells. The authors frame the design as a way to widen the drug options for stubborn inside-cell infections.
pmc-13363464:
Valer Donca and a large team report a 2026 study of vitamin D in 1,438 hospital patients aged 65 and older in central Romania. Each patient had a full geriatric workup: blood vitamin D, two thinking tests, mood scales, and ratings of daily self-care. The team sorted vitamin levels into lacking, low, and enough, then tested how each band lined up with brain and body function.

Over two fifths of the patients were frankly lacking in vitamin D. Lower levels tracked with worse thinking scores, heavier depressive symptoms, and more dependence in daily tasks, even after other health factors counted. The sharpest drop sat below the lacking threshold, while the low band behaved closer to the enough band. The authors urge attention to vitamin D in geriatric care.
pmc-13365864:
Rui Sun and co-workers read in 2026 the fast switch marks that male hormone flips in Sertoli cells, the nurse cells of sperm growth. The team feeds mouse cells the hormone for set spans and maps near thirteen thousand switch sites on cell proteins. Marks group into six waves by time.

Rich paths in the mark set run cell growth and grip work. Block tests show the switch net guards the blood testis wall seal. The map gives fresh leads on how male hormone steers sperm growth and where care for low sperm counts could aim.
pmc-13366364:
Juana Claus leads a team that tests in 2026 how two germ drug routes change germ mixes in youth with sore, drain ear ill. Youth took one week of mouth drug or ear drops by lot. The team reads germs in ear flow, nose, and stool at set points up to three months.

Ear drain clears in near all youth on both routes. Mouth drug cuts nose germs of one key type more than drops, but lifts two kin types. Gut germs and drug proof genes hold near still on both routes. Route choice can rest on such trade offs.
pmc-13367964:
MaKenna Browne and co-workers build in 2026 a tighter mouse mod of a harsh child soft flesh cancer driven by a fused gene pair. Past mods spark tumors with no switch, which blurs study. Their new mod needs two switch hits to wake the fused gene, in place and time of choice.

A drug hunt in human cells from the ill flags a drug that blocks gene read work. It kills ill cells by wear of the read gear's big part. The drug shrinks tumors in the new mouse mod and in human grafts. Past safe trials clear a path to patient tests.
pmc-13372664:
Xiaocui Lu and co-authors found a drug that breaks down a cancer helper in a 2026 study. The work looks at colon cancer with a gene fault that shows in about one in ten patients. Drugs for that fault often fail fast, since the cancer finds new paths to grow.

The team built a drug that tags a growth helper for the cell's trash system. A deep scan showed the drug glues the helper to the trash lead, so the helper is cut up and lost. In lab tests the move slowed tumor growth. The find opens a fresh line of attack for a hard cancer type, though patient tests are still to come.
pmc-13373864:
Iñaki Odriozola and co-authors mapped a soil fungi group round the world in a 2026 study. The fungi live with heath family plants and help turn soil carbon. Their world map was a blank next to that of other fungi groups.

The team pooled more than 39,000 soil samples and more than 13 million gene reads. Richness of types peaked at the far north and south. Soil mix beat weather and plant cover as a guide to where types thrive. Where soil carbon was high, the fungi took a large share of all fungi. The map helps land and climate work that counts on soil life.
pmc-13377864:
Yaniv Grosskopf and co-authors give a spare math tale for trauma stress in a 2026 paper. Just one to two in ten folk struck by trauma stay ill for long, while the rest heal at a spread of paces. Why that split falls was not clear in past frames.

Their tale has one driver that feeds its own growth, held by a clear-out pull. One trait, grit, sets who tips to the ill state. At mid grit, heal times spread wide, which fits true logs from many groups. Care must pass a bar to hold, the sums say. Spare tales can still guide who gets what care, and when.
pmc-13379764:
Krzysztof Kaczmarek and colleagues report a 2026 case where a heart device stopped working well and heart failure worsened as a result. The device, called cardiac contractility modulation, sends gentle signals that strengthen the heartbeat without using extra oxygen. It suits patients who cannot have another common device therapy.

Their patient, a 58-year-old man with a weak, enlarged heart, improved greatly after the device was fitted. Years later he declined, and checks showed the device was delivering its signals only sometimes. Surgery found worn insulation on all three leads. Replacing the leads restored the therapy, and his exercise ability and heart function improved again over long-term follow-up.
pmc-13379864:
Loukas Rentifis and co-authors report a 2026 study of bacteria growing on bile duct stents placed before major pancreas surgery. Such stents drain bile to reduce complications, but germs can colonise them and affect later care. Records covered 313 patients who had the surgery for tumours between 2010 and 2022.

Of 171 patients who had stents, 115 stents were tested for germs. Most tested positive, with gut-type bacteria most common and fungi found in over a third of samples. Some bacteria resisted many antibiotics. Longer waits between stent placement and surgery were linked with positive cultures. The findings matter for choosing preventive antibiotics around surgery.
pmc-13380664:
Ala Bala Babiker Abdalla and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review of a blood test used to diagnose acute heart failure in emergency departments. Breathlessness in the emergency room has many causes, and sorting them quickly is hard. The test measures a marker called NT-proBNP, which rises when the heart is stretched.

Following standard review guidance, the authors searched four databases for studies from 2021 to 2026 in adults with suspected heart failure. Eight studies were included, and their quality was assessed with a standard tool. A low marker level proved strong for ruling the condition out across the prospective studies. The review also examines which cut-off levels work best and how performance varies between patient groups.
pmc-13382764:
Shoushun Chen and co-authors review how solid-state NMR helps reveal the inner structure of metal-organic frameworks in a 2027 article. These porous crystals, built from metal nodes and organic links, now number in huge variety and serve many uses. Their range also makes it hard to link local structure to how a material behaves.

The review covers probes of metal centers and linkers, plus studies of guest molecules held inside the pores. New hardware and pulse methods that sharpen what the technique can show receive close attention. For labs designing frameworks for real use, the piece maps where NMR can guide choices and where limits still remain.
pmc-13386564:
Khalil Kargar Shooroki and colleagues report wrist masses that first revealed systemic amyloidosis in a 2026 case report. A 75-year-old man had swelling at both wrists with weak, numb hands and a history of repeated carpal tunnel syndrome. MRI showed the bilateral masses behind the returning symptoms.

Surgery removed the masses, and tissue testing confirmed amyloid deposits of the wild-type transthyretin kind. He stayed free of symptoms through four years of follow-up, the authors report. The case argues for biopsy and body-wide checks when wrist masses accompany repeating carpal tunnel problems.
pmc-13391664:
Marie Gudmundsson and colleagues build, in 2026, a grounded theory of how people using mental health services experience recovery through a nature-based programme. Nature-based interventions support recovery-oriented care, yet how users themselves live the recovery process inside them was little known.

Twenty participants took part in a newly developed programme at a farm-based rehabilitation centre, including horse-assisted therapy in groups. In-depth interviews, gathered by purposeful sampling, were analysed with constructivist grounded theory into an account the authors frame as an embodied journey. Mental health practitioners gain a user-voiced process model that can shape how farm and nature programmes are designed and paced.
pmc-13391964:
Hasan Alchalabi and colleagues pool, in 2026, evidence on shrinking the prostate's blood supply before shaving it from inside for men with very large glands. Large-volume benign prostate enlargement makes transurethral resection harder, with more bleeding, longer operations, and more complications.

The review pools the two paths. One path blocks gland blood flow first, then resects. The other resects at once. The pooled data cover time in theatre, blood loss, and harm rates. Urologists gain a joint estimate of a key trade. Does the extra step pay for itself in a smoother, safer cut? The doubt is greatest for the largest glands.
pmc-13392664:
Nuraini Nuraini and colleagues fermented cassava peel with an oyster mushroom fungus, then fed the product to broiler chickens at five rates up to a fifth of the diet. Raw cassava peel is a cheap farm residue but a poor feed, and fermentation was meant to upgrade it. The trial ran thirty-five days and tracked growth, carcass traits, gut shape and germs, blood fats, and meat quality.

Birds on fermented peel grew faster and heavier, most clearly at the highest rate, without eating more or wasting feed. Carcass share rose, the thymus immune organ grew, gut villi lengthened, harmful Escherichia coli fell while friendly lactic bacteria rose, and blood fats shifted in a healthier direction. Meat carried more of the prized omega fatty acids, though its cholesterol stayed put. The authors rate fermented peel as a working functional feed.
pmc-13393064:
Mohammed Mosharraf Hossain Khandaker and four colleagues describe a 60-year-old man who developed clots in the brain's venous drainage channels just after finishing treatment for pneumococcal meningitis. The infection itself had settled on two weeks of intravenous ceftriaxone, with blood tests back to normal and no weakness or focal signs. A lasting headache and neck stiffness refused to fit that tidy recovery.

Fresh brain imaging explained the mismatch: widespread cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, a rare but known complication most often tied to this meningitis germ. Blood-thinning treatment cleared the clots on later scans, although headaches hung on even after the channels reopened. The convention took effect in 2001 and joined a growing web of anti-terror law.
un-ga-res-a-69-64:
Trust between states, built in the open, is the theme of Resolution A/69/64, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. Its subject is trust-building steps in the field of standard arms: tanks, guns, and the like, short of mass-kill arms. Such steps, taken by free choice of the states involved, can lift the whole state of peace and safety in a region.

The text holds that swapping facts on these steps builds grasp and trust between states. It notes the two-way gain: calmer regions make arms cuts easier, and arms cuts calm regions in turn. Past votes from 2004 on are recalled as the base for the call.
un-ga-res-united-nations-general-assembl:
Hosted under the Resolution 52/164 label, the text here is the International Convention for the Suppression of Terrorist Bombings. The General Assembly adopted the treaty through that resolution. Its opening pages note the spread of attacks with bombs and other lethal devices. They also note the gaps in older treaties. Those gaps left such attacks hard to punish across borders.

The convention makes it a crime to set off an explosive or other lethal device in certain places. The places are a public place, a government site, public transport, or a key public system. The act must mean to kill, injure, or cause major loss. States must punish these acts at home. They must claim the right to try offenders. They must extradite or prosecute those found on their soil.

Resolution 69/64, adopted by the General Assembly at its sixty-ninth session in 2014, concerns information on confidence-building measures in the field of conventional arms. It welcomes the measures states have taken and the information they have supplied voluntarily. It asks the Secretary-General to keep the database of such measures up to date. He is to help states, on request, organize seminars and workshops. Those events share practical experience.
un-sc-res-1364:
Abkhazia, the breakaway region of Georgia, is the subject of United Nations Security Council Resolution 1364. The Council adopted it on 31 July 2001. Killings and hostage takings in the Gali district that spring and summer had frozen peace talks. The Abkhaz side had walked out of a planned meeting in protest.

The text extends the United Nations Observer Mission in Georgia, called UNOMIG, until 31 January 2002. It presses both sides, above all the Abkhaz side, to return to talks on core issues. It demands the release of hostages and justice for those behind the attacks. Refugees, the Council repeats, keep the right to go home in safety and dignity.
un-sc-res-1464:
Côte d'Ivoire's political forces had signed a peace deal in France in January 2003. On 4 February 2003 the Security Council endorsed the Linas-Marcoussis Agreement. West African states had already decided to send a peacekeeping force. The Council backed that effort and the African Union's work for a settlement. It restated Côte d'Ivoire's sovereignty and unity. Good relations between neighbors framed the text.

The deal provided for a government of national reconciliation. The Council called on all Ivorian forces to build it without delay. A balanced and stable government was the goal. The agreement also set up a monitoring committee. Its members had to watch compliance closely. All parties were urged to cooperate with that watch.
un-sc-res-1564:
Darfur's crisis brought a warning and an inquiry on 18 September 2004. The Secretary-General's report of 30 August found Sudan had not met all its duties under resolution 1556 (2004). Aid access had improved, but security had not. The African Union's president had appealed for support to grow the Union's mission in Darfur. Four Council members abstained.

The Council declared its grave concern at Khartoum's failure to meet its obligations. It backed the African Union's plan to enlarge its Darfur mission and urged states to give gear, money, and transport. Sudan and the rebels were called to work fully with the Union's force and to stop all violence. The Council asked the Secretary-General to set up an international commission of inquiry at once. It would study reports of grave breaches in Darfur, decide whether genocide had occurred, and name those responsible.
un-sc-res-1664:
Lebanon asked for a court to try the killers of its former prime minister. Rafiq Hariri died in a bombing in February 2005. An international team was investigating the attack. On 29 March 2006 the Security Council welcomed the Secretary-General's report on the probe. It asked him to negotiate a deal with Lebanon's government. The deal would create a tribunal of an international character. It would rest on the highest standards of criminal justice.

Setting the court's legal base would not fix its start date. Its parts could be phased in over time. Timing would follow the investigation's progress. The Secretary-General had to update the Council as talks advanced. The tribunal that resulted sat in the Netherlands. It tried suspects in the Hariri case in their absence.
un-sc-res-1764: Under the number 1764, a formal decision of the fifteen-member Security Council survives through a Wikisource transcription of the record. The body's texts are built to be quoted: each operative paragraph stands alone and numbered. The entry preserves the quotable whole, from the opening grounds the members stated to the final instruction they issued.
un-sc-res-1864:
Nepal's mission was kept on with a drawn-down shape on 23 January 2009. The constituent assembly elections of 10 April 2008 had been held with success. The assembly's first session had declared Nepal a federal democratic republic. A democratically elected government now sat in Kathmandu. A special committee had formed to oversee the Maoist army's integration and rehabilitation. The government asked for the mission to stay.

The Council extended UNMIN's mandate in line with the government's request and the Secretary-General's advice. A phased, gradual drawdown of the mission's staff was endorsed as the way ahead. The current arms monitoring arrangements would stay while the parties finished the integration question. All parties were called to use the mission's expertise as the peace process closed out. The Secretary-General had to keep the Council informed. Kathmandu was pressed to complete the steps needed for the mission's orderly end.
un-sc-res-264:
South Africa's hold on Namibia faced a direct legal challenge in 1969. The General Assembly had ended South Africa's mandate over the territory in 1966. It had taken direct responsibility for Namibia until independence. On 20 March 1969 the Security Council recognized that act as valid. France and Britain abstained in the vote. The rest of the Council backed the Assembly's move.

South Africa's continued presence, the Council said, is illegal. It runs against the Charter and past United Nations decisions. It also harms the people of the territory. South Africa had to withdraw its administration at once. Pretoria refused, and the occupation lasted two more decades.
un-sc-res-364: Resolution 364 of the Security Council reaches readers here as an official record text, catalogued under the year 1966. Behind each numbered text lies a meeting, a draft, and a vote, even when the final wording runs to a few lines. Read in sequence with its neighbours, it helps trace how Council practice grew across the postwar decades.
un-sc-res-464: Saint Vincent and the Grenadines was recommended for United Nations membership by the Security Council on 19 February 1980. The Council had weighed the young Caribbean state's bid to join. It told the General Assembly that Saint Vincent and the Grenadines should be admitted. The one-paragraph text is the standard admission step, sending the application on to the Assembly for the final vote.
un-sc-res-564:
Street fighting in Lebanon in 1985 fell heavily on civilians. Palestinian refugee camps suffered some of the worst attacks. On 31 May 1985 the Security Council voiced its deepest concern. It counted a heavy cost in lives and in destroyed property. The Council's president had already spoken on the rising violence a week earlier. Members now put their alarm into a resolution.

All concerned had to end violence against civilians at once. That duty applied above all in and around the refugee camps. The Council restated Lebanon's sovereignty and territorial integrity. It called for steps to ease suffering and to let aid groups work. The United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees needed room to operate.
un-sc-res-64: Four days after it ordered the release of Indonesia's leaders, the Council found them still held. On 28 December 1948 it told the Dutch government to free the president of the Republic of Indonesia at once. All other political prisoners had to go free as well. The Dutch also had to report back within a day. The whole text is one sentence. It backed up the demand made in resolution 63 of 24 December.
un-sc-res-united-nations-security-counci:
Violence in Georgia's Abkhazia conflict zone mars Resolution 1364, adopted on 31 July 2001. Killings and hostage-taking in the Gali district and elsewhere in April, May, and July had halted talks, and the Abkhaz side had pulled out of the planned Coordinating Council session. Two UNOMIG observers had been seized in the Kodori Valley. Both sides had held military drills that broke the 1994 Moscow ceasefire deal.

The Council extends the UN Observer Mission in Georgia, UNOMIG, until 31 January 2002. It regrets that the draft paper on sharing powers between Tbilisi and Sukhumi has not yet gone to the sides and stresses its early delivery as a spur to talks. It calls on the parties, above all the Abkhaz side, to get past the deadlock and settle the status of returnees to Gali as a first step. It demands the hostages be freed and those to blame face justice.

Côte d'Ivoire split in two after a rebellion in September 2002. Peace talks in France produced the Linas-Marcoussis Agreement on 24 January 2003. Resolution 1464, adopted unanimously on 4 February 2003, threw the Council's weight behind that deal. Ivorian leaders were told to build a balanced reconciliation government.

Members condemned rights abuses committed since the uprising began. Perpetrators had to face justice. Acting under Chapter VII, the Council backed regional troops already on the ground. ECOWAS soldiers and supporting French forces could protect their own people. They could also shield civilians facing immediate violence. The authority lasted six months. A special UN representative for the country was requested as well.

Darfur's crisis deepens in Resolution 1564, adopted on 18 September 2004. Sudan's government had promised in Resolution 1556 and a July joint statement to protect civilians and disarm the Janjaweed militias. The Secretary-General reported that those promises were not fully kept. The Council deplored fresh ceasefire breaches, including helicopter attacks and militia raids on villages in late August.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council backs a much larger African Union monitoring mission in Darfur and urges states to supply it with gear, money, and support. It asks the Secretary-General to set up an international commission of inquiry at once to probe abuses in Darfur, judge whether acts of genocide had occurred, and name those to blame. It warns that if Sudan fails to comply, the Council will weigh measures under Article 41, including steps aimed at the oil sector.

Fighting between France and Tunisia produced Resolution 164, adopted on 22 July 1961 by ten votes to none. French forces still held the naval base at Bizerte after Tunisian independence, and a Tunisian move to blockade it had triggered open clashes. The Council said it was acting while debate on the question continued, given the gravity of the situation.

Its orders were interim but firm: a cease-fire at once, with all armed forces back at the spots they held before the clash. The Council then decided to keep debating the item rather than close the file. The brief text shows the Council working as an emergency brake, stopping the shooting first and leaving the harder argument over the base's future for later sessions.

Resolution 1664, adopted on 29 March 2006, moves Lebanon closer to a court for the bombing that killed former Prime Minister Rafiq Hariri. Lebanon's government had asked for a court with an international character to try those blamed for the February 2005 attack. UN and Lebanese officials had reached a shared understanding on the court's main features.

The Council asked the Secretary-General to negotiate an agreement with Lebanon to create that tribunal, built to top world standards of criminal justice. It noted that setting the legal basis would not fix the timing, which depended on the investigation's progress. Progress reports were requested as talks moved forward, and the process led to the Special Tribunal for Lebanon.

A new High Representative for Bosnia and Herzegovina is welcomed on 29 June 2007. The Peace Implementation Council's Steering Board had designated Miroslav Lajčák on 19 June 2007, in succession to Christian Schwarz-Schilling. The designation is agreed to, and tribute is paid to the outgoing holder's work in the post.

The importance of the High Representative's role in driving the peace agreement's implementation is restated. That role includes guiding and coordinating the civilian organizations and agencies helping the parties carry out the agreement. Support for Bosnia and Herzegovina's path toward closer ties with European institutions is also reaffirmed, and the situation stays under review.

Nepal's peace process after a long civil war is the subject of Resolution 1864, adopted on 23 January 2009. The government and the Communist Party of Nepal (Maoist) had signed a Comprehensive Peace Agreement in November 2006. Votes for a Constituent Assembly followed in April 2008, and that body chose to make Nepal a federal democratic republic. The UN Mission in Nepal, UNMIN, watched over arms and fighters.

Nepal asked for a smaller UNMIN for six more months, and the Council renews the mandate until 23 July 2009. It backs a slow, phased drawdown of UNMIN staff, including arms monitors. It calls on all parties to finish the work on managing arms and armed personnel. It also calls on them to free minors held in cantonment sites. It calls for terms that let the mission close and leave by the end of the period.

AMISOM is kept in Somalia and ordered to grow in Resolution 1964, adopted on 22 December 2010. Al Shabaab's attacks on the Transitional Federal Government, AMISOM, and civilians continued. Humanitarian funding was falling. The African Union's July summit and October Peace and Security Council meeting pressed for a stronger mission. Uganda and Burundi supplied the troops.

Acting under Chapter VII, the Council authorizes African Union member states to maintain AMISOM until 30 September 2011 with its mandate. It asks the AU to raise its strength from 8,000 to 12,000. The Secretary-General must keep providing the UN logistical support package for up to 12,000 troops, excluding fund transfers. Future decisions will track benchmarks: progress on transitional tasks and constitution-making, a national security plan and Somali forces, reconciliation outreach, and AMISOM-backed consolidation of security. The Council also recalls its intent to consider a UN peacekeeping operation once conditions allow.

South Africa's grip on Namibia faced a blunt legal verdict in 1969. The land had been run by Pretoria since the First World War. The Assembly had cut that mandate in 1966 and claimed the land for the UN. Pretoria refused to leave. Resolution 264 passed on 20 March 1969 by thirteen votes to none. France and Britain held back.

The Council backed the Assembly's move in full. South Africa's stay was ruled against the law. Its rule had to be pulled out at once. Plans to split the land into tribal zones were banned. A new South African law for the land was ruled out of bounds. If Pretoria kept defying the UN, the Council warned, it would meet fast to weigh firm steps.

Five months after the Cyprus crisis of the summer, the island's peacekeeping force came up for a new term. A report from the Secretary-General, dated 6 December 1974, said the force was still needed. Its work maintained the cease-fire and helped the search for a peaceful settlement. Cyprus agreed it should remain beyond 15 December. Resolution 364 was adopted on 13 December 1974.

The Council reaffirmed its older Cyprus resolutions. It also reaffirmed the run of crisis texts passed in July and August 1974. The parties were urged to show the utmost restraint and to speed up their joint efforts. The force's stay was extended to 15 June 1975. Progress toward a final solution might then allow a withdrawal or a reduction. All parties were again asked to cooperate fully with the force.

Resolution 464, adopted unanimously on 19 February 1980, recommends Saint Vincent and the Grenadines for United Nations membership. The Council had examined the Caribbean island chain's application. Saint Vincent and the Grenadines had become independent from Britain the previous October, one of the last British Caribbean territories to take that step.

The single operative sentence asks the General Assembly to admit the new state. Small island countries placed real value on that seat: a General Assembly vote counts the same for them as for a superpower. The resolution's brevity is typical of admissions, where agreement is reached in advance and the Council's recommendation simply unlocks the Assembly's vote.

Lebanon was deep in civil war when the Council adopted Resolution 564 unanimously on 31 May 1985. Fighting had spread into civilian neighborhoods and Palestinian refugee camps, causing heavy deaths and destruction. The members said they were alarmed at how the violence kept growing and spreading.

The text calls on everyone involved to stop attacks on civilians, above all in and around the camps, and it repeats the Council's support for Lebanon's sovereignty and unity. It also asks all parties to ease suffering by letting UN aid agencies and the Red Cross reach victims safely, and it asks the Secretary-General to follow up and report.

The Dutch had four days to free Indonesia's leaders, and this text is the chase-up. On 28 December 1948, the Council adopted Resolution 64. Eight members voted yes and none voted no. Belgium, France, and Britain held back. Resolution 63, passed on Christmas Eve, had ordered the release. The Council now records that no release has come.

The Netherlands must set the prisoners free at once, the text says. It must report to the Council within twenty-four hours of the vote. Deadline pressure this sharp was rare for the young Council. The order showed how far Dutch standing had fallen after the December offensive. Within a year, The Hague handed sovereignty to Indonesia.
van-helmonts-workes-1664: Van Helmont's Workes of 1664 gathered the Flemish physician's writings. The Helmont corpus. Early modern medicine. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe for everyone. The archive keeps the paper open to all who seek it.
verne-journey-centre-of-the-earth-1864:
Jules Verne wrote A Journey to the Centre of the Earth in 1864. F. A. Malleson gave the tale its English dress used here. A German sage finds an old note that tells of a path down. The note points to a peak in Iceland with a shaft at its heart.

The sage, his kin, and a stout guide climb down through old lava tubes. They find a vast cave sea, lit by strange light, with live beasts of the old world. Storms, thirst, and a blocked path tax their strength to the end. The tale is the great subterranean trip of the age.
vogt-lectures-on-man-1864:
Carl Vogt, a Swiss-German man of science, gave these bold talks on man in Geneva, and James Hunt put them in English in 1864. Vogt was a famed voice for the view that all life is stuff and force alone. The talks deal with man's place in the world of beasts.

He makes the full case for man's ape kin, from skulls, brains, and the races of men. His scheme came before Darwin's own book on man's descent, and it reached a wide public. The book is the most strong famed plea of its kind from those years.
wallace-origin-human-races-1864:
Alfred Russel Wallace read this paper on the races of man to a London learned group in 1864. It was the first use of the new law of natural selection on the theme of man. Wallace had found that law on his own, far from Darwin's home and desk.

He holds that man's body was shaped by selection in a far past age. Once the mind grew strong, he says, selection bore on the mind more than on the frame. The step set him on the path that led, in time, to his split with Darwin on man.
walpole-castle-of-otranto-1764:
Horace Walpole wrote The Castle of Otranto in 1764. He first said it was a tale turned from old Italian print. The tale is set in a grim pile in the south of Italy. Prince Manfred holds the pile by a claim of thin right.

A vast helm falls from the sky and crushes Manfred's son on his wed day. Portraits sigh, statues bleed, and a hid curse drives all the fates. Walpole's brief tale set off the whole Gothic line in prose. Its stock of ghosts, tyrants, and hid sins still feeds tales now.
warren-commission-report-1964:
President Lyndon Johnson set up the Warren Commission days after President John Kennedy was shot in Dallas in November 1963. Chief Justice Earl Warren led the inquiry, which worked for ten months with a large staff. Its report, issued in September 1964, runs to 888 pages with volumes of evidence behind it.

The commission concluded that Lee Harvey Oswald fired the shots that killed Kennedy, and that he acted alone. It also found that Jack Ruby acted alone when he killed Oswald on live television. Doubts about those findings began at once and have never faded. The report remains the official account of the assassination, and the most argued-over government inquiry in American history.
whittier-in-war-time-1864:
John Greenleaf Whittier published In War Time, and Other Poems in 1864, while the Civil War still raged. Whittier, a Massachusetts Quaker, had spent thirty years as abolitionism's bard, editing antislavery papers and risking mobs. This volume is his wartime voice at full power.

The poems cheer Union soldiers, mourn the dead, and demand emancipation as the war's true purpose. Barbara Frietchie, his most famous ballad, tells of an old Maryland woman waving the Union flag at Stonewall Jackson's troops. Other pieces honor nurses, chaplains, and the enslaved people walking to freedom. Whittier's plain Quaker verse spoke to farmhouses and camps alike. The collection stands as the home front's own record of the war years.
